 Moment of Silent Reflection 

Land Acknowledgement 
The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is 
located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can.

 78th STUDENT SENATE 
 Legislation Cover Sheet 

 Senate PCA #: 004 

 Primary Sponsor(s): Perantoni, Gurtis 
 Co-sponsor(s): Bigenho, Le, Tizon, Macalintal, Kelbert 

Short Title: An Amendment to the Student Body Constitution to Create a Formal Vehicle for 
Entering into Agreements and Memorandums. 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This legislation would empower the Student Body President to formally negotiate and sign on to 
agreements and memorandums, with the advice and consent of 2/3rds of the Student Senate. The 
Amendment covers Article III, Section 3 of the Constitution, and also governs the ability for the Student 
Body President to leave agreements and memorandums. 
 
Background Information: 
This amendment comes in the context of increasing volumes of Memorandums of Understanding and 
previous conflict between entering into contracts with outside lobbying forces. The Constitution and 
Student Body Statute currently lacks any formal mechanism for entering into MOU’s, which places 
potential concern on strife between the Executive and Legislative branch in terms of what the Student 
Government will agree to enter unto. With the recent need to renegotiate the Memorandum of 
Understanding as it comes to the Activities and Services Fee distribution, having a mechanism in place 
allows consultation across the Government. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Legislative outreach covered the Student Government Advising Office (specifically, advisor Andy 
Johnson), the Student Body President, Student Attorney General, Senate leadership (President, 
President Pro-Tempore), Senate Judiciary Chair and Vice-Chair, Senate Internal Affairs Chair, Senate 
Finance Chair and Vice-Chair, and the Executive Branch Cabinet Director. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This Amendment would create a formal mechanism to enter into and exit agreements or Memorandums 
of Understanding, allowing a legal process that avoids strife and major disagreements across the 
Student Government. This will make sure that agreements are entered into legally, and will provide 
guidance for future agreements to properly gain consensus to be carried out.

Short Title: Campaign Contribution Submission Clarification 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This bill clarifies the due date of the Campaign Contribution Statement, as per the request of 
the Supervisor of Elections, to be one week before the first election day. This bill, if 
Amendment #1 is adopted, will also increase the non-election period campaign expense limit 
at the Supervisor of Elections request, and will clarify Schedule violations that were previously 
unclear. 
 
Background Information: 
This is an issue that was not resolved by the prior Bill #78-033 and was identified by the Supervisor of 
Elections. If the current language were to remain, the campaign contribution statement would be due on 
the first Monday of an Election period, which would be 5 weeks before the election. This is an 
unrealistic timeline since most parties and candidates wouldn’t have all of their contributions by this 
point. 
 
As the Fall semester began, the Supervisor of Elections realized that under the current conditions of 
Chapter 709, it would need to be specified what campaign expenses were; for the Office of Elections, 
that would mean either auditing every single purchase from a party and deliberating on whether it would 
count as a campaign expense once the Final Expense Statement was submitted, or simply considering 
every expense from a party or candidate’s account to be a campaign expense. If the latter option were 
chosen, the current non-election period expense limit of $2,000 would no longer be sufficient to allow 
parties to effectively function outside of the election period. 
 
Finally, currently Chapter 710 is unclear on whether violations of Chapter 709 constitute a Schedule 
One or Schedule Three violation. There is currently only one specified Schedule One violation in 
Chapter 709, so Chapter 710 needs to be updated to ensure that these violations are clear and easy to 
interpret for parties and independent candidates. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
This language was drafted alongside the Supervisor of Elections to best fit the needs of both the 
Elections Office and candidates when it pertains to the submission deadline for campaign contributions. 

 Page 17 of 21
The new non-election period expense limit was estimated by both the sponsor and the Supervisor of 
Elections, before being presented to SGA party chairs to be reviewed after the situation was explained. 
Upon verification from both parties that the new expense limit was sufficient, Amendment #1 was 
drafted so that this could be clarified as quickly as possible. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation would change the submission deadline for the campaign contribution statement to be 
one week prior to the first election day, rather than the first Monday of the election period 5 weeks 
before the election. This gives parties more time to collect their campaign contributions and finalize 
their statement, and gives the Elections Office more clarification. 
 
If Amendment #1 is adopted, this bill will also include an increase to the non-election period expense 
limit, from $2,000 to $6,000 for each school year. This bill will also clarify that only specific violations of 
709 that are explicitly stated to constitute a Schedule One violation will be Schedule One violations, and 
all other violations of Chapter 709 that do not have a specific Schedule violation listed will be 
considered Schedule Three violations.

Short Title: An Amendment to the Student Body Constitution to Create a Formal Vehicle for 
Entering into Agreements and Memorandums. 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This legislation would empower the Student Body President to formally negotiate and sign on to 
agreements and memorandums, with the advice and consent of 2/3rds of the Student Senate. The 
Amendment covers Article III, Section 3 of the Constitution, and also governs the ability for the Student 
Body President to leave agreements and memorandums. 
 
Background Information: 
This amendment comes in the context of increasing volumes of Memorandums of Understanding and 
previous conflict between entering into contracts with outside lobbying forces. The Constitution and 
Student Body Statute currently lacks any formal mechanism for entering into MOU’s, which places 
potential concern on strife between the Executive and Legislative branch in terms of what the Student 
Government will agree to enter unto. With the recent need to renegotiate the Memorandum of 
Understanding as it comes to the Activities and Services Fee distribution, having a mechanism in place 
allows consultation across the Government. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Legislative outreach covered the Student Government Advising Office (specifically, advisor Andy 
Johnson), the Student Body President, Student Attorney General, Senate leadership (President, 
President Pro-Tempore), Senate Judiciary Chair and Vice-Chair, Senate Internal Affairs Chair, Senate 
Finance Chair and Vice-Chair, and the Executive Branch Cabinet Director. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This Amendment would create a formal mechanism to enter into and exit agreements or Memorandums 
of Understanding, allowing a legal process that avoids strife and major disagreements across the 
Student Government. This will make sure that agreements are entered into legally, and will provide 
guidance for future agreements to properly gain consensus to be carried out.

that would mean either auditing every single purchase from a party and deliberating on whether it would 
count as a campaign expense once the Final Expense Statement was submitted, or simply considering 
every expense from a party or candidate’s account to be a campaign expense. If the latter option were 
chosen, the current non-election period expense limit of $2,000 would no longer be sufficient to allow 
parties to effectively function outside of the election period. 
 
Finally, currently Chapter 710 is unclear on whether violations of Chapter 709 constitute a Schedule 
One or Schedule Three violation. There is currently only one specified Schedule One violation in 
Chapter 709, so Chapter 710 needs to be updated to ensure that these violations are clear and easy to 
interpret for parties and independent candidates. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
This language was drafted alongside the Supervisor of Elections to best fit the needs of both the 
Elections Office and candidates when it pertains to the submission deadline for campaign contributions. 

 Page 11 of 15
The new non-election period expense limit was estimated by both the sponsor and the Supervisor of 
Elections, before being presented to SGA party chairs to be reviewed after the situation was explained. 
Upon verification from both parties that the new expense limit was sufficient, Amendment #1 was 
drafted so that this could be clarified as quickly as possible. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation would change the submission deadline for the campaign contribution statement to be 
one week prior to the first election day, rather than the first Monday of the election period 5 weeks 
before the election. This gives parties more time to collect their campaign contributions and finalize 
their statement, and gives the Elections Office more clarification. 
 
If Amendment #1 is adopted, this bill will also include an increase to the non-election period expense 
limit, from $2,000 to $6,000 for each school year. This bill will also clarify that only specific violations of 
709 that are explicitly stated to constitute a Schedule One violation will be Schedule One violations, and 
all other violations of Chapter 709 that do not have a specific Schedule violation listed will be 
considered Schedule Three violations.

The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is

Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with

work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to

 Legislation Cover Sheet 

 Senate Bill #: 041 

 Primary Sponsor(s): Gurtis

Short Title: Bureau Clean Up Act 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This bill will remove any remaining mentions of bureaus from Student Statute, and insert 
Institutes into areas where other Executive Entities are being referenced, to ensure that 
Statute is reflective of all entities under the Executive Branch. 
 
Background Information: 
This legislation originated from Senate leadership, who had written a similar bill in the past that never 
got enrolled. Bureaus no longer exist within SGA, and have been all but removed from virtually every 
other area of Municode. In addition, given that Institutes are considered to be a part of the Executive 
Branch, it was decided to include them in areas where other Executive entities such as Agencies and 
Affiliated Projects were being discussed. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
This legislation was reviewed by Senate leadership, and was written with guidance from Internal Affairs 
Committee leadership to ensure correct information was being put into place. In addition, the 
recommendation for this legislation came from the Student Senate Advisor in SG&A. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation would remove final mentions to Bureaus within Student Statute, and would ensure that 
Institutes are being included in the relevant areas of Student Statute where other Executive entities are 
being included.

Short Title: An Amendment to the Student Body Constitution to Create a Formal Vehicle for 
Entering into Agreements and Memorandums. 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This legislation would empower the Student Body President to formally negotiate and sign on to 
agreements and memorandums, with the advice and consent of 2/3rds of the Student Senate. The 
Amendment covers Article III, Section 3 of the Constitution, and also governs the ability for the Student 
Body President to leave agreements and memorandums. 
 
Background Information: 
This amendment comes in the context of increasing volumes of Memorandums of Understanding and 
previous conflict between entering into contracts with outside lobbying forces. The Constitution and 
Student Body Statute currently lacks any formal mechanism for entering into MOU’s, which places 
potential concern on strife between the Executive and Legislative branch in terms of what the Student 
Government will agree to enter unto. With the recent need to renegotiate the Memorandum of 
Understanding as it comes to the Activities and Services Fee distribution, having a mechanism in place 
allows consultation across the Government. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Legislative outreach covered the Student Government Advising Office (specifically, advisor Andy 
Johnson), the Student Body President, Student Attorney General, Senate leadership (President, 
President Pro-Tempore), Senate Judiciary Chair and Vice-Chair, Senate Internal Affairs Chair, Senate 
Finance Chair and Vice-Chair, and the Executive Branch Cabinet Director. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This Amendment would create a formal mechanism to enter into and exit agreements or Memorandums 
of Understanding, allowing a legal process that avoids strife and major disagreements across the 
Student Government. This will make sure that agreements are entered into legally, and will provide 
guidance for future agreements to properly gain consensus to be carried out.

32 Section 2. Statement of Intent. 
33 The following Statement of Intent shall be included on the ballot as required by §711.2, Student Body 
34 Statutes: 

35 The Student Government Association occasionally enters into memoranda of understanding and 
36 similar agreements with other entities of Florida State University. This amendment would establish a 
37 formal process for such agreements. Under this process, an agreement would require approval by the

INTERNAL AFFAIRS COMMITTEE 
 September 14, 2026 at 6:30 PM 
 Location: fla.st/sga-meet-ia 
 MEETING MINUTES 

 Call to Order 
 Chair Bigenho called the meeting to order at 6:31 PM. 

Land Acknowledgement 
The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is 
located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can. 
 
 Chair Bigenho acknowledged the Land Acknowledgment. 

 Roll Call and Verification of Quorum 
 Vice Chair Gaynor administered roll call and verified quorum. 
 
 Present: Bigenho, Aihe, Britto, Macedo, Frazee, Gaynor, Hamlin, Le, Rivas, White, 
 Holliday, Behar, Kaplan, Gentile

 ■ Maria Fernandez, Director of the Hispanic Latine Student Union, spoke highly

 • Vice Chair Gaynor welcomes the committee back to Internal Affairs, expressing 
 confidence in the capabilities of senators to fulfill their responsibilities. • Chair Bigenho confirms the sentiment expressed by Vice Chair Gaynor: Internal 
 Affairs is the last Student Senate committee to have their first fall semester

Old Business 

New Business 

• Destinee Britto - D&I Institute, Director (Assigned to Internal Affairs, 
 09.09.26) 
 
 ■ Candidate Britto gives an opening statement imploring senators to confirm

 • Candidate Britto details her experience with the Diversity and

 • Senator Aihe motions to move into roundtable discussion.

 confidence that, based on her work ethic within Student Senate, she 
 will be the exact type of leader the D&I Institute needs. • Senator Rivas speaks in pro of Candidate Britto, expressing high 
 praise for her character and leadership proficiency. 
 • Senator Aihe speaks in pro of Candidate Britto, describing her as an 
 outstanding leader and one capable of serving as D&I Institute 
 Director. 
 • Senator Le speaks in pro of Candidate Britto, expressing character

 • Senator Macedo motions to table Candidate Wilson

• Jade Jacotin - Black Student Union, Assistant Director (Assigned to Internal

 ■ Candidate Jacotin gives an opening statement imploring senators to

 • Candidate Jacotin introduces herself as the Assistant Director elect 
 of the Black Student Union, and as a 4th-year public health scholar

 Candidate Jacotin platforms her experience as a co-founder of a

• Candidate Jacotin provides more context on the Jacotin Foundation,

• Senator Aihe motions to move into roundtable discussion. 
• Senator Le seconds the motion to move into roundtable discussion. 
• Senator Rivas objects to the motion to move into roundtable 
 discussion. 
• Senator Aihe does not withdraw the motion to move into roundtable 
 discussion. 
• Vice Chair Gaynor administers vote regarding the motion to move 
 into roundtable discussion. 
• The motion to move into roundtable discussion passes on a 10-1-0 
 vote. 
• Chair Bigenho announces that the committee has moved into 
 roundtable discussion. 
• Senator Aihe speaks in pro of the candidate, offering a personal

• Senator Rivas questions Candidate Jacotin on why issues with the

• Advisor Nelson interjects, Candidate Jacotin expresses a desire to

 advisors. Commends senators for questioning her, and for following

• Vice Chair Gaynor questions Candidate Jacotin regarding her

• Vice Chair Gaynor raises a point of inquiry regarding whether his

• Chair Bigenho rules Vice Chair Gaynor's question as germane, as it

• Candidate Jacotin restates that she does not see the issue as

• Vice Chair Gaynor speaks in pro of Candidate Jacotin 
• Senator Kaplan motions to call the question. • Senator Le seconds the motion to call the question.

• Reta Pineda - Mental Health Council, Executive Director (Assigned to 
 Internal Affairs, 09.09.2026) 
 
 ■ Candidate Pineda gives an opening statement imploring senators to confirm

 • Candidate Pineda introduces herself as a senior majoring in nursing

 commitment to mental health advocacy, which began when she

 Here, she gained hands-on experience educating the community on,

 • Senator Aihe questions Candidate Fechter on specific initiative

 • Vice Chair Gaynor motions to move into roundtable discussion.

 public speaking efforts.

 previously began the legislative process to update language. 
 • Senator Le speaks in pro of the bill. 
 • Senator Le motions to call the question.

 for their time and praise. 

 The question is called.

 The bill passes in a 11-0-3 vote. 
• Constitutional Amendment #78-004 
 ■ Chair Bigenho reminds senators that constitutional amendments are very 
 serious, imploring the committee to take the legislation seriously despite the 
 late time. 

 • Sponsor Gurtis gives an opening statement regarding a proposed 
 constitutional amendment that would affirm the Student Body 
 President's power to form agreements on behalf of Student 
 Government, pending the approval of the Student Senate and 
 signature from the Vice President of Student Affairs. She cites the 
 amendment exposition as being related to the Flying High Circus 
 summer senate memorandum agreement, which allocated $70,000 
 from the creative and development fund for an HVAC unit for the 
 Flying High Circus, under the premise that remaining funds would 
 return to the Senate. The agreement was not expressly stated as a 
 power belonging to the Student Body President, which is what the 
 amendment hopes to clarify.

 • Chair Bigenho opens a period of general questioning. 
 • Vice Chair Gaynor asks Sponsor Gurtis for clarification regarding 
 steps in the newly proposed agreement process.

 the constitutional amendment is correct.

 her to elaborate on what the Presidential power looks like in the 
 absence of the amendment.

 • Senator Aihe seconds the motion to move into roundtable 
 discussion.

 stating that it addresses a major gap within the Student Body 
 Constitution with the proper balance of governmental powers.

 • Senator Le seconds the motion to call the question. 
 • Sponsor Gurtis gives a closing statement thanking the committee for 
 their time and reiterating the amendment's purpose. 

 The question is called.

 The constitutional amendment passes in a 12-0-2 vote. 

Closing Announcements 
 
 • Vice Chair Gaynor expresses gratitude to committee members in the 
 midst of a difficult meeting. 
 • Vice Chair Gaynor extends particular praise to Chair Bigenho. • Chair Bigenho expresses pride for the Internal Affairs Committee, 
 echoing sentiments presented by Vice Chair Gaynor. 
 • Chair Bigenho announces he will drop a poll in the chat regarding 
 which baked good he should prepare for the upcoming Wednesday 
 meeting.

 • Final roll call is taken. 
 • Senator Macedo motions to adjourn. 
 • Vice Chair Gaynor seconds.

Short Title: Bureau Clean Up Resolution 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution will remove any remaining mentions of bureaus from Senate Rules of 
Procedure and insert Institutes into areas where other Executive Entities are being referenced, 
to ensure that Rules of Procedure are reflective of all entities under the Executive Branch. 
 
Background Information: 
This legislation originated from Senate leadership, who had written similar legislation in the past that 
never got enrolled. Bureaus no longer exist within SGA, and have been all but removed from virtually 
every other area of Municode. In addition, given that Institutes are considered to be a part of the 
Executive Branch, it was decided to include them in areas where other Executive entities such as 
Agencies and Affiliated Projects were being discussed. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
This legislation was reviewed by Senate leadership, and was written with guidance from Internal Affairs 
Committee leadership to ensure correct information was being put into place. In addition, the 
recommendation for this legislation came from the Student Senate Advisor in SG&A. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation would remove final mentions to Bureaus within Senate Rules of Procedure, and would 
ensure that Institutes are being included in the relevant areas of Rules of Procedure where other 
Executive entities are being included.

Short Title: An Amendment to the Student Body Constitution to Create a Formal Vehicle for 
Entering into Agreements and Memorandums. 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This legislation would empower the Student Body President to formally negotiate and sign on to 
agreements and memorandums, with the advice and consent of 2/3rds of the Student Senate. The 
Amendment covers Article III, Section 3 of the Constitution, and also governs the ability for the Student 
Body President to leave agreements and memorandums. 
 
Background Information: 
This amendment comes in the context of increasing volumes of Memorandums of Understanding and 
previous conflict between entering into contracts with outside lobbying forces. The Constitution and 
Student Body Statute currently lacks any formal mechanism for entering into MOU’s, which places 
potential concern on strife between the Executive and Legislative branch in terms of what the Student 
Government will agree to enter unto. With the recent need to renegotiate the Memorandum of 
Understanding as it comes to the Activities and Services Fee distribution, having a mechanism in place 
allows consultation across the Government. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Legislative outreach covered the Student Government Advising Office (specifically, advisor Andy 
Johnson), the Student Body President, Student Attorney General, Senate leadership (President, 
President Pro-Tempore), Senate Judiciary Chair and Vice-Chair, Senate Internal Affairs Chair, Senate 
Finance Chair and Vice-Chair, and the Executive Branch Cabinet Director. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This Amendment would create a formal mechanism to enter into and exit agreements or Memorandums 
of Understanding, allowing a legal process that avoids strife and major disagreements across the 
Student Government. This will make sure that agreements are entered into legally, and will provide 
guidance for future agreements to properly gain consensus to be carried out.

Short Title: Recognizing the Seminole Boosters New Towing Policy for Fountain Throws 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution commends the work of the Student Senate and Student Government Association to 
protect the Fountain Throwing tradition at Heritage Fountain. Additionally, it informs the Student Senate 
of the delayed towing enforcement before gamedays for “Booster Parking Lot C – University Center A 
North” in response to student concerns. 
 
Background Information: 
On September 2nd, 2026, during a regular meeting of the Student Senate, members of the student 
body raised concerns regarding pre-gameday towing procedures near Heritage Fountain. Previously, 
on August 28th (prior to the first football home game), a towing company responsible for enforcing the 
rule brought a large fleet of tow trucks to the lot closest to Heritage Fountain and began towing vehicles 
immediately as it turned midnight. This resulted in students, who often look forward to this tradition for 
their entire collegiate careers, having to immediately run back to their cars in hopes that their car 
remained in the lot. Outreach was immediately conducted after learning of this issue, and in partnership 
with the Seminole Boosters, it was agreed to begin pre-gameday towing enforcement at 1 AM for 
“Booster Parking Lot C – University Center A North.” 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Student Senate, Executive Branch, Transportation and Parking Services, Office of Student Governance 
and Advocacy, Seminole Boosters. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation:

STUDENT LIFE COMMITTEE 
 September 10, 2026 at 7:00 PM 
 Location: (Location or Zoom Link) 
 MEETING MINUTES 

 Call to Order 
 Chair Rico called the meeting to order at 7:02 PM. 

Land Acknowledgement 
The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is 
located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can. 
 Chair Rico acknowledged the Land Acknowledgment. 

 Roll Call and Verification of Quorum 
 Chair Rico verified quorum in the absence of Vice Chair Macalintal. 

 Public Comment 

 Opening Announcements 
 
 • Chair Rico welcomes senators and visitors back to the Student Life 
 Committee meeting, requesting that at least one meeting participant 
 turns their Zoom camera on. 

 Old Business 

 New Business 
 • Chair Rico reminds committee members to take the time to ask 
 questions and understand the legislation presented in the meeting 

• Constitutional Amendment #78-004 
 
 ■ 
 • Sponsor Gurtis gives an opening statement regarding a proposed 
 constitutional amendment that would affirm the Student Body 
 President's power to form agreements on behalf of Student 
 Government, pending the approval of the Student Senate and 
 signature from the Vice President of Student Affairs. She cites the 
 amendment exposition as being related to the Flying High Circus 
 summer senate memorandum agreement, which allocated $70,000 
 from the creative and development fund for an HVAC unit for the 
 Flying High Circus, under the premise that remaining funds would 
 return to the Senate. The agreement was not expressly stated as a 
 power belonging to the Student Body President, which is what the 
 amendment hopes to clarify. 
 • Sponsor Gurtis yields with 1:48 for her closing. 
 • Chair Rico opens a period of general questioning. 
 • Chair Rico, in the absence of questions from senators, reminds the 
 committee that constitutional amendments are rare and encourages 
 senators to ask questions regarding the proposition. 
 • Senator Dawkins motions to move into roundtable discussion. 
 • Senator Finman seconds the motion to move into roundtable 
 discussion. 
 • Senator Dawkins speaks in pro of the proposed amendment, noting 
 particular appreciation for updates on the amendment since he last 
 heard about it. 
 • Senator Nturubika questions Sponsor Gurtis on the importance of 
 having the constitutional amendment. 
 • Sponsor Gurtis explains that the proposed constitutional 
 amendment is the formalization of a power already used by the 
 Student Body President and that the amendments purpose is to 
 develop clarity and structure for successive administrations. 
 • Senator Nturubika moves to adopt Amendment #78-004. 
 • Senator Finman seconds the motion to adopt Amendment #78-004. 
 • Constitutional Amendment #78-004 is adopted. 

 Senator Nturubika motions to call the question. 
 Chair Rico notes that the motion is seconded. 
 
 Chair Rico conducts a role count vote, affirming the amendment in a 8-0-1 
 vote. 
• Resolution #78-043 
 
 ■ 
 • Sponsor Gaynor gives an opening statement regarding a resolution 
 that acknowledges the parking and towing advocacy raised at the 
 09/02 Student Senate meeting and proposes that Booster Parking Lot C at University Center A North begins towing at 1 AM instead of 
 12 AM. 
 • Sponsor yields with 3:53 for their closing. 
 • Chair Rico opens a period of general questioning. 
 • Senator questions Sponsor Gaynor about whether the resolution will 
 apply to the entire campus or just the specified lot. 
 • Sponsor Gaynor clarifies that the resolution will only apply to 
 Booster Parking Lot C at University Center A North, but asks 
 Student Life to monitor whether more space is needed. 
 • Senator Nturubika questions Sponsor Gaynor as to why this issue 
 was addressed through a resolution and not a memorandum of 
 understanding. 
 • Sponsor Gaynor expresses that there is no firm legislative need, 
 and that the status of "resolution" is language designed to assure 
 the student body of a concrete solution. Clarifies that a 
 memorandum of understanding is for more formal agreements. 
 • Senator Nturubika motions to enter roundtable discussion. 
 • Senator Owens seconds the motion to enter roundtable discussion. 
 • Senator Nturubika speaks in pro of the resolution. 
 • Senator Nturubika motions to pass the resolution by unanimous 
 consent. 
 • Senator Ownes seconds the motion to pass the resolution by 
 unanimous consent. 

 Resolution #78-043 passes by unanimous consent. 
• Affiliated Project Liaison 
 
 ■ 
 • Chair Rico reminds the committee that members will be appointed to 
 liaison positions for affiliated projects, and assures senators who 
 were not present at the previous meeting that she will be reaching 
 out to them shortly. 
 • Chair Rico expresses that she and President Holliday are in the 
 process of finalizing details regarding liaison assignment. 
 
• Committee Legislation 
 
 ■ 
 • Chair Rico presents the Student Life Legislation Ideas form and 
 asks that each senator within student life submits at least 1 Student 
 Life related idea 
 • Chair Rico announces that she will send out Google Form with 
 submitted legislation ideas. 

Closing Announcements 
 
 • Chair Rico expresses a desire for a more interactive committee, and 
 asks senators to reach out to her or Vice Chair Macalintal with any 
 suggestions on how to make the space more inviting and comfortable. She reminds the committee that everyone is human, encouraging 
 cameras and mistakes within committee time. 

 Final Roll Call and Adjournment 
 
 • Final roll call is taken. 
 • Senator Nturubika motions to adjourn. 
 • Senator Owens seconds. 

 Meeting Adjourned at 7:35 PM.

Short Title: Impeachment Procedure Revision 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
Amends Section 405 of Student Statute relating to impeachment procedure to implement 
safeguards to our current process, and clarify the Judiciary Committee’s role in the process. In 
addition, clarifies the appeal process and how suspension of an official works while they are 
undergoing the impeachment process. 
 
Background Information: 
 While looking through Section 405, it was noticed that under the current process, students could 
file impeachment charges that were falsified with little to no evidence, and the Committee would still 
have to hear them as though they were true and call the accused officer into a hearing. It was then 
decided that additional safeguards, such as a preliminary hearing with the accuser arguing their case 
that the accused doesn’t have to attend, could positively benefit our current system. 
 In addition, upon looking at SGA Statutes from other public Florida universities, our Statutes 
lacked a clear procedure that would be uniformly used for all hearings, so it was also decided that 
adding in a clear process could also streamline the hearing process. Along with this, the hearing 
process that we use didn’t reflect what other universities use and find success with, so it was decided 
that by making the appeal process optional it could potentially mitigate unnecessary cases for the 
Student Supreme Court if there is a clear preponderance of evidence. 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
This legislation was originally brainstormed and drafted with current and former Senator input, before 
being looked over by Senate leadership to assure that the language was clear and the process was 
acceptable. After this, it was reviewed by Student Governance & Advocacy, who provided input about 
the length of how long opening and closing statements should be, as well as some advice relating to 
the appeal process and the preliminary hearing. Finally, a final draft was sent to both the Student 
Supreme Court Chief Justice and Attorney General for review, to ensure that all branches of SGA were 
aware of potential changes and to receive any relevant feedback. Both of these branches found no 
issue with the proposed legislation, with the Chief Justice choosing to defer to the Attorney General’s 
opinion, and the Attorney General approving the bill without proposed change. 

 Page 6 of 13
Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
 If this bill were to be enrolled, it would create a clear process for impeachment: after articles are 
filed against an officer, the individual who filed the articles must appear in front of the Judiciary 
Committee with their evidence to argue the validity of their claim. If the Judiciary Committee proves the 
validity of the claim, the accused officer then must appear in front of the Judiciary Committee to defend 
themselves, and then the Committee votes on whether the case should be forwarded to the Student 
Senate as a whole, and if the Senate votes to impeach the officer, that individual then has the option to 
appeal to the Student Supreme Court, the VPSA, or accept the vote and vacate their office. 
 If the preliminary charges are accepted, the accused officer is suspended until the case is 
finished being considered by the Senate; if they continue the appeal process their suspension will also 
continue. Suspension includes the restriction of making official actions within that position, as well as 
suspension of OPS wages.

This legislation is being presented to allow RSOs to use A&S funds to purchase plastic water 
bottles for student events. Given Florida's high temperatures and the number of outdoor events

environment, and ensures attendees have access to hydration during periods of extreme heat.

 feedback was incorporated to extend committee presentation limits 
 from 5 to 10 minutes (with chair discretion to extend further). Chief 
 Justice Branca remained impartial. 
 o Sponsor yielded remaining opening time. 
• Questioning Period: 
 o Senator Serpenguzel: Inquired why this procedure was previously lacking 
 and how it aligns with practices at other institutions. 
 o Sponsor Response: Gurtis noted existing statutes were scarce on details. 
 Other Florida universities use separate temporary impeachment 
 committees, but Gurtis and Senate President Holiday agreed to utilize the 
 standing Judiciary Committee instead of creating extra committees. 
• Roundtable Discussion: 
 o Motion: Senator Kaighin moved to enter roundtable discussion. 
 o Second: Senator Tanner seconded. 
 o Discussion Points: 
 ▪ Senator Cineas: Spoke in favor, noting the bill simplifies and 
 streamlines the process. 
 ▪ Senator Kaighin: Spoke in favor, supporting making Supreme Court 
 appeals optional 
 ▪ Senator Thompson: Spoke in favor and asked if any negative 
 feedback had been received 
 ▪ Sponsor Response: Gurtis clarified SG&A questioned excluding 
 accused officers from initial preliminary hearings, but the structure was maintained to give officers the choice not to appear. Timing 
 adjustments suggested by SG&A were adopted, and general senator 
 feedback has been positive 
 • Call to Question & Vote: 
 o Motion: Senator Kaighin moved to call the question 
 o Second: Senator Serpenguzel seconded 
 o Vote: 6 Yes, 0 No, 0 Abstain. Bill 78-39 Passes 
 ▪ Yes: Senators Cineas, Thompson, Kaighin, Tanner, Serpenguzel, 
 Belman 
 o Vice Chair Rodriguez relinquished the chair back to Chair Gurtis 

2. Bill 78-40: 

 • Legislation Presentation: 
 o Presented by Senator Dewey 
 o Opening Statement: 
 ▪ Amends Chapter 802 to permit Recognized Student Organizations 
 (RSOs) to use A&S funds to purchase plastic water bottles (and 
 reinstates plastic straws and styrofoam) 
 ▪ Aims to prevent heat stroke and heat-related illnesses during warm 
 months. The prior ban was unenforced across campus, and 
 environmental impacts are considered minor relative to health risks. 
 ▪ Sign-offs obtained from the Office of Sustainability, Senate President, 
 and Student Body Treasurer. 
 o Sponsor yielded remaining opening time. 
 • Questioning Period: 
 o Vice Chair Rodriguez: Asked if the Department of Sustainability was 
 consulted regarding the rationale for lifting single-use plastic restrictions. 
 o Sponsor Response: Dewey confirmed Office of Sustainability approval, 
 noting Chair Perantoni handled sustainability outreach, and offered to follow 
 up with Perantoni for specific details prior to the full Senate session 
 • Roundtable Discussion: 
 o Motion: Vice Chair Rodriguez moved to enter roundtable discussion 
 o Second: Senator Cineas seconded 
 o Outcome: Entered roundtable 
 o Discussion Points: ▪ Vice Chair Rodriguez: Expressed reservation over missing specific 
 reasoning from sustainability officials, stating she would await full 
 details on the Senate floor before committing a yes vote 
 ▪ Senator Cineas: Spoke in favor, citing the need for student hydration 
 year-round due to campus weather and walking distances 
 • Call to Question & Vote: 
 o Motion: Senator Kaighin moved to call the question 
 o Second: Senator Cineas seconded 
 o Outcome: Sponsor gave closing remarks, promising to obtain sustainability 
 feedback details from Chair Perantoni before the Senate session 
 o Vote: 5 Yes, 0 No, 2 Abstentions. Bill 78-40 Passes 
 ▪ Yes: Senators Kaighin, Serpenguzel, Cineas, Thompson, Belman 
 ▪ Abstain: Vice Chair Rodriguez 

Closing Announcements 

 • Chair Gurtis: Thanked members for active participation and high engagement; 
 noted upcoming agendas will grow heavier 
 • Vice Chair Rodriguez: Elaborated on her voting philosophy, advising that 
 committee members should abstain or vote cautiously when critical information is 
 missing from sponsors 

Final Attendance & Adjournment 

 • Final Quorum Verification: Conducted by Vice Chair Rodriguez 
 o Present: Senators Tanner, Kaighin, Serpenguzel, Cineas, Thompson, 
 Belman, Vice Chair Rodriguez, Chair Gurtis 
 • Adjournment Motion: 
 o Motion: Senator Serpenguzel moved to adjourn 
 o Second: Senator Kaighin seconded 
 • Meeting Adjourned: Meeting adjourned at 7:22pm

 2 Section 1. Amendment to Student Body Statutes Chapter 802, “General Guidelines 
 3 and Restrictions on Expenditures”. 

 4 Section 802 of the Florida State University Student Body Statutes, entitled “General Guidelines and 
 5 Restrictions on Expenditures” is hereby amended to read as follows: 

 6 Chapter 802 General Guidelines And Restrictions On Expenditures 

 7 1. The A&S Fee Guidelines were promulgated jointly by the Student Government Association and 
 8 Florida State University. The allocation and expenditure policies and procedures contained in the 
 9 A&S Fee Guidelines are obligatory upon Student Government Association. 

10 2. Activities funded must not conflict with the purpose or regulations of the Florida State University, 
11 Board of Trustees policies, or state and federal laws. 

12 3. No A&S monies shall be dispersed to pay for previous expenditures without prior approval. SGA 
13 shall only be obligated to pay where a legitimate purchase order has been properly issued, or other 
14 paperwork as designated by the SGA Accounting Office. This clause may be waived by an appeal in 
15 the form of a resolution to the Senate Finance Committee. The appeal must include a letter of 
16 explanation as to why the expense did not receive pre-approval as well as the financial statement 
17 and expense reports from the event. A representative for the organization requesting the appeal 
18 must be present. The appeal must pass the Finance Committee by three-fourths (3/4) and receive a 
19 three-fourths (3/4) vote of the Student Senate. Should either vote fail, SGA shall not be liable for the 
20 expense. 

21 a. SGA shall not fund any item pertaining to an event or travel in the past including, but not 
22 limited to: clothing, awards, and promotional items. The selection process for any awards 
23 paid for by A&S monies must occur after the initial request presentation, and the recipient 
24 must be notified that their award was paid for by SGA. 

25 4. Accessibility of Meetings & Events: Exempting SGA-sponsored concerts, no FSU student shall be 
26 charged admission for any event funded in whole or in part by A&S monies, unless the student is 
27 unable or unwilling to provide proof of studentship that shall include, but not be limited to, their valid 
28 FSU ID. All SGA-funded events and meetings must also be well publicized and conducted in an 
29 environment that is generally accessible to the public. 

30 a. No event or meeting at which A&S Fees are utilized may be conducted in a private 
31 residence. This includes, but is not limited to, apartments, homes, and condominiums. This 
32 does not apply to community clubhouses. Exceptions to this rule shall require a two-thirds 
33 (2/3) vote of the Student Senate. 

34 b. Evidence of an adequate advertisement plan of A&S Fee utilizing meetings and events must 
35 be presented at the time the expenditure is initially presented to the Student Body Treasurer. 
36 Failure to properly promote an event is grounds for rejection of all expenditures associated 
37 with the event. 

38 c. SGA-sponsored concerts shall include Headliners concerts, Homecoming Live, and any 
39 other concerts that attain the sponsorship of SGA via Senate resolution. Such concerts must 
40 have their ticket prices approved by Senate through resolution. 

41 d. Events should be held on campus if appropriate accommodations on campus are available. 
42 Agencies, affiliated projects, and SGA offices must have off-campus events approved via a 
43 resolution of the Student Senate. Funding for undergraduate RSOs to host events off 
44 campus shall require a majority vote of approval by the RSO Allocation Committee and the 
45 Student Senate. Graduate RSOs must have approval as outlined in the COGS Code. 

46 5. Limitation on Outside (Non-FSU) Benefits: 

 Page 3 of 7
47 a. Funds may not be expended to support a candidate for political office, nor for contribution to 
48 political activity directly seeking to affect the passage, defeat, or status of any legislation 
49 except as provided by Florida Law. This statute shall by no means be interpreted as 
50 restricting the lobbying efforts of the Student Body President, Student Senate, or the Office 
51 of Governmental Affairs. 

52 b. Items/services purchased with A&S money may not be used for the primary benefit of

62 State University. A&S Fees shall not be used to: endorse a political candidate on or off 
63 campus or advance political messages and ideologies off-campus. 

64 e. Religious based student groups may receive funding for awareness/advertising of their RSO 
65 on campus, RSO events, and travel that advances their mission at Florida State University. 
66 Funding for proselytizing is prohibited. Religious based organizations providing service are 
67 exempt from being registered as a service organization. Religious groups can request money 
68 for service projects or service travel, but must not proselytize their religion. Religious topics 
69 or lectures may be offered during travel or events; however, if requested by a participant, an 
70 alternate activity must be arranged. 

71 6. Acknowledgment of SGA Funding: 

72 a. All online and printed materials purchased or manufactured with A&S Fees must include the 
73 FSU SGA logo, or the logo of the SGA-budgeted entity purchasing the item(s). On printed 
74 materials, the SGA logo shall be no less than 1/30 of the size of the area in which the logo is 
75 placed on materials not advertising a specific event, the logo may be substituted with the 
76 words “Paid for by SGA” or “Paid for by Student Government Association” in clearly visible 
77 font. One of the following areas on printed materials must be used to meet the logo 
78 requirement: 

79 (1) On the front of posters and flyers 

80 (2) On the front or back cover of pamphlets and other publications 

81 (3) Inside the front cover of publications 

82 (4) On either the front or the back of t-shirts or tank tops. 

83 b. All audio and video advertising funded by non SGA-budgeted entities in whole or in part with 
84 A&S Fees shall publicly acknowledge SGA funding by including the statement “Paid for by 
85 FSU SGA” or “Funded in part by FSU SGA”. Classified advertisements must either include 
86 the FSU Student Government logo or the words "Paid for by FSU SGA.” 

87 c. Any printed materials sponsored by an A&S recipient must include the name of recipient. 

88 d. All printed materials and broadcasts expressing a political message must also include, with 
89 the SGA logo: "The views expressed herein do not necessarily reflect those of the FSU 
90 Student Government Association."

 91 7. No personal gifts may be purchased with A&S money. Items given for recognition may only be 
 92 funded from the Clothing & Awards Category. 

 93 8. Alcohol may not be purchased with A&S monies, either specifically or as part of a facility rental 
 94 agreement or any other package. 

 95 9. Disposable plastic water bottles and disposable plastic straws may not be purchased with A&S 
 96 monies. In lieu of disposable plastic water bottles, RSO may not purchase other environmentally

 99 methods of water distribution are hindered, plastic water bottles may be purchased.

105 that utilize these items for the purpose of sport under the purview of Campus Recreation, however 
106 Campus Recreation must have policies in place around the purchase and use of their firearms and 
107 weapons.

 78th STUDENT SENATE

 Senate Bill #: 040 
 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Dewey, Perantoni

Short Title: To Remove Water Bottle Purchasing Restrictions for SGA Funded Entities 

Summary of Legislation: 
This bill would amend chapter 802, Student Body Statutes, to allow RSO’s to purchase plastic 
water bottles with A&S funds. 

Background Information: 
This legislation is being presented to allow RSOs to use A&S funds to purchase plastic water 
bottles for student events. Given Florida's high temperatures and the number of outdoor events 
hosted by RSOs, access to water is important for student health and safety. This change 
would provide organizations with greater flexibility in planning events while helping ensure 
students have access to hydration and reducing the risk of heat-related illnesses. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

SGA Business Manager, Senate President, Tanner McKinley, Student Body Treasurer, 
Sustainability 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation would permit Registered Student Organizations to use A&S funds for the 
purchase of plastic water bottles. Providing water at student events helps support a safe event 
environment, and ensures attendees have access to hydration during periods of extreme heat.

located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can.

 A PROCLAMATION 
 Recognizing the Tragedy of 9/11, 25 Years Later 

 1 WHEREAS, the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, represent the single deadliest foreign attack 
 2 on American soil, including the hijackings of: United Airlines Flight 175, which struck the South Tower, 
 3 which collapsed upon New York City an hour later; American Airlines Flight 11, which struck the North 
 4 Tower, which collapsed upon New York City two hours later; American Airlines Flight 77, which struck 
 5 the Pentagon; United Airlines Flight 93, which was forcefully crashed into an open field in Pennsylvania; 
 6 and, 
 7 
 8 WHEREAS, September 11, 2001, claimed the lives of 2,977 innocent people, including 343 firefighters 
 9 and paramedics, 23 New York City Police Officers, 37 Port Authority Police Officers, 125 Pentagon 
10 Staff, and 261 flight passengers, forever changing the United States, reminding future generations of 
11 the cost of hatred and the strength of the human spirit; and, 
12 
13 WHEREAS, amidst unimaginable tragedy, countless individuals displayed extraordinary courage, 
14 including Rick Rescorla, who safely evacuated more than 2,700 Morgan Stanley employees before 
15 returning to help others and sacrificing his life; and, 
16 
17 WHEREAS, bravery included Moira Smith, an NYPD officer who repeatedly entered the World Trade 
18 Center to lead the injured to safety before losing her own life; and, 
19 
20 WHEREAS, bravery included Welles Crowther, the "Man in the Red Bandanna," who saved as many 
21 as 18 people by climbing up the South Tower stairwell to floors above where United Airlines Flight 175 
22 struck, guiding and carrying individuals to the safety of the staircases; and, 
23 
24 WHEREAS, bravery included Benjamin Clark, a chef at Fiduciary Trust Company, who successfully 
25 helped evacuate the entire 96th floor, and was last seen helping a handicapped individual during the 
26 collapse of the South Tower; and, 
27 
28 WHEREAS, bravery included John Perry, an NYPD officer who, despite being hours from retirement 
29 and off-duty, rushed into the North Tower to help evacuate people, last seen helping a woman escape 
30 the North Tower when it collapsed; and, 
31

 Page 2 of 60
32 WHEREAS, bravery included Danny Lewin, who attempted to halt the hijackers of American Airlines 
33 Flight 11, and was stabbed to death onboard the plane; and, 
34 
35 WHEREAS, bravery included Leonard Hatton, a former marine and volunteer firefighter, who sprung to 
36 action outside of working hours to join the New York City firefighters as they evacuated the North 
37 Tower. He was last seen in the North Tower when the building collapsed; and, 
38 
39 WHEREAS, bravery included William Rodriguez, a maintenance worker, who led firefighters up the 
40 North Tower with the emergency exit keys, helping hundreds of people escape the tower; and, 
41 
42 WHEREAS, bravery included Ronald Bucca, a New York Fire Marshall who was found passed away in 
43 the debris of the South Tower. His protective coat was found wrapped around several other civilians; 
44 and, 
45 
46 WHEREAS, bravery included Jason Thomas and Dave Karnes, marines who rushed into the World 
47 Trade Center to save two police officers under 20 feet of debris; and, 
48 
49 WHEREAS, bravery included Kathy Mazza, a port authority police officer captain, who worked to 
50 evacuate people from the North Tower lobby, including carrying a disabled woman down into the lobby 
51 with her team. She made extra exits by shooting out the lobby’s windows with her service weapon, and 
52 her body was found in the collapsed rubble with the woman she attempted to save; and, 
53 
54 WHEREAS, bravery included officers Thomas Jurgens, Mitchel Wallace, and William Thompson, who 
55 all jumped in from unrelated posts to evacuate an individual who suffered a heart attack, and another 
56 who suffered a head injury. After numerous entries into the World Trade Center, they were told it was 
57 unsafe for them to go in again. Defying orders, they went in to save more people. They did not return; 
58 and, 
59 
60 WHEREAS, bravery included the passengers and crew of Flight 93, who fought back against the 
61 plane’s hijackers to seize back control of the plane, causing it to crash into an empty Pennsylvania field, 
62 preventing the striking of either the White House or Capitol Hill; and, 
63 
64 WHEREAS, bravery included the coast guard and civilian captains who rescued half a million civilians 
65 from the soot and debris of the collapsed World Trade Center, ferrying them to safer areas around New 
66 York City; and, 
67 
68 WHEREAS, bravery included rescue dogs and their handlers, who worked for 14-hour shifts for periods 
69 up to four weeks, searching for survivors, including the final survivor identified by rescue dog Trakr, 
70 Genelle Guzman-McMillan, who had been trapped under debris for 27 hours; and, 
71

Short Title: Recognizing the Tragedy of 9/11, 25 Years Later 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This proclamation recognizes the extraordinary sacrifices and stories of the victims and heroes of the 
9/11 terrorist attacks. It names each victim by name who died that day, and calls for remembrance on 
the 25th anniversary of this act of hatred. 
 
Background Information: 
2026 marks 25 years since the tragedy of 9/11. Many individuals at Florida State were shaken, 
especially the members of our Veteran community, or had parents/loved ones impacted by 9/11. 
Overall, the attacks heavily impacted the psyche of the American people and our country’s response on 
the world stage, making the largest attack on American soil one to remember for the innocents and 
heroes who were lost that day. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Outreach with the Veteran Student Union and research into the history of 9/11. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This proclamation recognizes and encourages remembrance for the 9/11 attacks, especially on the 25th 
anniversary. It would highlight the stories and heroism displayed during the attacks, and recognize the 
innocent victims.

calendar month while the Student Senate is in session, the balance, activity, and transaction ledger of

Executive Projects formalizing a practice the Senate already follows informally.
