The 78th Student Senate 
 Judiciary Committee 
 Meeting Minutes 
 June 24, 2026 at 7:00 PM | (Location or Zoom Link) 

 Call to Order 
 The meeting was called to order at 7:02 pm. 

Land Acknowledgement 
The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is 
located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can. 
 Chair Gurtis Acknowledged the Land Acknowledgement. 

 Roll Call and Verification of Quorum 
 Present: 
 Morgan Gurtis 
 Kayla Iarossi 
 Isabel Tanner 
 Colby Kaighin 
 Nadia Noble 
 Eddie Fordham 
 Mackenzie Malone 
 Ian Rodriguez 
 Melyne Cineas 
 
 Not Present: 
 Anne Bristol 
 Meredith Helming 
 
 Quorum is verified. 

 Public Comment 
 N/A 
Opening Announcements 
 Chair Gurtis: So excited to start this meeting can't wait to hear from everyone! 

Old Business 

• Ben Jolly - Executive Branch, Solicitor General (Assigned to Internal Affairs, 
 Judiciary, 06.03.2026) (Tabled in Internal Affairs, 06.08.2026) (Tabled in 
 Judiciary, 06.10.2026) 
 
 ■ Opening Statement: 
 Candidate: I am excited to be here, excited to hear your questions, and 
 aside from that, I don't really have too much to add. I'm ready whenever you 
 are. 
 
 General Questioning: 
 Senator Kaighin- Can you into further depth about your experience please? 
 - The candidate stated that they are in law school and have 
 developed familiarity with legal systems and government structure through 
 both academic and practical experience. They noted an internship with the 
 Florida Attorney General’s Office, where they gained exposure to the 
 executive branch legal process. They also referenced involvement in law 
 school student government through the Law School Council, where they 
 worked on budgeting and appropriations processes and gained experience 
 with organizational statutes and procedures. Additionally, they described 
 undergraduate experience on a club lacrosse team, which provided 
 perspective on student organizations’ interactions with student government 
 and challenges in obtaining funding and administrative support. Overall, the 
 candidate characterized their background as well-rounded across legal, 
 governmental, and student organizational contexts. 
 
 Senator Cineas- Because this position involves advocating for the 
 university's interests, can you describe a time when you had to argue or 
 support a position that did not align with your personal values, and how you 
 approached that situation? 
 - The candidate explained that law school has provided significant 
 experience arguing from multiple perspectives. Through classroom 
 exercises, particularly in criminal law, students are often assigned to 
 represent either the defense or prosecution in hypothetical cases and must 
 advocate effectively regardless of their personal beliefs. They noted that 
 these experiences have strengthened their ability to analyze issues from 
 different viewpoints, make persuasive arguments based on the same set of 
 facts, and professionally represent positions they may not personally hold. 
 They believe this training would translate well to the role and prepare them 
 for legal advocacy in their future career. 
 
 Vice Chair Iarossi- legislation that could conflict with student body statutes, 
 how would you advise your clients? 
 -The candidate stated that in both court and governmental 
 procedure, any action that violates law or the student constitution is 
 presumed to be not allowed unless otherwise permitted. They explained 
 that this would serve as the baseline starting point for interpreting 
 arguments and making decisions within the system. 
 Vice Chair Iarossi- What improvements would you make to the office? 
 - The candidate stated that they are aware of some controversies 
 from the previous year and are still learning the full procedural framework in 
 their current role. They expressed a preference for prioritizing quick dispute 
 resolution, ideally through agreement between parties when possible, rather 
 than proceeding to full trials or oral arguments. The candidate added that 
 this approach would generally guide their vision for handling disputes, even 
 though they are currently involved in oral argument processes. 
 Senator Malone: If a student that was to file agreements against an SGA 
 official who happens to be possibly like a close friend or maybe like a 
 political ally or someone you know, how would you go about leading your 
 office to handle that prosecution? 
 - The candidate stated that in the event of a real or perceived 
 conflict of interest, they would step aside from direct involvement in the 
 case to avoid bias. They explained that responsibility would then be 
 delegated to the Attorney General or Deputy Solicitor General, ensuring the 
 matter is handled by individuals without conflicts while maintaining proper 
 representation and process integrity 
 
 Round Table: 
 Senator Rodriguez: Are you affiliated with any organization that would effect 
 your nonpartisan role? 
 -No. 
 
 Closing Statement: 
 Candidate: I would like to thank everyone for their time today. 
 
 Vote: 
 
 YAY: 
 Isabel Tanner 
 Colby Kaighin 
 Nadia Noble 
 Eddie Fordham 
 Mackenzie Malone 
 Ian Rodriguez 
 Melyne Cineas 
 
 NAY: 0 
 
 Candidate passes with unanimous consent. 

• Haven Branca - Judicial Branch, Chief Justice (Assigned to Judiciary, 
 06.07.2026) (Tabled in Judiciary, 06.10.2026) 
 
 ■ Opening Statement: 
 The candidate stated that they have been serving as Acting Chief Justice of 
 the FSU Student Supreme Court for approximately one month and 
 previously served as an Associate Justice for six months. They also noted 
 additional legal experience, including serving as an Executive Editor on the 
FSU Law Review, a fellow in the Chambers of Justice Francis on the 
Florida Supreme Court (with plans to return in the fall), a teaching assistant 
for legal writing, and a research assistant for Professor Eisler focusing on 
constitutional law issues. 
The candidate outlined two primary goals if confirmed as Chief Justice: first, 
establishing a roster or system of student legal representatives to provide 
representation for students appearing before the Student Supreme Court, 
particularly in cases where current representation is limited to SGA counsel 
or executive/legal officers; and second, updating and revising the Court’s 
Rules of Procedure to improve clarity and functionality. 
The candidate concluded by yielding the remainder of their time. 
 
General Questioning: 
Senator Cinceas- If you were to get the position, what do you think would 
be one of your biggest challenges, and why? 
 - The candidate identified two primary anticipated challenges in 
implementing their proposed initiatives. First, regarding the creation of a 
student representative organization for appearances before the Student 
Supreme Court, they noted that establishing an RSO is a time-sensitive 
process. They shared that they have already begun outreach and learned 
that organization applications are not expected to reopen until at least June 
30, which may delay formation. They emphasized the importance of early 
outreach and planning so that the organization can later pursue funding for 
training, case preparation resources, and administrative materials. Second, 
regarding the revision of the Court’s Rules of Procedure, the candidate 
highlighted the balance between comprehensiveness and accessibility. 
They referenced the Florida Rules of Civil Procedure as an example of a 
highly detailed system and explained that while thoroughness is necessary 
to ensure proper governance, the rules must remain understandable and 
usable for students who are not legal professionals.The candidate 
concluded that while these challenges are significant, they believe 
collaboration within the Court will allow the goals to be successfully 
achieved. 
 
Senator Fordham- As Chief Justice, would you proactively recommend 
changes to rules or statutes to improve fairness and equal access for both 
sides, or would you wait for the Senate to initiate those changes? 
 - The court is taking a proactive approach under the Student 
Body Statutes and Constitution by exercising its authority to amend its own 
rules of procedure, updating outdated requirements—such as eliminating 
mandatory physical copies in favor of more accessible digital processes—to 
improve efficiency and reduce unnecessary student costs. 
 
Senator Rodriguez- Are you involved with any organizations that you will 
impact your bias or partiality? Such as Burning Spear? 
 - no. 
Vice Chair Iarossi: In pro 
Senator Rodriguez: In pro 
 
Closing Statement: 
Candidate: Great! Well, thank you so much, everyone, for being here 
tonight to listen to me. The Supreme Court is a passion project of mine, and 
I'm really excited just to get to work with this court next year 
 
 Vote 
 YAY: 
 Isabel Tanner 
 Colby Kaighin 
 Nadia Noble 
 Eddie Fordham 
 Mackenzie Malone 
 Ian Rodriguez 
 Melyne Cineas 
 
 Candidate passes by unanimous consent. 

New Business 

• Bill #78-024 
 
 ■ Opening Statement: 
 Sponsor Tanner: The sponsor introduced the bill as their first piece of 
 legislation and expressed enthusiasm in presenting it. The bill amends the 
 Student Body Statutes by removing the requirement that the Student 
 Senate President Pro Tempore sign enrolled copies of legislation. 
 The sponsor clarified that the legislation does not alter or diminish the role 
 or authority of any position, but rather streamlines the enrollment process 
 by requiring only the Student Senate President’s signature before 
 legislation proceeds to enrollment. The sponsor concluded that the change 
 is intended to simplify and improve procedural efficiency. 
 
 General Questioning: 
 Senator Fordham: How removing the requirement for the Student Senate 
 President Pro Tempore to sign enrolled legislation might increase the risk of 
 procedural or clerical errors going unnoticed. Specifically, they inquired 
 whether the Pro Tempore’s additional review step could serve as a 
 safeguard for catching textual or formatting mistakes before legislation 
 reaches the Student Senate President for final signature. 
 - The sponsor acknowledged the concern and stated that 
 legislation typically undergoes a significant review process prior to 
 enrollment, making additional signature requirements less necessary 
 Vice Chair Iarossi: What was the background into deciding this piece of 
 legislation? 
 -The bill argues this creates unnecessary procedural 
 redundancy because both roles are largely ministerial in the enrollment 
 process. It proposes removing the Pro Tempore signature requirement 
 while keeping the Senate President’s certification authority intact. 
 Senator Rodriguez- motion to propose amendment strike of like 44. 
 Passes. 
 
 Closing: 
 Sponsor Gurtis: Thank you all for your questions and time. 
 
 Vote: 
 YAY: 
 Isabel Tanner 
 Colby Kaighin 
 Nadia Noble 
 Eddie Fordham 
 Mackenzie Malone 
 Ian Rodriguez 
 Melyne Cineas 
 
 Bill passes by unanimous consent. 
• Bill #78-025 
 
 ■ Opening Statement: 
 Sponor Bigenho: This just allows for leadership to run for another term. 
 Until last year there was no term limit. All previous presidents loved this 
 idea. This legislation does not create indefinite leadership or diminish 
 accountability. Instead, it establishes a clear and balanced structure 
 allowing Senate leadership to serve a second term if the body chooses, 
 reflecting the value of experience, institutional knowledge, and proven 
 performance. At the same time, it preserves electoral oversight by keeping 
 leadership fully subject to the will of the Senate. 
 Additionally, this bill modernizes our organizational procedures by removing 
 an inflexible timing requirement for the organizational session, ensuring that 
 logistical constraints do not interfere with our ability to govern efficiently and 
 responsibly. 
 
 General Questioning: 
 Senator Fordham- I believe in the section 400.8 F there needs to be an 
 additional definition of term, why have you not defined term and leadership? 
 - The threshold is that you cannot be sworn into the senate president 
 twice. These are questions of law that we already have with real offices and 
 that why we did not put another definition. Our definition of a term would be 
 a limit on getting sworn in. 
 
 Round Table: 
 Senator Rodriguez: Speak in pro 
 Senator Iarossi: Speak in pro 
 
 Closing Statement: 
 This is a safeguard for senate, thank you all for listening. 
 
 VOICE VOTE!!!! UNANIMOUS !!!! PASSES!!! 

Closing Announcements 
 Chair Gurtis: I am so proud of you all. Engagement has been amazing. 
 
 Vice chair Iarossi: Please text me if you will not be able to go to the meetings 
 in the future. 
Final Roll Call and Adjournment 
 Present: 
 Morgan Gurtis 
 Kayla Iarossi 
 Isabel Tanner 
 Colby Kaighin

FINANCE COMMITTEE 
 June 24, 2026 at 5:45 PM 
 Location: (Location or Zoom Link) 
 MEETING MINUTES 

 Call to Order 
 Chair Perantoni begins committee meeting at 5:49pm. 

Land Acknowledgement 
The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is 
located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can. 
 Chair Perantoni acknowledges the Land Acknowledgment. 

 Roll Call and Verification of Quorum 
 Vice Chair Tizon calls the roll and verifies the quorum. 
 
 Present: Perantoni, Tizon, Gentile, Dewey, Costello, Scarpone, Rodriguez, 
 Bollinger, Kaul. 
 Excused: White, Oria, Hidalgo 

 Public Comment 

 Opening Announcements 
 Chair Perantoni welcomes the finance committee and Rama Naem, who is 
 presenting for the Sports Club Distribution Council. Vice Chair Tizon 
 welcomes the committee and acknowledges that this is the final summer 
 meeting for Senator Gentile, who is taking a leave of absence beginning the 
 following week. Chair Perantoni reccomendeds committee members to co-
 sponsor his new piece of legislation regarding RSOAC reform. 

 Old Business 
 No old business. 
New Business 

• Presentation by Sports Club Distribution Council 
 
 ■ Chair Perantoni introduces speaker Rama Naem with the Sports Club 
 Distribution Council, who is the current Chair. 
 
 Speaker Naem expresses her excitement for the Sports Club and the 
 upcoming year. Speaker Naem explains how the club's process works, 
 overseeing 50+ sports club at FSU. Responsibilities: Budget hearings, tier 
 review, sports club funding. Sports clubs submit budget requests with a 
 spreadsheet of all finances, alongside a presented presentation which is 
 reviewed during their hearings. Allocations are voted on and notified via 
 email of their tier and funding allocation. Tier system from highest to lowest: 
 Garnet Tier, Gold Tier, White Tier, and Probationary. 
 
 Sen. Gentile asks what are the incentives to move up tiers. 
 
 Speaker Naem explains how advancing in tiers allows for more allocation of 
 funding for clubs, roughly a $2,000 increase. 
• Anthony Naranjo-Abraham - Hispanic/Latin Student Union, 
 Treasurer (Assigned to Finance, 06.17.2026) 
 
 ■ Tabled to next finance committee meeting, July 8th. 
• Allocation Resolution #78-008 
 
 ■ Vice Chair Tizon introduces allocation resolution #78-008, proposing the 
 allocation of $118.556.00 to various Sports Clubs who request funds from 
 the Sports Club Distribution Council. 
 
 Vice Chair Tizon motions for non-senators to speak. 
 Sen. Costello seconds. 
 
 Sen. Costello asks a question regarding the Sports Club Distribution 
 Council. 
 Speaker Naem responds. 
 
 Sen. Dewey asks about travel funding for clubs. 
 Speaker Naem responds. 
 
 Sen. Dewey questions why dance funding is higher than other clubs. 
 Speaker Naem explains that they are garnet tier, and explains that the 
 funding is dependent on how much the club requested, how dance 
 requested more funding than many other clubs. 
 
 Chair Perantoni asks how sports clubs can be successful regarding 
 allocation. 
 Speaker Naem highlights women basketball, who started as a probationary 
 club who worked hard and passionately to move up in tiers for increased 
 funding. 
 
 Chair Perantoni asked which clubs have gotten a reduction in tiers and 
 what was the most common reason. 
 Speaker Naem responds and highlights two examples of clubs that had a 
 tier reduction. 
 
 Vice Chair Tizon calls the question and the vote, resolution passes with 8 
 yes, 0 no, 1 abstention. 

 Closing Announcements 
 Chair Perantoni discusses the next meeting's contents on July 8th. Chair 
 Perantoni reminds the senators of his office hours. Vice Chair Tizon wishes 
 the best to Speaker Naem and the Sports Club Distribution Council. 

 Final Roll Call and Adjournment 
 Vice Chair Tizon motions to adjorn. Sen. Gentile, seconds. Vice Chair Tizon 
 calls final roll. 
 
 Present: Perantoni, Tizon, Gentile, Dewey, Costello, Scarpone, Rodriguez, 
 Bollinger, Kaul. 
 Excused: White, Oria, Hidalgo 
 
 Meeting adjourned at 6:18pm.

 Members present: Mr. Ian Seibert, Dr. Dei Allard, Mr. Camden Reuthe, Mr. Josh 
 Turner, Ms. Sela Teplin, Mr. Gilman Page, and Mr. Maddox Goodman 
 
III. Public Comment 
 
 No public comment was submitted in advance or presented during the meeting. 
 
IV. Chairs Remarks 
 Ian Seibert, Chair 
 
 Mr. Seibert thanked the committee members and presenters for their presentations 
 during the previous meeting. Mr. Seibert stated the committee could make 
 recommendations for the next three fiscal years. 
 
V. Committee Deliberations and Recommendation 
 
 Ms. Teplin expressed support for Athletics. 
 
 Ms. Teplin recommended an increase for athletics. Ms. Teplin added the importance 
 of keeping athletic tickets free for students. 
 
 Mr. Maddox Goodman said the A&S fees are being stretched as much of it can be. 
 RSOs, Agencies, Institutes, and Affiliated Projects are feeling the effect of not 
 enough A&S fees. 
 
 Mr. Turner discussed the importance of police presence at athletic events for student 
 and fan safety. 
 
 Mr. Reuthe spoke about minimum wage increases and how inflation is outpacing the 
 minimum wage. 
 
 Ms. Teplin asked Mr. Turner if the police presence is funded by local fees or by the 
 state. Mr. Turner stated that Athletics covers the FSU PD fees. 
 
 Dr. Allard supports a dollar increase to A&S fees. 
 
 Mr. Reuthe moved to increase the health fee by 35% over the next three fiscal years. 
 Ms. Teplin seconded the motion. This motion passes unanimously. 
 
 Ms. Teplin asked whether the committee wished to reconsider the health fee 
 recommendation. 
 
 Chair Seibert stated they could consider a one-year increase rather than a three-year 
 recommendation. 
 
 Mr. Goodman expressed support for increasing A&S fees by 40% and Athletic fees 
 by 25%. 
 
 Mr. Reuthe stated he supported Mr. Goodman's statement. 
 
 Ms. Teplin moved to by a maximum of a 5% increase A&S fees by 40% over the next 
 three fiscal years. Mr. Goodman seconded the motion. This motion passes 
 unanimously. 
 
 Mr. Goodman moved to by a maximum of a 5%, increase Athletic fees by 25% over 
 the next three fiscal years. Ms. Teplin seconded the motion. The motion passes 
 unanimously. 
 
 Mr. Reuthe moved to a maximum 5% increase Health Fees by 25%, A&S Fees by 
 40%, and Athletic Fees by 25% over the next three fiscal years. Mr. Goodman 
 seconded the motion. The motion passes unanimously. 
 
 Ms. Brown noted that the recommendation should specify FY 2027-28 through FY 
 2029-30. The committee agreed to revise the motion accordingly. 
 
 Mr. Reuthe moved to a maximum 5% increase for the next 3 fiscal years, distributed 
 35% to the Health Fee, 40% to A&S, and 25% to Athletics. Mr. Page seconded the 
 motion. The motion passes unanimously. 
 
 The final recommendation of the committee a maximum 5% increase for the next 3 
 fiscal years, distributed 35% to the Health Fee, 40% to A&S, and 25% to Athletics. 
 
VI. Open Discussion for Committee Members 
 
VII. Chairs Closing Remarks 
 Ian Seibert, Chair 
 
VIII. Adjournment 
 The meeting adjourned at 2:51 pm.

Welcome and Introductions
Committee Members

 ● Chair – Ian Seibert, Student Body President
 ● Staff Member – Dei Allard, Assistant Vice President, Housing, Childcare, Study Away, & PCC SA
 ● Staff Member – Gil, Page, Director, Office of Student Finance

 ● Student Member – Maddox Goodman, Student Body Treasurer

 ● Ex-officio Member – Cassandra Brown, Division of Student Affairs Chief Financial Officer
Types of Fees 

A&S Fee: Funds student organizations, events, and campus amenities to enrich 
student life and foster inclusivity.
Health Fee: Supports on-campus health facilities for student medical care, including 
general healthcare, mental health, and emergencies.
Athletic Fee: Subsidizes athletic programs and facilities, offering discounted or free 
event access to boost school spirit.
Background 

 Current Fees: $34.73 per credit hour 
 ○ Activity & Service: $12.86
 ○ Athletics: $7.90 
 ○ Health: $13.97

 Under Florida Statute (FS) 1009.24, the Local Fee Committee is authorized to 
 increase aggregate local fees by up to 5% or $1.73 per credit hour, effective in 
 Fall 2024.

 The maximum allowed for all local fees is 40% of the legally set tuition of 
 $105.07, putting the cap at $42.02. Currently, local fees at FSU stand at 33% of 
 the tuition.
Past Percentage Distribution of General Fee Increase

Last fee Raise: 2013
o (40%) A&S: $0.36
o (25%) Athletics: $0.62
o (35%) Health: $0.55

If the Local Fee Committee recommends increasing these fees by $1.73 and we 
recommend the same distribution, the allocation at the start of fall term 2027 could be as 
follows:
o 40% to A&S results in $.69 increase - New rate per credit hour = $13.55
o 25% to Athletics results in $.43 increase - New rate per credit hour = $8.33
o 35% to Health results in $.61 increase - New rate per credit hour = $14.58

This would bring the new total to $36.46. Well under the 40% cap of $42.02

media accounts, including Agencies and Departments, and requires them to use available 
accessibility features to accommodate students with sight and hearing impairment. In addition, 
this resolution states that Senate will work with the Press Secretary to put out educational 
materials showing how to use accessibility features, so there is no confusion on how to use 
available tools. 
 
Background Information: 
This issue was brought to attention by a former Senator with impaired vision. The goal of this resolution 
is to ensure that those who are impaired, either by vision or hearing, can still access necessary 
information from social media posts, given that SGA social media posts are generally used to advertise 
events and other important media. In addition, this resolution also proposes that the Press Secretary 
release educational materials regarding how to use social media accessibility tools. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
This resolution was drafted in consultation with the Press Secretary, as well as the current Student Life 
Chair. In addition, this resolution was sent to the Senate President for review. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution would follow up the codification of accessibility features being used on SGA-affiliated 
posts with a statement that educational materials will be released relating to how to use these tools. It 
also ensures that the Press Secretary and Department of Communication are aware of this change and 
support it.

False or Malicious Charges: Allegations that knowingly, deliberately or recklessly mislead, or attempt to

Proposed Amendment: 
False or Malicious Charges: Allegations that knowingly, deliberately or recklessly with knowledge of their

filed for the purpose of harassing, intimidating, or gaining an unfair competitive advantage over the accused 
party. A complaint filed in good faith based on a reasonable interpretation of the facts and the Election Code

amendment raises the mental state requirement to actual knowledge of falsity, adds a purpose element, 
and creates an express safe harbor for good-faith complaints.

Explanation: 
We’ve reorganized the burden of proof requirements to give both the Supervisor of Elections and the Student 
Supreme Court clear guidelines as to how different Schedule violations should be treated. 
While having a “preponderance of evidence” for Schedule 4 violations as well as Schedule 1, 2, and 3 
violations may seem illogical, we have reasoning for this decision. Schedule 4 violations are generally done 
knowingly, and as such are covered up and relatively difficult to find evidence for. If the standard for Schedule 
4 violations were to be “clear and convincing evidence,” it would become very difficult to prove an 
individual/party’s guilt, which removes the purpose of a Schedule 4 violation. By keeping this at “a 
preponderance,” more discretion is given to both the Supreme Court, the Elections Commission, and the 
Supervisor of Elections. Moreover, keeping other Schedule violations at “a preponderance” makes sense 
because evidence for these violations is easily obtained via photographs and paper trail. 
It’s also important to note that by making the burden of proof for all Schedule violations a preponderance of 
evidence, it follows Florida Statutes regarding disciplinary proceedings (Title IX, Academic Honor Policy, 
etc.). 
Given the severity of Schedule 4 violations (immediate disqualification of an individual or party), further 
safeguards make sense; the Election Commission’s oversight provides further ability for Schedule 4 violations 
to remain at “a preponderance,” in addition to any disqualifications immediately being review by the Student 
Supreme Court. 
The striking of Clause (h) is done because it has been moved to an above section given that it is somewhat out 
of place here.

 Senate Bill #: 022 

 Primary Sponsor(s): Gurtis 
 Co-sponsor(s): Holliday 

Short Title: Free Rights in Elections & Expression Act 

Summary of Legislation: 
This bill goes through the entire Election Code (Chapter 7 of Student Statute) and changes current 
regulations pertaining to time, place, and manner restrictions. It opens up the campaigning period to be 
year-round, changes locational restrictions to reflect University policy, and changes current policies 
relating to posting materials, campaign finances, and free speech protections. 
 
Background Information: 
This legislation is needed because our current Election Code and the restrictions within it restrict 
expression rights that are protected by both the United States and Florida Constitutions. While the 
University can restrict certain forms of expression based on location and potential harm to others, they 
cannot restrict a specific form of free speech such as campaigning, as our Election Code does. 
 
Once it was found that our Election Code needed to change, other universities’ election codes and 
statutes were examined to see how they imposed election restrictions while also ensuring that students’ 
right to expression was protected. Universities such as the University of Alabama had similar problems 
of election code being too restrictive, so served as good framework to begin drafting our own changes. 
 
Once it was found that current time restrictions on campaigning would need to be removed, the 
question was raised of how this would impact campaign finances. This bill pertains almost entirely to 
free speech and expression rights, so including additional section to change campaign finances 
seemed extensive. There are plans to follow up this bill, should it be approved, with additional 
legislation that addresses the changes that need to be made to campaign finance expenditures. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
This bill was worked on extensively with Senate leadership and SG&A. The document went through 3 
separate drafts before eventually being proposed to University Admin, as well as General Counsel. 
From there a final draft was created and looked over by all parties, as well as the Student Body 
President. Party leadership was also contacted and notified of the legislation so that they are prepared 
for the changes being made to campaigning and other areas of the Election Code. 

 Page 24 of 37
 
Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
Should this legislation be approved, it will lift current campaign restrictions to allow for year-round 
campaigning. It also removes the locational ban of campaigning from dining halls, academic buildings, 
the Student Union, and libraries. It also adds additional free speech protections to ensure that students 
retain their right to expression and election violations pertaining to expression have set guidelines to be 
followed. It also changes rules related to the Spring Debate and Executive Question and Answer Event 
to set better guidelines to be followed by the Supervisor of Elections. 
 
Finally, this bill sets more narrow restrictions on expression. Any locational time, place, and manner 
restrictions are those that are already in place for all forms of speech by the University, such as posted 
quiet hours in residence halls and appropriate conduct in the Student Union. All relevant time, place, 
and manner restrictions are cited directly in the bill for easy access and can be updated by SG&A if and 
when these citations need to change.

162 Section 704.3 of the Florida State University Student Body Statutes, entitled “Political Parties” is hereby 
163 amended to read as follows: 

164 a. Any group of students may organize as a student political party and nominate candidates. 
165 b. The Supervisor of Elections shall officially recognize a political party no later than one (1) day prior to 
166 the filing deadline of an election when the party does all of the following: 
167 (1) Files with the Supervisor of Elections an accurate copy of its Constitution and an up-to-date 
168 list of Officers. 
169 (2) Nominates at least one candidate for office per year. 
170 (3) Files a party name, acronym, or logo that does not duplicate or blatantly resemble the name, 
171 acronym, or logo of any other existing FSU campus political party, nor utilizes the 
172 copyrighted image or symbol not authorized for use by the individual using the image or 
173 symbol, or any individual without their consent. Party names may not be vulgar or offensive 
174 contain the following: 

 Page 29 of 37
175 (A) Obscene material as defined by Florida Statute §847.001. 
176 (B) Content otherwise prohibited by the FSU RSO Handbook. 
177 The acceptance of names shall be at the discretion of the Supervisor of Elections, who shall 
178 inform the individual(s) who filed for the political party with the discarded name within forty-
179 eight (48) hours of receiving the filing. If a political party would like to appeal the decision of 
180 the Supervisor of Elections, they may file an appeal to the Elections Commission within three 
181 business days of being informed of the decision. 

182 (4) Is a Registered Student Organization with Student Organizations and Involvement. 
183 (5) Has not been disqualified in a past election within the previous four (4) years due to violations 
184 of the Election Code. 

185 Section 7. Amendment to Student Body Statutes Chapter 705.1, “General Elections”. 

186 Section 705.1 of the Florida State University Student Body Statutes, entitled “General Elections” is 
187 hereby amended to read as follows: 

188 a. All candidates in a general election shall declare their candidacy with the Supervisor of Elections no 
189 later than 4 p.m. Eastern Time on Monday, three (3) weeks before election day. 
190 b. General Elections shall take place on the eighth Monday and Tuesday of the semester in which they 
191 take place. In the case of a conflict or a religious holiday, the Supervisor of Elections shall determine 
192 the date of election day to be on a Monday and Tuesday between the sixth and eighth week of the 
193 semester. The Supervisor of Elections shall announce the date of election day no later than the third 
194 Wednesday of the semester. 
195 (1) The Supervisor of Elections shall notify the Student Body President, Vice President, Chief of 
196 Staff, Senate President, Senate Pro Tempore, COGS Speaker of the House and the SGA 
197 Advisor of the date and calendar of each General Election, no later than twenty-four (24) hours 
198 after deciding the date of any General Election. 
199 A. For the Fall General Election, the Supervisor of Elections shall notify the Student Body 
200 President, Student Senate President, COGS Speaker, the Chair of the Campus 
201 Recreation Board, and the SGA Advising Office of the date and seats up for election 
202 no later than twenty-four (24) hours after deciding the date of the Fall General Election. 
203 B. For the Spring General Election, the Supervisor of Elections shall notify the Student 
204 Body President, the Student Senate President, the Senior Class President, the Chair 
205 of the Union Board, and the SGA Advising Office of the date and seats up for election 
206 no later than twenty-four (24) hours after deciding the date of the Spring General 
207 Election. 
208 (2) Once the date of the election is determined, the Supervisor of Elections shall send the 
209 elections calendar to the SGA Webmaster to be published on the SGA website no later than 
210 twenty-four (24) hours after deciding the date of any General Election. 

 Page 30 of 37
211 c. Campaigning is prohibited prior to 12:00 a.m. Eastern Time on the Monday one week prior to 
212 the date of the elections. Nothing in this section shall be construed to prohibit any student from 
213 engaging in political speech, including the solicitation of support for or against any candidate, 
214 political party, or ballot item, at any time. 

215 Section 8. Amendment to Student Body Statutes Chapter 708.1, “Regulation of 
216 Campaign Material and Other Activities”. 

217 Section 708.1 of the Florida State University Student Body Statutes, entitled “Regulation of Campaign 
218 Material and Other Activities” is hereby amended to read as follows: 

219 Regulation of Campaign Material and Other Activities: 

220 a. Campaign materials may be placed in university owned academic buildings in places provided 
221 for general information such as billboards or community posting boards. Any marking of 
222 university property must be approved by the proper university authority or authorities. Any 
223 posting or placement of campaign materials must be consistent with applicable University 
224 regulations, which can be found at http://posting.fsu.edu or its successor website. 

225 b. Active campaigning by soliciting support from students is forbidden inside university academic 
226 buildings and residence halls. Campaigning in university academic buildings is subject to the 
227 same content-neutral time, place, and manner restrictions that apply to all other forms of student 
228 expression in those buildings, including applicable noise, posting, and space-reservation policies 
229 administered by the university. Campaigning in university residence hall common areas, 
230 including lobbies, community rooms, and shared social spaces, is subject to the same rules that 
231 govern all other forms of solicitation and student expression in those spaces, and is not 
232 permitted during posted quiet hours. Unsolicited door-to-door canvassing of individual residence 
233 hall rooms is prohibited during posted quiet hours. No restriction on campaigning in residence 
234 halls shall be applied in a manner that grants access to any university entity, student 
235 organization, or governing body while denying equivalent access to candidates or political 
236 parties. 

237 c. All material and activity located on FSU campuses shall be in accordance with rules and 
238 regulation of Campus Event Services, Union Posting Guidelines, University Housing Guidelines, 
239 the Student Conduct Code and any other relevant entities. 

240 d. There shall be no campaigning through the campus email system. 

241 (1) A student may not use FSU email servers to campaign for political office. This 
242 includes sending emails from their own FSU email or to another student’s FSU email. 

243 c. Campaign communications sent through the university email system are subject to the same 
244 acceptable-use policies that govern all other student use of university email, including any university 
245 policies prohibiting mass unsolicited electronic communications. Acceptable-use policies that govern 
246 student use of university email can be found at https://policies.vpfa.fsu.edu/policies-and-
247 procedures/technology/electronic-mail-policy or its successor website. No student shall be prohibited 
248 from sending campaign-related communications to individual recipients or to recipients who have 
249 opted to receive such communications solely because the content of the communication constitutes 
250 campaigning. 

251 d. Campaigning inside of university owned libraries, dining halls, and the Student Union is prohibited. 
252 Campaigning inside university-owned libraries is subject to the same noise and conduct policies that 
253 apply to all other activities in those facilities, which may be found at 
254 https://www.lib.fsu.edu/about/community-standards or its successor website. Campaigning in 
255 university dining halls and the Student Union is permitted and is subject to the same content-neutral 
256 space reservation, tabling, and posting policies that apply to all other student organizations and 
257 activities in those facilities. 

 Page 31 of 37
258 e. Students shall not be prohibited from wearing properly registered campaign clothing materials. 

259 (1) Within the Student Senate Chambers, candidates and designated party representatives 
260 who are formally presenting before the Student Senate shall be expected to not display or 
261 distribute campaign materials during their presentations. This restriction does not apply to 
262 attendees, observers, or candidates who are not actively presenting before the body, but 
263 these individuals are also expected to abide by the dress code, to the extent practicable, 
264 while in the Student Senate Chambers. 

265 Section 9. Amendment to Student Body Statutes Chapter 709.4, “Campaign 
266 Contributions”. 

267 Section 709.4 of the Florida State University Student Body Statutes, entitled “Campaign Contributions” is 
268 hereby amended to read as follows: 

269 a. Political parties and candidates must be able to account for all contributions. The contribution shall be 
270 a part of the campaign contribution statement and final expense statement and must detail which 
271 individual or organization donated the campaign contribution. Registered Student Organizations 
272 (RSO), excluding SGA political parties, and SGA entities are prohibited from donating to SGA political 
273 parties or candidates in any SGA election. 
274 (1) SGA entities — excluding political parties, Affiliated Projects and SGA Agencies — are 
275 prohibited from engaging in campaigning. No SGA entity may expend Activity and Service Fee 
276 funds, or funds derived from mandatory student fees, for the purpose of endorsing or opposing 
277 any candidate, political party, or ballot item. SGA entities shall be allowed to educate voters in 
278 a nonpartisan manner. Individual members, officers, and employees of SGA entities retain the 
279 right to engage in campaign financing in their personal capacity, using their personal resources 
280 and personal finances, regardless of their SGA affiliation. 
281 b. Campaign finance obligations, including spending caps, expense reporting requirements, and 
282 contribution disclosure requirements, shall apply to expenditures and contributions made on or after 
283 12:00 a.m. Eastern Time on the Monday one week prior to the date of the elections. 
284 c. In cases where campaign materials are sold (i.e. shirts, cups, etc.) to raise funds for a political party 
285 or candidate, individual records must be kept in accordance with Section 709(4)(a). Regardless of 
286 profit or involvement of campaign goods, anytime “Membership” is extended in return for dues or fees, 
287 the donating individual or organization must be recorded. 
288 d. No money may be accepted by a campus political party or candidate from a 501(c)(4) organization as 
289 defined by Title 26 of the U.S. Internal Revenue Code. 
290 e. The campaign contribution limit of individual or organizational donors to a candidate or party shall be 
291 established as $200 per election cycle. 
292 (1) Party-candidate membership dues submitted by an individual shall not exceed the campaign 
293 expense limits of the position the candidate is running for. 
294 f. If an individual is donating as a proxy for someone who donated via a money transfer service such as 
295 Venmo, Zelle, CashApp, etc., receipts must be provided of the entire exchange. 
296 g. If an individual is donating as a proxy for an organization, the entirety of the exchange should be 
297 documented. 

298 Section 10. Amendment to Student Body Statutes Chapter 710.4, “Reporting 
299 Procedure”. 

300 Section 710.4 of the Florida State University Student Body Statutes, entitled “Reporting Procedures” is 
301 hereby amended to read as follows: 

302 Reporting Procedures: 

303 a. All alleged violations shall be brought to the Supervisor of Elections in accordance with Section 
304 703(2) of the Student Body Election Code, and must include: 
305 (1) The name of the party or individual alleging the violation; 
306 (2) The name of the party or individual who allegedly violated the Elections Code; 

 Page 32 of 37
307 (3) The specific statute(s) in the Elections Code which was allegedly violated; 
308 (4) Any and all evidence to support the claim of an alleged violation; and 
309 (5) A short and plain statement describing the occurrence of the alleged violation. 
310 b. When an alleged violation is filed against an individual candidate, independent candidate, 
311 political party, or a member of a political party, the Supervisor of Elections shall notify the 
312 recipient(s) and listed witnesses of the alleged violation within twenty-four (24) hours after 
313 receiving the alleged violation. 
314 c. All students will have the option to present their case directly to the elections commission, 
315 choose a third-party to represent them, or be appointed a law student by the Supreme Court 
316 to represent their case before the Elections Commission. 
317 d. The Supervisor of Elections and Deputy Supervisor(s) shall have the power to receive and 
318 review alleged violations. The time, place, and manner of such violations shall be recorded 
319 and submitted to the Elections Commission. 
320 e. All alleged violations and appeals must be presented to the Supervisor of Elections 
321 electronically by the end of two (2) business days from their discovery. 
322 (1) Any complaint that lists an alleged violation after two (2) business days from its original 
323 discovery shall be dismissed by the Supervisor of Elections. 
324 f. The final deadline for all alleged violations and appeals to be filed by an individual or political 
325 party for a particular election is forty-eight (48) hours following the close of polls from an 
326 election, unless it alleges a failure to submit a complete or rectified final expense statement. 
327 (1) If an alleged violation is submitted less than twenty-four (24) hours before the deadline 
328 to submit alleged violations, the Supervisor of Elections shall be allowed to notify 
329 individuals of an alleged violation after the close of the filing deadline. 
330 (2) The final deadline for an alleged violation and appeal to be filed by an individual or 
331 political party alleging a failure to submit a complete or rectified final expense 
332 statement is the Wednesday following an election by 4 p.m. 
333 g. The burden that a party alleging a violation of the Student Body Election Code must meet in 
334 order to prove a violation shall be by “clear and convincing evidence”. Burden of Proof 
335 (1) The burden of proving an alleged violation of the Student Body Election Code shall 
336 rest at all times with the petitioner. 
337 (2) The applicable standard of proof for all alleged Election Code violations shall be a 
338 “preponderance of the evidence,” meaning that the existence of a fact is more likely 
339 true than not true. 
340 (3) Procedural Protections for Schedule 4 Findings 
341 (A) A finding of responsibility for any Schedule 4 violation shall require the 
342 affirmative vote of no fewer than two-thirds (2/3) of the members of the 
343 Elections Commission present and voting. 
344 (B) Any disqualification imposed on the basis of a Schedule 4 violation shall be 
345 subject to automatic review by the Student Supreme Court, regardless of 
346 whether the respondent files an appeal under Chapter 711. 
347 (4) Failure to satisfy the applicable burden shall result in dismissal of the alleged violation 
348 with prejudice for the current election cycle. 
349 h. Students shall not be prohibited from properly registered campaign materials which are 
350 clothing, except in the Student Senate Chambers. 
351 (1) Wearing clothing which is a campaign material is strictly prohibited in the Student 
352 Senate Chambers. The only exception to this rule is when the results of an election 
353 are read aloud to the Senate by the Supervisor of Elections on the day of an election. 

354 Section 11. Amendment to Student Body Statutes Chapter 710.5, “Implementation of 
355 Violations”. 

356 Section 710.5 of the Florida State University Student Body Statutes, entitled “Implementation of 
357 Violations” is hereby amended to read as follows: 

358 Implementation of Violations: 

 Page 33 of 37
359 a. Each occurrence, event, or time that violates the Election Code shall constitute an alleged Election 
360 violation that must be heard by the Elections Commission. Violations do not count against a candidate 
361 or political party until ruled upon by the Elections Commission. 
362 (1) In the event that a party found to be responsible by the Elections Commission appeals to the 
363 Student Supreme Court, the violation will not be counted until the Supreme Court issues their 
364 ruling. 
365 b. Disqualification shall occur according to the following provisions: 
366 (1) Party Disqualification: 
367 a. A political party that has either been found guilty of a schedule 4 violation or has 
368 accumulated twenty-five (25) or more penalty points during a single election cycle shall 
369 be disqualified. A candidate or individual that has either been found guilty of a schedule 
370 4 violation or has accumulated fifteen (15) or more penalty points during a single 
371 elction election cycle shall be disqualified. 
372 b. In the case that a political party is disqualified, all candidates running in that election 
373 with that party shall become disqualified. Any candidate disqualified shall be barred 
374 from running for an elected office or being a member of a political party for one (1) 
375 election cycle following their disqualification. 
376 c. The disqualified political party is barred from participating in future elections for a 
377 period of four (4) years. 
378 d. All party officers and members of the party leadership board shall be barred from 
379 participating in student government elections as members of political parties or running 
380 for office for one (1) election cycle following their disqualification. 
381 (2) Winning Candidate Disqualification: 
382 a. If a candidate who won an election is then disqualified, the Supervisor of Elections 
383 shall call a Special Election pursuant to Student Body Statute Section 705(2) for the 
384 office won by the disqualified candidate. 
385 (3) Individual Disqualification: 
386 a. In the event of an individual disqualification, the candidate or individual is barred from 
387 running in an election, or participating in any political party, or advocating/campaigning 
388 for individual candidates, political parties, or ballot items for one (1) election cycle 
389 following their disqualification. 
390 (4) Special Election After Disqualification: 
391 a. If there is a special election following disqualification of a candidate or political party, 
392 the following rules will be obeyed: 
393 (1) Inability to use the political party’s name or logo on campaign materials and 
394 during campaigning. 
395 (2) Inability to use the party funds. 
396 (3) A disqualified political party cannot endorse a candidate or candidates. 
397 c. When an Election violation is alleged against a party as opposed to an individual, naming the party as 
398 the respondent, it must meet one or more of the following standards: 
399 (1) The violation is perpetrated by any person acting as an officer of a party. 
400 (2) The violation involved the collaboration of more than one member of the same party. 
401 (3) The violation is in a series of violations which constitute a systematic attempt by a party to 
402 violate the Elections Code. 
403 (4) The violation is part of a clear pattern of violations perpetrated by individuals internal to a party 
404 which represent systemic ignorance of the Elections Code. 

405 Section 12. Amendment to Student Body Statutes Chapter 710.6, “Violations of the 
406 Code”. 

407 Section 710.6 of the Florida State University Student Body Statutes, entitled “Violations of the Code” is 
408 hereby amended to read as follows: 

409 a. No violations will contest or come into contradiction with Section 710(4). 
410 b. If a candidate or political party is accused of any election violation and does not challenge the validity 
411 of the allegation, they may be eligible for a reduced punishment in exchange for an admission of guilt 
412 to the Elections Commission. 

 Page 34 of 37
413 (1) This section shall not apply if an individual, candidate, or political party is accused of 
414 a Schedule 3 Violation or Schedule 4 Violation. 
415 (2) After admitting guilt to the Elections Commission, a respondent or petitioner cannot 
416 appeal the alleged violation to the Supreme Court. 
417 (3) The vice-chair of the Commission shall move to approve reduced punishments by 
418 acclimation unless any member of the Elections Commission objects. If an objection 
419 is raised, the reduced punishment must be approved by a majority vote of no less than 
420 quorum. 
421 (4) An individual, candidate, or political party may have up to three (3) punishments 
422 reduced per election cycle. Reduced punishments eliminate all points associated with 
423 a violation. 

424 c. Schedule one (1) Violations of this Code shall be assigned as follows: 
425 (1) Removing, obscuring, or damaging another candidate’s or political party’s campaign 
426 materials within a given space such as a bulletin board or general flyer area. 
427 (2) Engaging in any action against Chapter 709 of the Student Body Election code, 
428 including but not limited to violations of university posting guidelines. 
429 (3) Using campaign materials which fail to comply with University regulations, building 
430 regulations, or fail to comply with such regulations in academic classrooms. 
431 (4) Having posted campaign flyers in an academic building or classroom. Posting 
432 campaign materials in a manner that violates applicable university posting policies, 
433 including but not limited to policies administered by Campus Event Services, Facilities, 
434 or University Housing. 
435 (5) Failing to remove campaign materials within thirty-six (36) hours of the closing of the 
436 polls, and campaign materials from previous election cycles that have failed to be 
437 removed. 
438 (6) Submitting an incomplete Final Expense Statement, consistent with Section 709(2)(f). 
439 A. If an allegation of an incomplete final expense statement is made, the 
440 recipient shall have until the Tuesday following the election by 4 p.m. Eastern 
441 Time to correct any issues with the document. If all issues are not corrected 
442 by the following Tuesday at 4 p.m. Eastern Time this violation will turn into a 
443 Schedule 4 Violation. 
444 d. Schedule two (2) Violations of this Code shall be assigned as follows: 
445 (1) Bringing false or malicious charges against another candidate, political party, or 
446 political member. 
447 (2) Posting, utilizing, or distributing, either electronically or physically, campaign material 
448 that is publicly defamatory against a candidate for an elected office of the student body, 
449 or is defamatory against any person or entity within the content of a campaign material. 
450 Posting, utilizing, or distributing, either electronically or physically, campaign material 
451 containing a provably false statement of fact concerning an identified person, made 
452 with knowledge of its falsity or with reckless disregard for whether it was true or false, 
453 that causes demonstrable reputational harm. Statements of opinion, political rhetoric, 
454 satire, parody, hyperbole, and commentary on candidates' public records and policy 
455 positions do not constitute violations of this section. 
456 A. This shall apply to political party’s executive board members, candidates, 
457 and/or dues-paying members in the current semester. 
458 (3) Defacing or damaging official election materials created and distributed by the 
459 Supervisor or Elections. 
460 (4) Campaigning prior to one (1) week before the election. 
461 (5) Performing an activity that would intentionally place another party or candidate in 
462 violation of the election code. Deliberately fabricating or manipulating evidence, 
463 communications, or circumstances with the specific intent to cause another party or 
464 candidate to be charged with or found responsible for a violation of this Code that the 
465 party or candidate would not otherwise have committed. 
466 (6) Using the past and/or present SGA logo on campaign items. 
467 (7) Utilizing any Student Government owned equipment for express endorsement or 
468 support for or against any candidate, platform, political party, or ballot item. 

 Page 35 of 37
469 (8) Campaigning physically or electronically using the funds or official institutional 
470 resources, platforms, or authority of an SGA entity. which is not a political party, 
471 Affiliated Project, or Agency. 
472 e. Schedule three (3) Violations of this Code shall be assigned as follows: 
473 (1) Vandalism or any unauthorized marking of university or private property for campaign 
474 purposes. 
475 (2) Falsely representing oneself on behalf of the Supervisor of Elections or the SGA Office 
476 of Elections. 
477 (3) Engaging in any action against Chapter 709 of the Election Code. 
478 (4) Failing to appear at any elections commission hearing if listed as a petitioner without 
479 giving prior notice to the Supervisor of Elections, five (5) hours prior to the Elections 
480 Commission hearing, of inability to appear 
481 f. Schedule four (4) Violations of this Code shall be assigned as follows: 
482 (1) Submitting a fraudulent final expense statement. This includes parties or individuals 
483 failing to submit a complete final expense statement by the Tuesday following the 
484 election at 4 p.m. Eastern Time. 
485 A. This is an allegation that can only be made by the Supervisor of Elections 
486 and/or the Deputy Supervisors of Elections. 
487 (2) Providing another individual or group with or receiving personal login information (FSU 
488 ID and password) in which they use to cast votes for another person. These votes shall 
489 be considered fraudulent. 
490 (3) Any attempt to perpetrate a fraudulent election. This shall include, but is not limited to, 
491 providing false information regarding filing or elections procedures, voting more than 
492 once, or attempting to vote with another person’s student identification (FSU ID). 
493 (4) Offering money, gift cards, or other forms of payment in exchange for votes in any 
494 election. 
495 (5) Offering goods or services in exchange for votes, not including campaign materials as 
496 specified in Chapter 701 of the Election Code. 

497 Section 13. Effective Date. 

498 The provisions of this bill shall take effect upon signature of the Vice President for Student Affairs.

Land Acknowledgement 
The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is 
located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can.

Summary of Legislation: 
This bill would recommend that the Executive Branch to initiate a public information campaign about 
proper e-scooter/bike operation. The Senate additionally requests the Executive Branch cooperate with 
the marketing department to create a video detailing many safety precautions drivers of e-
scooters/bikes should undertake. Finally, the Senate initiates willingness to support with funds should 
the project require it. 
 
Background Information: 
Administration wishes to see tangible steps on increasing pedestrian safety on campus, prior to 
pursuing previously intended investments in electric scooter infrastructure by the SGA across campus. 
This is one of many avenues that the Senate may take to increase pedestrian safety on campus, by 
uniting campus partners to educate the population. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Outreach included the VP of Finance, TAPS Director Richard Rind, and SGA Advisor Andy Johnson.

This resolution would encourage the Executive Branch to initiate a public information campaign, ideally 
leading to enhanced student safety with e-scooters/bikes.

Short Title: The “Better Ed” Bill of 2026 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This bill alters Chapter 207 of the Student Body Statutes to address shortfalls found in current training 
requirements throughout SGA. Additionally, this bill codifies transition documents, ensuring a smooth 
transfer of power and preventing information deficits. Lastly, this bill seeks to revitalize the Professional 
Development opportunities that are available for the SGA space, creating a comprehensive list of local, 
state, and national events that are accessible for FSU students. 
 
Background Information: 
Previously, Chapter 207 had loose guidelines for the expectations and responsibilities for SGA entity 
leaders for the trainings given to its members. Due to the lack of oversight and accountability, this 
expectation was not uniformly applied, resulting in a patchwork of training provided across the SGA 
space. This bill seeks to close that gap, while still respecting autonomy and nuances within each entity. 
While on the mission of filling gaps, the gap of information that newly elected leadership receives from 
their predecessor is solely dependent on that person’s willingness to cultivate a strong relationship with 
them. We seek to codify the practice that all elected leaders should follow; assisting those who will 
come after them. Lastly, the Professional Development clause in Chapter 207 is underutilized in the 
status quo, which harms the SGA’s ability to produce well-rounded leaders throughout their time at 
FSU. By reimagining what Professional Development can look like in the SGA space, we ensure that 
this Senate, and the student body, continue to progress into the future. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Senate President, Senate President Pro Tempore, Office of Student Governance and Advocacy, 
Student Body President, Student Body Treasurer, Chief Justice of the Student Supreme Court, Chair of 
the Union Board, Chair of the Campus Recreation Board, Class Council Presidents, Speaker of the 
Congress of Graduate Students, Directors of Affiliated Projects, Funding Board Chairs, Student Body 
Vice President, Student Body Attorney General, Senate Standing Committee Leadership, Senate 
College Delegation Leadership, Executive Institute Directors, Homecoming Director. 

 Page 12 of 15
Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation would reorganize the list and requirements for SGA entities regarding training. It would 
create a requirement for transition documents to be gathered, kept, and transferred through the Office 
of Student Governance and Advocacy after new leadership assumes office. It specifies requirements, 
outside of New Senate Orientation, for Committee Leadership and College Delegation Leadership 
training. It creates a mechanism for compliance through the Office of Student Governance and 
Advocacy. It creates a running document, managed by an administrative officer within the Office of the 
Student Body President, to inform SGA officeholders of on-campus, local, state, and national 
opportunities for professional and leadership development.

About the organization: 
The Iranian Student Association at Florida State University aims to enrich the campus community 
with Iranian culture, traditions, and heritage. A wide range of events and activities are organized 
by the association to educate and create a sense of community among Iranian students and those 
interested in Iranian culture. The Iranian Student Association has seen significant growth recently, 
with their Facebook membership increasing from 200 to 500 and Instagram followers growing 
from 89 to 297. This surge of interest demonstrates a desire among students to engage with Iranian 
culture and become part of the community. The overarching goal of this Association is to foster 
cross-cultural connections and understanding between diverse groups at the university. 
 Purpose & Description of the Tirgan Festival (Jashn-e Tirgan): 
Tirgan, an ancient Iranian festival, is celebrated in honor of Tishtrya, the deity of rain, and marks 
the mid-summer season in the Iranian calendar. This vibrant celebration occurs in the month of Tir 
(June or July), symbolizing gratitude for water and the blessings of nature, highlighting themes of 
renewal, hope, and joy. With roots tracing back to Zoroastrianism, Tirgan is one of the oldest and 
most cherished festivals celebrated by Iranians and many others around the world. 
The Tirgan Festival (Jashn-e Tirgan) aims to: 
 Educate: Provide insights into the history, significance, and rituals associated with Tirgan, 
 promoting a deeper understanding of this ancient celebration. 
 Unite: Bring together students, faculty, staff, and the broader Tallahassee community to foster 
 cultural exchange and mutual respect. 
 Build Community: Strengthen the sense of community among Iranian students and those 
 interested in Iranian culture through shared experiences and celebrations. 
 Celebrate Key Themes: Focus on themes of gratitude, renewal, and the joy of life, which are 
 central to the spirit of Tirgan. 
 The Tirgan Festival (Jashn-e Tirgan) is more than just an event; it’s an immersive experience into 
 the culture that has celebrated this mid-summer festival for thousands of years. Central to Tirgan 
is the tradition of tying colored bands on wrists, symbolizing wishes for prosperity and happiness. 
Participants also engage in water splashing, a playful and symbolic act representing the 
 purification and renewal of the soul. Our goal is to create a space that not only showcases the 
 tradition of Tirgan but also spreads its messages of gratitude, renewal, and community. 
 Advertisement: 
We will advertise this event via various channels, including our Facebook page, Instagram account, 
 and our Telegram channel and group, to ensure widespread awareness and participation. 
 Funding Request: 

 We kindly request a fund of $1100.43 to support the Tirgan Festival (Jashn-e Tirgan) organized by 
the FSU Iranian Student Association. The funds will be used to cover expenses such as food for 
 the participants and disposable glasses for the water-pouring activity. These elements are integral 
to the cultural experience and enjoyment of the festival. 
The Tirgan Festival (Jashn-e Tirgan) is a significant cultural event that not only celebrates Iran's 
heritage but also fosters inclusivity, diversity, and cross-cultural understanding within the Florida 
State University community. Your generous contribution will help us create an unforgettable 
experience that promotes cultural appreciation and enriches the university's multicultural 
environment. 
We appreciate your consideration and support. Please let us know if you need any additional 
information.

Short Title: Declaring the Senate’s Intent for an Electric Scooter Certificate Program 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This legislation will declare the Senate’s official intent to pursue an Electric Scooter Certificate Program 
with FSUPD. The Resolution details exactly what the Senate wishes to see of the program, and states 
the Senate’s intent of supporting the project with a contribution of free u-lock bike locks for graduates of 
the program. 
 
Background Information: 
Administration wishes to see tangible steps on increasing pedestrian safety on campus, prior to 
pursuing previously intended investments in electric scooter infrastructure by the SGA across campus. 
This is one of many avenues that the Senate may take to increase pedestrian safety on campus, by 
uniting campus partners to educate the population. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Initial project ideas were passed by the VP of Finance, Kyle Clark. Senate Advisor Andy Johnson was 
also consulted in regards to the project. TAPS Director Richard Rind additionally supports this 
measure. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution would give the authority to the Sponsors to speak with FSUPD on behalf of the Senate 
for an official certificate program they wish to be implemented, and measure the ability of such a 
program to be implemented.

Short Title: Update to Statutory Subdivision 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This bill amends Chapter 100.3 of Student Statute, which addresses the formatting of subdivisions 
within Statute. This bill intends to give a better example of what subdivision within Statute should look 
like, as well as change our current formatting to better reflect that of the Florida legislature. 
 
Background Information: 
With the current language, our Student Statute’s subdivisions go against this statute, and all of our 
current legislature is improperly formatted. In addition, the language used in this clause makes it difficult 
to understand how formatting should be done, making the process of drafting legislation more difficult 
for newer Senators. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
This legislation was drafted in consultation with the Senate President. Given that the primary 
stakeholders for this legislation will be Senators, having input from their primary representative was 
crucial. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If enacted by the Student Senate, this bill will amend Student Statute to reflect a better example of how 
subdivisions should be formatted, providing clearer guidelines to new Senators regarding how they 
should format their drafted legislation. Moreover, this change would allow our Student Statutes to better 
reflect the current formatting adopted by the Florida Legislature, which our Student Statutes are 
modeled after.

Short Title: Encouraging a Pedestrian/Scooter Safety Campaign 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This bill would recommend that the Executive Branch to initiate a public information campaign about 
proper e-scooter/bike operation. The Senate additionally requests the Executive Branch cooperate with 
the marketing department to create a video detailing many safety precautions drivers of e-
scooters/bikes should undertake. Finally, the Senate initiates willingness to support with funds should 
the project require it. 
 
Background Information: 
Administration wishes to see tangible steps on increasing pedestrian safety on campus, prior to 
pursuing previously intended investments in electric scooter infrastructure by the SGA across campus. 
This is one of many avenues that the Senate may take to increase pedestrian safety on campus, by 
uniting campus partners to educate the population. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Outreach included the VP of Finance, TAPS Director Richard Rind, and SGA Advisor Andy Johnson. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution would encourage the Executive Branch to initiate a public information campaign, ideally 
leading to enhanced student safety with e-scooters/bikes.

Senate’s standard practice for debate is.

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This would amend the Finance Committee’s rules of procedure for more efficient operation.

 A RESOLUTION 
 The I.D.E.A. Act (Integrity of Delegation Elections Act) 

WHEREAS, Rule 16 of the Senate Rules of Procedure defines College Delegations, including their 
structure and election process as adopted by the Florida State University Student Government 
Association; and 
 
WHEREAS, College Delegation elections serve as the bridge between delegation members, their 
subsequent leadership, and the college they represent; and 
 
WHEREAS, It is critical each duly elected Senator to this Student Government Association Senate can 
make their vote heard in the makeup of College Delegation leadership; and 
 
WHEREAS, Allowing leadership elections to occur in line with Committee Leadership elections allows 
for a more streamlined process that both increases representation and decreases time between 
inauguration and Delegation elections ; and 
 
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED by the 78th Student Senate at Florida State University that: 
Rule 16 of the Senate Rules and Procedure entitled “College Delegations” is hereby amended and shall 
read as follows; 
 
RULE SIXTEEN – College Delegations 

 1. A College Delegation shall consist of all Senators elected from the same academic college or unit 
 as defined by Student Body Statutes and Senate apportionment. 
 a. Each Delegation shall be recognized as a formal body within the Student Senate for 
 purposes of coordination, representation, and constituency outreach. 
 b. Meetings of College Delegations shall be required to be compliant with Chapter 203 and 
 Chapter 210. 
 c. Each College Delegation is required to meet at least once per semester. 
 (1) Absences to College Delegation meetings shall be recorded according to Rule 13. 
 2. Elections of College Delegation Leadership: 

 Page 1 of 3 

 Page 3 of 16
 a. After the ratification of the Senate President and Senate President Pro-Tempore, College 
 Delegations shall convene to elect from among its members a Delegation Chair pursuant 
 to Standing Committee elections in Rule 5.5. 
 b. Election shall be by simple majority of the Delegation members present. 
 c. Standing Committee Chairs shall be ineligible to serve as Delegation Chairs. 
 (1) This clause shall not be in effect if a Standing Committee Chair is a Senator within 
 a college of two Senators or less. 
 (2) When a college is apportioned only one Senate seat, the senator shall be required 
 to submit at least one instance of correspondence with their college’s 
 administration to the Student Senate President and Student Senate President Pro-
 Tempore. 
 1. They are not subject to fulfill the duties outlined in Rule 16.3 or Rule 16.5. 
 (3) In colleges apportioned two Senate seats, the most senior senator shall 
 automatically serve as Delegation Chair unless they submit via email their intent 
 to abdicate the role of Delegation Chair to the Student Senate President and 
 Student Senate President Pro-Tempore. 
 (4) In college apportioned two Senate seats, and both senators have the same amount 
 of tenure, then the Student Senate President has the right to appoint one of the 
 two senators as College Delegation Chair. 
 1. The other senator shall serve as the College Delegation Vice-Chair. 
 (5) The term of office for a Delegation Chair shall run concurrent with the session of 
 Senate in which they were elected. standing committee leadership, pursuant to 
 Rule 5.5, Senate Rules of Procedure. 
 1. Elections shall take place following Standing Committee elections, and 
 shall be performed during the same meeting of the Senate. 
 d. Delegation shall elect a Vice Chair to assist the Chair and serve in their absence. 
 (1) In colleges apportioned two Senate seats, the most Junior Senator shall 
 automatically serve as Delegation Vice Chair, unless the most senior senator 
 abdicates Delegation Chair to the most Junior Senator. In this instance, a College 
 Delegation Vice-Chair shall not be required. 
 e. The Student Senate President or a designee from the Office of the Student Senate 
 President or the Student Governance & Advocacy Office shall have the authority to 
 preside over Delegation Chair and Vice Chair elections. 
3. The Delegation Chair shall perform the following duties: 
 a. Represent the interests and concerns of their College Delegation before the Student 
 Senate as a whole. 
 b. Preside over College Delegation meetings. 
 c. Serve as the official liaison between the Student Senate and their academic college’s 
 Student Leadership Council, if such a body exists. 
 (1) If the Student Leadership Council does not exist, the College Delegation shall 
 serve as the official liaison to their College’s administration. 
 d. Organize and oversee the Delegation’s outreach initiatives to students in their college, 
 including (but not limited to): tabling events and email correspondence. 
 e. In the absence of the Chair, the Vice Chair shall assume all of the above duties. 
4. The Delegation Vice Chair shall perform the following duties: 
 a. Take minutes at College Delegation meetings. 
 (1) The deadline to submit minutes shall be pursuant to Rule 5.11. 
 b. Preside over Delegation meetings in the absence of the Delegation Chair. 
 c. Ensure that all members of the Delegation are notified of scheduled meetings and shall 
 monitor attendance of Delegation members. 
 d. Assist the Delegation Chair in coordinating outreach initiatives and constituency concerns 
 as directed. 
 e. In the absence of the Vice Chair, the Chair shall assume all of the above duties. 
5. Each College Delegation is encouraged to organize itself to address the needs of its constituency 
 and to coordinate the legislative agenda of its members. 

 Page 4 of 16
 a. Constituency Reports shall provide a comprehensive summary of Delegation activities, 
 including but not limited to: 
 (1) An overview of business addressed at College Delegation meetings. 
 (2) An overview of business addressed with the College Delegation’s respective

 1. This includes the list of recognized College Delegations and their
