Short Title: The I.D.E.A. Act (Integrity of Delegation Elections Act) 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution would amend Rule 16 of Senate Rules of Procedure to change College Delegation 
elections to match Committee Leadership elections. This ensures Senators who were previously unable 
to vote for College Delegation leadership now can represent their interests through the election 
process. 
Background Information: 
College Delegations were recently established to unite the members of a given college to collaborate 
on issues pertaining to their constituents. Currently, Rule 16.2 defines leadership elections for College 
Delegations as needing to be held yearly after the Fall inauguration. This is inconsistent with Standing 
Committee leadership elections, which occur after each Inauguration. The purpose of holding 
leadership elections after each inauguration, both Fall and Spring, ensures that every elected senator, 
even those sworn in in the spring, can cast a vote regarding their leadership. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
The Office of the Senate President, The Office of the Senate President Pro Tempore. 
 
Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution seeks to apply the same principles of representation to College Delegation leadership 
and clarifies the timeline in which College Delegation elections should occur. This will codify the 
process by which Delegation elections should take place, taking place after Standing Committee 
leadership elections.

Short Title: Amending Rules of Procedure to adjust Affiliated Project Review. 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This Resolution would amend Rule Six of Senate Rules of Procedure, adjusting Affiliated Project 
Review to match recommendations from Senate Advisors. This would include shifting the review 
process to the fall semester, granting more time for deliberations to be held, and establishing a four 
year staggered cycle in order to not overwhelm the committee. 
 
Background Information: 
Affiliated Project Review has been the responsibility of the Student Life Committee since the passing of 
the Affiliated Project Act of 1994. During the 77th Student Senate, this process was also codified in the 
Student Senate Rules of Procedure to ensure the continued process for future Student Life Leadership. 
However, the offices of Student Governance & Advocacy and Student Engagement have expressed 
concerns over the process coinciding with the budget cycle in the Spring Semester, and possible 
redundancy. Therefore, the process is being moved per their recommendations to the Fall. It was also 
under their recommendation that the process is being shifted to a staggered four year cycle, in order to 
have a broader view of the project in the long-term efficiency rather than the changes on a yearly basis. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Andy Johnson and Veronica Nelson, Student Senate President 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
The legislation would move Affiliated Project Review to the Fall Semester, grant more time for the 
Student Life Committee to visit the projects and host the deliberations, and establish four year cycle in 
which the projects would be reviewed in a staggered manner. It would also establish guidelines for the 
review of new Affiliated Projects.

Short Title: Amending Rule Ten, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Clarify Definitions and 
Streamline and Codify the Amendment Process 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution updates Rule Ten of the Senate Rules of Procedure to clarify definitions of 
legislative instruments and establish a structured, transparent, and uniform amendment 
process. The changes align Senate procedural rules with recently adopted statutory standards, 
improve clarity for Senators and the public, and enhance efficiency and predictability during 
floor consideration of measures. 

Background Information: 
Rule Ten governs the submission, consideration, and amendment of measures before the 
Student Senate. Prior to this amendment the procedures for submitting and considering 
amendments lacked sufficient structure. Clerks, and Senate Leadership, were often burdened 
with tracking down specific language for amendments, and Senators experienced confusion on 
how to properly amend bills given statutory and procedural requirments to submit amendments 
in writing. This resulted in confusion during debate, last-minute changes to legislation, and 
reduced transparency for both Senators and the public. To aid in clarity, and fix an 
administrative discrepancy with no clear outlet to submit amendments, this amendment helps 
to create an Amendment Form. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
This bill was drafted with direct input from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate Leadership, 
and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 
A special thanks is given to SGA Webmaster Ben Young, Senate Program Coordinator 
Veronica Nelson, the Senate President and Pro Tempore, Judiciary Committee Chair Leila 
Jackson, and the Senate Rules Committee for its invaluable input in making this measure the 
successful, clear, and concise solution it is. 

 Page 15 of 16
Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution codifies procedures for submitting amendments in advance of Senate meetings 
and on the Senate floor. Collectively, these changes improve legislative transparency, protect 
public notice, reduce administrative confusion, and ensure a more orderly and deliberative 
amendment process.

 Senate Bill #: 018 
 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Bigenho, Nucatola 
 Co-sponsor(s): Mendez Arrango, Tumuluri 

Short Title: Creating Chapter 511, The Office of Auditor General, for Consolidated Oversight 
and Review Improvements. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This bill creates Chapter 511 of the Student Body Statutes, establishing the Office of the 
Auditor General as an independent oversight entity within the Student Government 
Association. It outlines the structure, selection process, qualifications, term length, renewal 
procedures, removal standards, and vacancy procedures for the Auditor General and Deputy 
Auditors General. 
 
The bill establishes a five-member Auditor General Selection Board composed of the Student 
Body President, Student Senate President, Student Body Treasurer, Chief Justice of the 
Supreme Court, and Speaker of the Congress of Graduate Students. The selected nominee 
must be confirmed by a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the Student Senate. 
 
The legislation further defines the powers and duties of the Office, including auditing financial 
activity, reviewing compliance with statutory and fiscal regulations, maintaining anonymous 
reporting mechanisms, issuing public reports, ensuring non-retaliation for whistleblowers, and 
publishing findings. Additionally, the bill amends Chapter 100 to designate the Auditor General 
and Deputy Auditors General as major offices within Student Government. 

Background Information: 
The Florida State University Student Government Association manages significant Activity & 
Service (A&S) fee funds and oversees numerous executive departments, agencies, boards, 
and affiliated projects. While existing statutes establish financial procedures and transparency 
requirements—including the Sunshine Act (Chapter 203), the External Transparency and 
Digital Records Act (Chapter 210), and Title VIII: The Finance Code—there is currently no 
independent internal oversight body charged exclusively with auditing compliance, 
investigating violations, and safeguarding institutional accountability across all branches of 
Student Government. 
 
In light of the increasing complexity of Student Government operations and financial 
allocations, the establishment of a structurally independent Office of the Auditor General would 

 Page 5 of 12

strengthen transparency, deter misconduct, ensure adherence to appropriations and proviso 
language, and provide a formal mechanism for anonymous reporting and systematic review. 
Creating this office codifies a permanent, neutral oversight authority within Student 
Government. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with the direct input of the Student Body Treasurer and other members of 
the Student Body Treasurers Office and RSO Allocation Committee. It was also discussed with 
members of the Department of Student Affairs, and with contact to the Office of Audit and 
Advisory Services. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
Upon passage, this legislation formally establishes a new, independent Office of the Auditor 
General within Student Government, creating a centralized authority responsible for 
investigations, audits, compliance review, and financial oversight. The bill introduces structured 
appointment and confirmation procedures, conflict-of-interest safeguards for the Selection 
Board, defined qualifications for service, and clear standards for removal. 
 
The Office will gain administrative access to relevant record systems, require the preservation 
of documents under review, and mandate the publication of audit reports and semesterly 
summaries. It also creates statutory protections for anonymous reporting and whistleblower 
non-retaliation, while ensuring that audited officers retain the right to respond before the 
appropriate Senate committee. 
 
By amending Chapter 100 to classify the Auditor General and Deputies as major offices, the 
bill subjects these positions to the same accountability and ethical standards applicable to 
other high-level Student Government officials. Overall, the legislation strengthens institutional 
transparency, enhances fiscal accountability, and establishes an enduring internal oversight 
framework within the Student Government Association.

 Senate Proclamation #: 010

Short Title: Recognizing the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory for its Scientific Contributions, 
Educational Outreach, and Partnership with Florida State University 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This proclamation recognizes the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory (MagLab) for its leadership 
in scientific research, innovation, and education. It highlights the MagLab’s contributions to advancing 
scientific knowledge, supporting student involvement from universities all over the nation, and 
developing community outreach within nearby elementary schools and individuals interested in learning 
about their processes. Additionally, this proclamation expresses support for continued collaboration 
between Florida State University and the MagLab 
 
Background Information: 
The National High Magnetic Field Laboratory is the largest and most powerful magnet laboratory in the 
world. It serves as a place for research in fields such as physics, chemistry, materials science and 
engineering, The MagLab also provides students of all ages with opportunities to engage with scientific 
concepts, research and collaboration with scientists. 
 
Through its outreach, including tours, elementary school visits, and community events, the MagLab 
plays a vital role in promoting science and inspiring future generations of researchers and scientists. A 
recent visit by the Student Senate has further highlighted the impact of the MagLab on the university 
community and the entire nation. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
This proclamation was developed in consultation with Student Senate members who attended the 
scheduled MagLab tour, students involved in research at the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory 
and a representative at the MagLab who guided the Senate tour. Additional information was gathered 
from public information posted on the MagLab website regarding their initiatives, mission, and research 
impact. 
Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If adopted, this proclamation will formally recognize the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory for its 
contributions to Florida State University and the scientific community. It will also demonstrate the 
Student Senate’s support for continued collaboration, student engagement, and outreach with the 
MagLab.

Land Acknowledgement 
The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is 
located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can.

located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can.

Short Title: Organizational Session Election Procedure Reform Act 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution would amend Rule 1,1.5 of Senate Rules and Procedures to adapt changes to how the 
Senate Conducts the Organizational Session by streamlining the nominations process to require only 
one second, eliminating con debate to improve efficiency, and permitting nominators to ask questions 
during candidate questioning. These amendments are to streamline the process of electing Senate 
Leadership and mirror the procedures of committee elections. 
 
Background Information: 
The Organizational Session is a critical meeting held at the start of each Senate term to elect the 
Student Senate President and President Pro Tempore and establish the body’s leadership structure. 
This process is governed by the Senate Rules and Procedures and is intended to ensure fairness, 
transparency, and orderly conduct. However, given that the Senate has only conducted one 
Organizational Session under the current framework, and that experience revealed procedural 
inefficiencies and challenges, there is a clear need to refine aspects of the process, particularly 
nomination requirements, debate structure, and questioning limitations, to better support an effective 
and functional election. 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
This resolution was drafted with the input of Advisor Andy Johnson. 
 
Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution will reduce the number of required seconds for nominations, eliminates the con debate 
portion of candidate evaluation, and permits nominators to ask questions during the questioning period. 
Collectively, these changes streamline the election process, remove unnecessary procedural barriers, 
and promote a more efficient, accessible, and effective Organizational Session while maintaining 
fairness and transparency.

Short Title: Amending Rule 9, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Fix the Implementation of 
Robert’s Rules of Order and Adding a Table to Reference Vote Totals and Thresholds. 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This legislation would amend Rule 9 of the Senate’s ROP to clean up the implementation of Robert’s 
Rules of Order Newly Revised, ensure there is a clear, in text, definition of governing documents and 
supremacy clauses, and creates a table to reference vote thresholds, totals, and other important pieces 
of information. We include this in Rule 9 because of its already existing title, Governing Authority, which 
we amend to fully read “Outlined Vote Thresholds and Governing Authority”, this properly captures 
what we are trying to do with this Resolution. To the table itself, we outline most of the in-statute 
requirements for different thresholds of voting, with descriptions attached and statute references 
attached as well, and place a mandate on the Senate to constantly update this table with any new vote 
thresholds. 
 
Background Information: 
Over the history of the Senates’ existence, different thresholds have been sprinkled into the Statutes. 
Three Fourths to amend Chapter 210, two thirds to impeach, majority vote to confirm, these are 
outlined in statutes not in ROP. The point of this legislation, is to make the job of a Senator easier, in 
history to prepare for Senate meetings the Parliamentarian, Senate Officers and Senators themselves 
were forced to find the appropriate title being amended, the statute they found relevant to this, or some 
other case before they could feel confident in voting and before it could be a legal vote. This table 
would provide an easy reference for the Senators. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Senate President Alexia Holliday, Senate Parliamentarian Simon Monteleone, Senators in the 
Governing Documents Working Group, Senate Advisor Veronica, and the Senate Officers team. 
 
Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
Reduce time spent by Senators attempting to cross reference information and understand vote 
thresholds for each vote, along with adding clarity to the Senates operating procedures in regard to 
which laws are applicable over the other.

 Co-sponsor(s): Ferris, Tumuluri 

Short Title: RSOAC Reforms to Chapter 816 “RSO Allocation Committee’ 
 
Summary of Legislation: 
This bill amends Chapter 816 of the Student Body Statutes to restructure and clarify the operations of 
the Registered Student Organization Allocation Committee (RSOAC). It revises committee composition, 
establishes clearer procedures for funding requests, and strengthens accountability measures for both 
committee members and student organizations. Additionally, it updates funding limits, eligibility 
requirements, and operational guidelines to improve efficiency and transparency. 
 
Background Information: 
The RSO Allocation Committee (RSOAC) plays a critical role in distributing Student Activity & Service 
Fee funding to Registered Student Organizations (RSOs). However, inconsistencies in structure, 
unclear procedures, and gaps in accountability have created inefficiencies in the funding process. This 
legislation is introduced to modernize and standardize RSOAC operations, ensuring fair access to 
funding while maintaining compliance with university policies and state regulations. 
 
The bill also responds to the growing demand for RSO funding and the need for clearer guidelines 
regarding eligibility, attendance requirements, and funding caps. By refining these processes, the 
legislation aims to better support student organizations while safeguarding responsible allocation of 
student funds. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
 - RSOAC Leadership (Chair and Vice Chair Ashley Wong and Ammiel Bowen) 
 - Senate Leadership (Senate President Alexia Holliday) 
 - Former RSOAC Leadership (Chair and Vice Chair Vince Nucatola and Caden Vandermeulen) 
 - SGA Accounting Head (Laurel McKinley) 
 - Incoming and Exiting Student Body Treasurer (Erica Wyatt and Maddox Goodman) 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If enacted, this bill will significantly restructure the RSOAC by adjusting its membership composition 
and formalizing leadership roles and responsibilities. It introduces stricter attendance and accountability 
policies for committee members and establishes clearer timelines and procedures for funding requests 
and approvals. 

 Page 16 of 25

The legislation also refines funding guidelines, including eligibility criteria, funding caps, and 
restrictions, ensuring that allocations benefit the broader student body. Overall, the bill improves 
transparency, consistency, and efficiency in the RSO funding process.

112 (1) An absence means failure to attend a noticed meeting of the RSOAC.

195 A. All organizations applying for funding must be currently registered with the Office of

198 B. An RSO must have received funding via the RSO Development Fund (Chapter 817,

201 C. Student organizations may not receive funding from the RSO Allocation Committee if they

205 D. Student organizations are limited to three funding requests from the RSO Allocation 
206 Committee per fiscal year. 
207 7. Funding Guidelines and Restrictions 
208 A. All requests must be for eligible uses of Student Activity & Service Fee revenues, as 
209 provided in the SGA Financial Manual. 
210 B. The Student Body Treasurer shall coordinate with the Department of Student Engagement 
211 to establish an online system for submitting funding requests. 
212 C. Funding requests shall generally be required to include a description of the intended use 
213 of funds and why the requested funding is needed. Student organizations shall be required 
214 to provide an estimate of the number of FSU students that are likely to attend an event or 
215 travel opportunity funded by SGA. 
216 D. Pursuant to §1009.24, Florida Statutes, SGA funding may only be used to benefit the 
217 student body in general. As such, funding from the RSO Allocation Committee may not 
218 benefit activities for which an admission fee is charged to students. Further, student 
219 organizations that charge membership fees may not exclude any student from 
220 participation in any events or programs funded by SGA as a result of a student’s inability 
221 to pay such fees. 
222 E. Funds may not be used to cover membership dues or fees associated with a student’s or 
223 organization’s national or international affiliations. 
224 F. The committee shall not recommend funding for events or programs that are likely to have 
225 only group members attend and/or have no general benefit to the student body. 
226 G. The committee shall not recommend funding for events that are exclusive to a club or 
227 organization’s executive board. 
228 H. Requests for clothing may only be approved once per fiscal year. Any clothing funded by 
229 SGA must directly promote the student organization. 
230 I. Organizations seeking funding for service trips must first demonstrate that they made a 
231 good-faith effort to participate in an open or public service opportunity offered by the 
232 Center for Leadership and Service, if such an opportunity was available. If participation in 
233 such a trip was not feasible due to scheduling, availability, or capacity, the organization 
234 may pursue independent service trip funding through the RSO Allocation Committee. In 
235 such cases, documentation of the organization’s outreach to CLS and explanation of why 
236 participation in a CLS-facilitated trip was not possible must be provided with the funding 
237 request. 
238 J. Student organizations shall generally be required to make a brief presentation to for the 
239 committee in support of their funding requests. If a representative of a student organization 
240 does not attend the committee Student Senate meeting at which its funding request is 
241 considered, the request shall be tabled. If a representative of a student organization does 
242 not attend for a second time, the request shall be zero funded and considered a complete 
243 request of the three allowed within a fiscal year. 
244 8. Funding Limits 
245 A. Travel 
246 (1) Maximum of $250 per student and $5,000 per organization. 
247 B. Events/Programming 
248 (1) Maximum of $3,000 per organization. 
249 C. Annual Cap per Organizations

250 (1) No organization may receive more than $10,000 5% of the entire RSOAC budget 
251 in total funding from the RSO Allocation Committee during a single fiscal year, 
252 regardless of the number of individual requests or categories funded.

254 events, programming, or any other expenditures recommended by the RSO 
255 Allocation Committee and approved by the Student Senate.

257 (1) An organization may not receive funding for more than one (1) request within the

263 A. In order to comply with University purchasing and travel guidelines, of the funding

265 (1) 5% shall be available for allocation beginning July 1 each year through the end of 
266 the Summer semester; 
267 (2) 47.5% shall be available for allocation in the Fall semester, in addition to any 
268 unexpended funds from earlier in the fiscal year; and 
269 (3) 47.5% shall be available in the Spring semester, in addition to any unexpended 
270 funds from earlier in the fiscal year. 
271 B. All final funding allocations must be approved by the Student Senate at least 30 calendar 
272 days before the event or travel is to take place. 
273 C. In addition to the requirement above, funding for events or travel scheduled during the 
274 months of May or June must be approved by the Student Senate before the conclusion of 
275 the Spring semester. There shall be no exceptions to this requirement, which is needed in 
276 order to maintain compliance with the University’s fiscal year-end closeout procedures. 
277 10. Post-Award Requirements 
278 A. All events funded by SGA must be publicly advertised on NoleCentral in a manner visible 
279 to the general student body. This shall serve as the baseline standard for public 
280 advertisement. Additional promotion through means such as social media, digital signage, 
281 newsletters, or tabling is encouraged but not required. 
282 B. Any events, programs, travel, or other activities supported by SGA funding must comply 
283 with the FSU Student Organization Conduct Code as well as all federal, state, and local 
284 laws. 
285 C. Every organization receiving funding from SGA must submit a post event evaluation form, 
286 along with receipts for any purchases made, to the SGA Accounting Office, within ten (10) 
287 business days following the event. 
288 D. If the requirements above are not followed by an organization, they shall be barred from 
289 requesting any further funding until their post-award violations are rectified with SGA 
290 accounting. 
291 11. Annual Review Requirement 
292 A. No later than the end of the Fall semester each year, the Student Body Treasurer shall 
293 conduct an evaluation of the RSOAC program. This review shall assess the overall 
294 effectiveness of the program and identify any areas for potential improvement. 
295 B. This evaluation shall include: 
296 (1) The number and nature of instances in which standard funding rules or limits were 
297 waived; 
298 (2) An analysis of how such waivers impacted student organizations and the broader 
299 student body; 
300 (3) The adequacy of the current funding level for the program; 
301 (4) Recommendations for enhancing the program’s structure, parameters, and 
302 allocation limits; and

303 (5) A breakdown of the number and types of organizations that receive funding, 
304 including both organizational status (USSO, ASO, GSO) and programmatic 
305 category (e.g. academic, cultural, special interest, political, community service). 
306 C. Following the evaluation, the Student Body Treasurer shall prepare a report of findings 
307 and recommendations. This report shall be submitted to the Student Senate Budget 
308 Committee during the annual SGA budget planning cycle. 
309 12. Policy Implementation: 
310 A. The Student Senate shall adopt a policy, pursuant to the requirements of Chapter 421, 
311 Student Body Statutes, to govern the operations of the RSO Allocation Committee, to 
312 establish procedures governing funding requests, and to establish criteria for the 
313 committee to use in evaluating funding requests. At minimum an established policy must 
314 create a rubric that the committee shall use for all allocations. 
315 13. Committee Member Elections 
316 A. Beginning in the 78th Student Senate Session, five (5) four (4) of the student-at-large 
317 seats on the RSO Allocation Committee shall be filled by election during the Fall SGA 
318 elections. 
319 B. The elected members shall: 
320 (1) Be currently enrolled undergraduate students; 
321 (2) Be in good academic and conduct standing with the University; 
322 (3) Must have completed financial certification at any time during the current fiscal 
323 year, beginning July 1st, and no later than the day before the candidate declaration 
324 filing deadline. 
325 (4) Cannot be the registered President or Treasurer of any Registered Student 
326 Organizations (RSOs). 
327 C. Candidates for these seats must file for candidacy and comply with all campaign and 
328 election requirements outlined in Title VII of the Student Body Statutes. 
329 D. Elected committee members shall serve a one-year term beginning at the Fall SGA 
330 Inauguration and ending at the following Fall Inauguration. 
331 E. In the event of a vacancy in one of the five elected student-at-large seats on the RSO 
332 Allocation Committee, the Student Body President may appoint a replacement pursuant 
333 to the procedures outlined in Chapters 201 and 202 of the Student Body Statutes, and any 
334 other applicable Executive Branch policies governing seat vacancies. The appointee must 
335 meet all eligibility requirements outlined in this Chapter and shall be referred to the Student 
336 Senate Finance Committee for confirmation prior to being considered by the full Student 
337 Senate. 
338 F. The number of elected seats and eligibility criteria may be reviewed and adjusted annually 
339 by the Student Senate as part of the RSOAC evaluation report submitted pursuant to 
340 Section 11 of this Chapter. 

341 Section 2. Effective Date. 

342 The provisions of this bill shall take effect upon the reconvention of the 78th Student Senate during

prioritize student health, wellness, and security through policy advocacy, 
preventative programming, and accessibility to essential resources.

The Department of Health, Wellness, and Safety actively advances its mission 
through tangible, student-centered initiatives. Through direct work on key issues, 
the department is increasing availability of essential health resources. 
Preventative efforts like social media campaigns and resource fairs promote 
awareness and informed decision-making. Ongoing collaboration with campus

Short Title: Amending Rule Ten, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Clarify Definitions and 
Streamline and Codify the Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This resolution updates Rule Ten of the Senate Rules of Procedure to clarify definitions of 
legislative instruments and establish a structured, transparent, and uniform amendment 
process. The changes align Senate procedural rules with recently adopted statutory standards, 
improve clarity for Senators and the public, and enhance efficiency and predictability during 
floor consideration of measures. 

Background Information: 
Rule Ten governs the submission, consideration, and amendment of measures before the 
Student Senate. Prior to this amendment, several key terms were either undefined or 
inconsistently applied, and procedures for submitting and considering amendments lacked 
sufficient structure. This resulted in confusion during debate, last-minute changes to 
legislation, and reduced transparency for both Senators and the public. Following the adoption 
of statutory reforms to the amendment process, it became necessary to revise Rule Ten to 
ensure consistency between the Senate Rules of Procedure and the Student Body Statutes, 
as well as to formally codify best practices that had developed informally over time. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with direct input from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate Leadership, 
and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution clarifies the definitions of legislative instruments, including bills, resolutions, 
amendments, committee substitutes, and late-filed amendments. It codifies procedures for 
submitting amendments in advance of Senate meetings, establishes clear voting thresholds 
and debate procedures for late-filed amendments, and formalizes processes for committee 
substitutes, confirmations, and statements of dissent. Collectively, these changes improve 

 Page 5 of 11

legislative transparency, protect public notice, reduce administrative confusion, and ensure a 
more orderly and deliberative amendment process on the Senate floor.

 A RESOLUTION 
 Clarifying Senate Rules of Procedure Regarding Forms of Legislation 

 1 WHEREAS, Rule 10 of the Senate Rules of Procedure currently defines and governs the forms of 
 2 legislation considered by the Senate of the Florida State University Student Government 
 3 Association; and 

 4 WHEREAS, proclamations serve a distinct ceremonial and honorary function, including the recognition 
 5 of individuals, organizations, events, causes, and achievements of significance to the student body 
 6 and the University community; and 

 7 WHEREAS, resolutions are intended to express the official position, recommendation, or intent of the 
 8 Senate on matters of policy, governance, or advocacy, and therefore should be clearly 
 9 distinguished from ceremonial proclamations; and 

10 WHEREAS, clarifying the definitions and procedural treatment of bills, resolutions, and proclamations 
11 promotes transparency, consistency, and orderly legislative practice; and 

12 WHEREAS, Student Body Statutes Chapter 401 “Forms of Legislation” has been updated, leaving 
13 Senate Rules of Procedures outdated and inconsistent; 

14 NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED by the 78th Student Senate at Florida State University that: 
15 Rule 10, 8.5, and 8.6 of the Senate Rules of Procedure entitled “Submission and Consideration of 
16 Measures” and “Senate Business” is hereby amended and shall read as follows: 

17 RULE TEN - Submission And Consideration Of Measures 

18 1. Definitions: 

19 a. A "Constitutional Amendment" shall be any measure proposing a change, deletion or 
20 addition to the Student Body Constitution. 

 Page 1 of 5 

 Page 7 of 11
 
21 b. A "Bill" shall be any measure proposing an amendment to the Student Body Statutes or 
22 any measure appropriating money. 

23 c. A " Resolution" shall be defined as a formal statement/amendment of Senate policy or 
24 intent. any measure which is not a bill, constitutional amendment, nomination, 
25 confirmation, or statement of dissent. 

26 d. An “Allocation Resolution” shall be defined as a resolution approving, and allocating 
27 funding recommendations originating from Student Government Association funding 
28 boards or committees established in Student Body Statutes or allocating or transferring 
29 Student Government funds to student organizations through processes expressly 
30 authorized by statute. 

31 e. A "Proclamation" shall be defined as a formal public declaration or official announcement 
32 issued by the Senate to recognize a specific individual, group, event, or cause. 

33 f. A "Nomination" shall be the name of any person who has been forwarded to fill a vacant 
34 position in Student Government that requires confirmation by the Senate. 

35 g. “Confirmation” shall be defined as the approval of a nomination by the Senate, in which 
36 case the nominee shall then immediately assume office. 

37 h. “Statement of Dissent” shall be defined as a written explanation expressing disagreement 
38 with any motion, action, or measure made the Senate. 

39 2. Any bill or resolution, or proclamation filed on time shall be drawn up by the Senate Staff and 
40 distributed to members of the Senate via email and/or packets CivicPlus. 

41 3. Any bills affecting Student Government funds which are restrictive shall state all restrictions, 
42 earmarks, stipulations and provisions as part of the proviso of the bill. 

43 4. All appropriations bills must be accompanied by an information form detailing the need for the 
44 money, the specific uses for the money, and alternative methods of funding which have been 
45 investigated. 

46 5. All bills, constitutional amendments, and resolutions, and proclamations shall include a purpose 
47 and description section detailing a statement of legislative intent. No bill shall be placed on second 
48 reading without a statement of legislative intent. 

49 6. All constitutional amendments, bills, and resolutions, and proclamations shall be submitted on the 
50 appropriate forms as designated by the Student Senate President. 

51 7. Any measure being brought before the Senate for the first time shall be placed on first reading, 
52 unless otherwise moved. 

53 8. Any measure reported out of committee(s) shall be placed on second reading to be heard by the 
54 full Senate at the next meeting. 

 Page 8 of 11
 
55 9. All nominees to Student Government offices requiring Senate confirmation shall have their 
56 completed applications forwarded to the appropriate Senate committee for consideration. The 
57 committee shall interview and question the nominee and then vote on whether to forward or deny 
58 them. Following the vote of the committee, all nominees forwarded by the committee shall be 
59 called to the floor of the Senate at its next meeting. The structure of debate for Senate 
60 confirmations shall be as follows: 

61 a. Nominees shall be allowed to give an opening statement lasting no longer than five (5) 
62 minutes, with their remaining time being allocated to their closing. 

63 b. Nominees may be questioned by any Senator on matters of their experience, 
64 qualifications, and goals for the respective position. 

65 c. Upon passage of a motion to enter debate by majority vote, Senators may speak freely as 
66 to the qualifications of any candidate. Nominees shall be permitted to remain in the Senate 
67 Chamber during debate if they so choose. 

68 d. Upon the passage of a motion to call the question on a candidate for confirmation, each 
69 nominee shall have the time remaining from their opening statement to give a closing 
70 statement as to why they should be confirmed. 

71 10. The primary sponsor of any bill, constitutional amendment, or resolution may withdraw 
72 consideration of the document from the Calendar of the Senate at any time without the need for 
73 a formal motion. 

74 a. In the event one or both primary sponsors are unable to present legislation due to 
75 extenuating circumstances, a present cosponsor may be delegated to present subject to 
76 the opinion of the presiding officer. 

77 11. Any amendment to a measure must be submitted in written form and must contain the exact 
78 language of the proposed amendment including that which shall be inserted and/or deleted. 

79 a. Motions to amend may be made during any round of debate and shall require a second. 
80 If the proposed amendment is germane and receives no objections, the presiding officer 
81 shall ask the primary sponsor if the amendment is favorable. If the sponsor finds the 
82 amendment favorable, the original measure shall be amended, and debate shall proceed 
83 on the measure as amended. 

84 b. If the motion to amend is objected to or the sponsor does not find the amendment 
85 favorable, debate on the primary measure shall halt and the Senate shall consider the 
86 amendment as a stand-alone measure. The Senator who made the motion to amend shall 
87 be considered the sponsor for purposes of debate. 

88 1. Debate on the amendment shall not address the merits of the original measure, 
89 unless it is pertinent to the merits of the amendment. Additionally, questions and 
90 points of information should only inquire on the facts of the amendment itself. 

91 c. Unless otherwise specified by the Student Body Constitution or Student Body Statutes, a 
92 motion to amend shall require a majority vote to pass. 

 Page 9 of 11
 
 93 d. All amendments that appropriate or transfer funds to organizations that are not part of the 
 94 originally submitted bill must be individually debated on the Senate floor, regardless if the 
 95 sponsor accepts them as friendly or unfriendly. 

 96 12. The Senate may, at any time following the proper motion, move to committee caucus for the 
 97 purpose of expediting the consideration of any measure. A motion to move to committee caucus 
 98 shall require a two-thirds vote of the Senate. The Student Senate President, or other presiding 
 99 officer, shall reconvene the Senate at the end of the caucus. 

100 13. Any Senator may, at any time, move to meet as a committee of the whole for the purpose of 
101 discussing any Senate business. A motion to convene as a committee of the whole may pass by 
102 consent or, if objected to, shall require a two-thirds vote of the Senate. A motion to adjourn such 
103 a committee meeting and return to a regular Senate meeting shall require a majority vote. 

104 a. The Student Senate President shall preside over a committee of the whole, unless they 
105 choose to relinquish the Chair. 

106 b. The Student Senate President Pro Tempore shall act as the Vice Chair of a committee of 
107 the whole, unless they choose to relinquish their position. 

108 c. When the Senate reconvenes, any senator may move to accept the decision of the 
109 committee as the decision of the whole. 

110 d. Should the Senate enter a committee of the whole, only members of the original committee 
111 who were on the prevailing side of a motion may move for a reconsideration of the vote 
112 on the said motion. 

113 14. Any senator may, during New Business, move to add a Statement of Dissent into the record. 

114 a. The statement must solely address a singular action, motion, or measure made during 
115 that meeting. 

116 b. There may only be one statement submitted per any action, motion, or measure per 
117 Senator. 

118 c. Senators who did not make the action, motion, or measure on the floor may cosign the 
119 Statement with the consent of the Senator who made the action, motion, or measure. 

120 d. The statement must be submitted to Senate Staff within two (2) school days following the 
121 meeting of the senate when the action, motion, or measure was made. 

122 15. A resolution recognizing all Florida State University students that have deceased shall be heard 
123 on the floor of the Senate during the meeting prior to the last Senate meeting of the session, or 
124 “Sine Die.” 

125 a. The list of students will be provided by the SGA Director. 

126 b. This resolution shall be proposed and advertised one (1) week prior to it being heard. 

127 c. This resolution shall be referred to the Student Life Committee after its first reading and 
128 shall be reported out of the committee in one (1) week.

129 d. No other resolutions recognizing students that have passed shall be considered unless 
130 this rule is waived by two-thirds (2/3) vote of the Senate. 

131 RULE EIGHT - Senate Business 

132 5. Any resolution, bill, or constitutional amendment, to be included on the calendar of a Senate 
133 meeting, must be filed with the Senate Advisor no later than 12 p.m. on the Monday before the 
134 Senate meeting. Any resolution, bill, or proclamation, to be included on the calendar of a Senate 
135 meeting, must be submitted to the Senate Advisor, Senate President, Senate President Pro 
136 Tempore, and Senate Clerk no later than midnight on the Friday before the Senate meeting. 

137 6. If a Senator wishes to introduce any bill, resolution, or constitutional amendment for First Reading 
138 after the submission deadline, it shall require a two-thirds (2/3) vote to be introduced during that 
139 Senate meeting. This Senator must provide a copy of the item to all senators present in order for 
140 the motion to be considered. If a Senator wishes to introduce any bill, resolution, or proclamation 
141 for First Reading after the submission deadline, it shall require a three-fourths (3/4) vote to be 
142 introduced during that Senate meeting. This Senator must provide a copy of the item to all 
143 senators prior to the meeting for the motion to be considered.

Short Title: Allocating $2,000 from Senate Projects for the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift 

Summary of Legislation: This legislation seeks to allocate $2,000 from the Senate Projects 
account to the Senior Class Council for the procurement and installation of communal seating 
as the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift. These funds will cover all costs associated with the 
purchase and shipping of high-quality couches to be permanently placed in the Oglesby 
Student Union terrace, providing a lasting enhancement to campus lounge spaces. By funding 
this initiative, the Senate will ensure a tangible contribution to the Florida State student 
experience.

Background Information:
The Class Councils are an executive entity of the FSU Student Government Association 
dedicated to fostering campus traditions and leaving a lasting impact on each graduating class. 
For the first time in years, the Senior Class Council is taking donations from Registered 
Student Organizations and the local community to furnish the Oglesby Student Union’s 
second-floor terrace. This legislation aims to allocate $2,000 from Senate Projects to procure 
and install communal seating for the student body to enjoy. 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with the co-sponsorship of Senate President Holliday and the Senior 
Class Council's leadership. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If enacted, this legislation will officially transfer $2,000 from the Senate Projects account to the 
Senior Class Council to finalize the funding for the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift. This 
transfer will result in the permanent installation of communal seating on the Oglesby Student 
Union’s second-floor terrace, directly enhancing the quality of shared lounge spaces for all 
students. Beyond the physical beautification of the Union, this bill strengthens the collaborative 
relationship between the Student Senate and the Class Councils by supporting shared 
student-led initiatives. Ultimately, the project fosters a more visible and engaged on-campus 
presence for student government while providing a lasting benefit to the Florida State 
community.

Short Title: Restructuring the Executive for Visibility, Accountability, Modernization, and 
Performance (REVAMP) Act of 2026 

Summary of Legislation: 
This legislation would reform many processes for the appointment of officers under the Student 
Body Statutes, specifying exactly which offices in the Executive Branch require confirmation by 
the Student Senate. The bill discusses many ‘staff roles’ throughout the Executive Branch and 
clarifies their functions and appointment process. The bill also creates a new role of special 
advisor, an individual with an 8 week acting capacity to help assist the President on larger 
projects on a temporary basis. 

Background Information: 
The current appointment structure of the Executive Branch has had frictions between the 
Legislative and Executive arms of the SGA, which has caused issues relating to opposing 
memorandums, judicial filings, and disagreements about interpretation. To rectify this, the 
Legislative Branch has conferred with the Executive Branch to find a middle point that solves 
problems on all sides. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Outreach has included the Senate President, the Chair and Vice Chair of Internal Affairs, 
Office of Attorney General and the President of the Student Government. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation would: specify the exact offices that need to be forwarded and confirmed by the 
Senate; allow for Executive appointment of staff roles; specifying promotion procedures;

community.

Short Title: Amending the Senate Rules of Procedure to Establish Standing Committee Chair 
Liaison Assignments to Executive Branch Departments 

Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution amends Rule Two of the Senate Rules of Procedure to designate specific 
Standing Committee Chairs as liaisons to corresponding Executive Branch departments. It 
also preserves the Senate President’s authority to appoint additional liaisons to other 
Executive Branch departments as needed. The changes are intended to improve interbranch 
coordination and clarify liaison responsibilities. 

Background Information: 

The Student Senate relies on liaison positions to maintain consistent communication and 
collaboration with Executive Branch departments and campus partners. Currently, liaison 
assignments are largely discretionary, which can lead to uneven engagement and unclear 
lines of responsibility between key Senate committees and their most closely related Executive 
counterparts. 

This legislation formalizes a limited number of high-alignment liaison relationships—specifically 
between Judiciary, Internal Affairs, Finance, and Student Life and their respective Executive 
departments—while preserving the Senate President’s flexibility to assign additional liaisons 
where operationally necessary. By creating clearer structural expectations, the Senate can 
strengthen oversight, improve information flow, and support more coordinated Student 
Government operations. 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This legislation was developed through consultation with Senate President Holliday, and 
Student Body President Dale. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If enacted, this legislation will formally designate certain Standing Committee Chairs as 
liaisons to specified Executive Branch departments while preserving the Senate President’s 
authority to appoint additional liaisons to other Executive Branch departments as needed. The

amendment clarifies expectations for interbranch communication and accountability, improves 
structural consistency in Senate liaison assignments, and strengthens coordination between 
the Legislative and Executive Branches without altering the Senate President’s broader 
appointment powers or existing liaison reporting requirements.

Short Title: Amending Rule Ten, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Clarify Definitions and 
Streamline and Codify the Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This resolution updates Rule Ten of the Senate Rules of Procedure to clarify definitions of 
legislative instruments and establish a structured, transparent, and uniform amendment 
process. The changes align Senate procedural rules with recently adopted statutory standards, 
improve clarity for Senators and the public, and enhance efficiency and predictability during 
floor consideration of measures. 

Background Information: 
Rule Ten governs the submission, consideration, and amendment of measures before the 
Student Senate. Prior to this amendment, several key terms were either undefined or 
inconsistently applied, and procedures for submitting and considering amendments lacked 
sufficient structure. This resulted in confusion during debate, last-minute changes to 
legislation, and reduced transparency for both Senators and the public. Following the adoption 
of statutory reforms to the amendment process, it became necessary to revise Rule Ten to 
ensure consistency between the Senate Rules of Procedure and the Student Body Statutes, 
as well as to formally codify best practices that had developed informally over time. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with direct input from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate Leadership, 
and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution clarifies the definitions of legislative instruments, including bills, resolutions, 
amendments, committee substitutes, and late-filed amendments. It codifies procedures for 
submitting amendments in advance of Senate meetings, establishes clear voting thresholds 
and debate procedures for late-filed amendments, and formalizes processes for committee 
substitutes, confirmations, and statements of dissent. Collectively, these changes improve 

 Page 9 of 21

legislative transparency, protect public notice, reduce administrative confusion, and ensure a 
more orderly and deliberative amendment process on the Senate floor.

Short Title: Amending Rule Thirteen of the Senate Rules of Procedure to Codify Disability 
Related Accommodations and Leaves of Absence 

Summary of Legislation: 
This legislation amends Rule Thirteen of the Student Senate Rules of Procedure to establish a 
formal process allowing Senators to request a temporary leave of absence during their term 
due to serious health conditions, family emergencies, or other significant circumstances. The 
amendment also clarifies that disability-related attendance exceptions may be approved by 
Senate leadership or the Rules Committee. The goal is to maintain accountability while 
providing reasonable flexibility for Senators facing circumstances that affect their ability to 
attend meetings. 

Background Information: 

The Student Senate maintains attendance requirements in order to ensure that Senators fulfill 
their responsibilities, maintain quorum, and effectively represent the student body. These 
expectations are essential for the orderly conduct of Senate business and for maintaining 
consistent representation of the student body. 

While the existing rules provide a structure for excused absences, they do not clearly establish 
a process for Senators who may need a temporary pause in participation due to significant 
personal circumstances. Situations such as serious health conditions, family emergencies, or 
other major disruptions may make it difficult for a Senator to maintain regular attendance for a 
limited period of time. 

Additionally, while the Senate has historically exercised discretion when evaluating attendance 
circumstances, the rules do not explicitly recognize that disability-related attendance 
exceptions may sometimes be appropriate. Clarifying this possibility ensures that Senate 
leadership has clear authority to make reasonable attendance determinations when necessary. 

Establishing a defined leave of absence process and clarifying the possibility of disability-
related attendance exceptions helps provide transparency and predictability for both Senators 
and Senate leadership. It also helps ensure that Senators facing temporary challenges are 
able to communicate openly with leadership while maintaining the overall functioning of the 
Senate. 

 Page 16 of 21

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Consultation occurred with current Student Senators and Senate leadership regarding the 
structure of Rule Thirteen and existing attendance practices. Outreach also included 
communication with the Director of the Office of Accessibility Services (OAS) to gather 
feedback regarding the inclusion of language recognizing disability-related attendance 
exceptions. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 

If enacted, this legislation would amend Rule Thirteen of the Student Senate Rules of 
Procedure to establish a formal process through which Senators may request a temporary 
leave of absence during their term for serious health conditions, family emergencies, or other 
significant circumstances. 

The legislation also explicitly states that disability-related attendance exceptions may be 
approved by the Student Senate President, Student Senate President Pro Tempore, and/or the 
Rules Committee. This clarification provides Senate leadership with the authority to make 
reasonable determinations regarding attendance when appropriate. 

During an approved leave of absence, the Senator would not accrue absences and would not 
be counted toward quorum. The Rules Committee would review leave requests and determine 
the conditions under which a Senator may return to active service.

Short Title: Amending the Student Body Constitution, Article III, Section 2, to establish the 
sperate election of Student Body President and Student Body Vice President. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would eliminate the election of the Student Body President and 
Student Body Vice President as a ticket. Instead, students would elect each by a plurality vote. 
The constitutional amendment also clarifies language within the Constitution relating to the 
naming of the Student Body Treasurer, consistently referring to the office as “Treasurer” to 
mirror references made to “President” and “Vice President.” 

Background Information: 
Florida State University has one of the longest and richest traditions of student self-
governance in the state. Student government at FSU predates the university itself: in 1935, 
while the institution was still the Florida State College for Women, the College Government 
Association was established with executive, legislative, and judicial branches. When men were 
admitted in 1946 and the institution became Florida State University in 1947, the CGA split 
briefly into separate Men's and Women's Government Associations before merging in 1948, 
when Charles McMillan was elected the first Student Body President of Florida State. In 1949, 
the body was renamed the University Government Association, and the modern era of FSU 
student governance began, a lineage the SGA celebrated with its 75th anniversary reunion in 
September 2024. 
 
From the earliest days of coeducation, the Student Body President and Student Body Vice 
President have been the two foundational elected executive officers of the student body. The 
presidency has carried extraordinary institutional significance: the Student Body President 
administers and enforces all laws of the Student Body and holds voting seats on the FSU 
Board of Trustees, the Student Affairs Advisory Council, the Athletics Board, and the 
Foundation Board of Trustees. The office has produced a Florida Governor (Reubin Askew, 
the 1950 Student Body President, who later signed the landmark 1974 Activity & Service Fee 
law), and in recent years, four of the last five FSU Student Body Presidents have been elected 
Chair of the Florida Student Association, earning a seat on the Florida Board of Governors. 

 Page 25 of 80 

The Student Body Vice President has similarly been an elected position since 1946, though its 
scope and responsibilities have evolved dramatically over the decades. In the early years of 
coeducation, men dominated the top two executive offices, it was not until 1957 that Jan 
Kaminis Platt became the first woman elected Vice President since the FSCW era. For much 
of SGA's history, the Vice President served primarily as a successor-in-waiting and general 
assistant to the President. Over time, however, the role has grown into the primary executive 
officer responsible for overseeing FSU's identity-based Agencies, the Asian American Student 
Union, Black Student Union, Hispanic/Latinx Student Union, Jewish Student Union, Pride 
Student Union, Veterans Student Union, and Women's Student Union, as well as the Bureaus, 
Leadership Institutes (including the Freshman Leadership Institute, founded in 2011, the 
Transfer Leadership Institute, and the Diversity and Inclusion Institute, developed in 2018), and 
the formulation and completion of Executive Projects. The Vice President's portfolio today 
encompasses the full breadth of SGA's student-facing programming, cultural advocacy, and 
leadership development operations, making the office substantively distinct from and 
complementary to the presidency in a way it was not in earlier decades. 
 
Notably, this joint-ticket structure has at times limited the pipeline between the two offices; 
when Stacey Pierre was elected Student Body President in 2018 after serving as Vice 
President, she was the first president in ten years to have previously held the vice presidency, 
suggesting that the running-mate model may discourage rather than encourage continuity of 
experienced executive leadership. 
 
The Student Body Treasurer represents a later but equally significant addition to the elected 
executive structure. The Treasurer's existence as an independently elected officer is 
inseparable from the passage of Chapter 74-312, Laws of Florida, in 1974, the Activity & 
Service Fee law that transferred authority over A&S fee allocation from university 
administrators to student governments. In 1974, Student Body President David Aronofsky, 
Vice President Jan Pietrzyk, and Senate President Doug Mannheimer became the first student 
leaders to set and allocate A&S fees, and in 1975, the first full A&S budget was established. 
This law transformed FSU's SGA from a purely advocacy-oriented body into a fiscal entity, one 
that today manages a budget of nearly $15.4 million. The need for an officer independently 
elected by and accountable to the full student body specifically for financial stewardship led to 
the creation of the Student Body Treasurer as a separately elected at-large position. Critically, 
the Treasurer has always run independently, not on a joint ticket with the President, giving the 
office its own electoral mandate as a fiscal check on executive spending. The Treasurer 
approves all activity and service fee expenditures and holds a constitutional place in the line of 
presidential succession. In 2019, the Pierre/Brown/Pimentel administration initiated the first 
official SGA Audit, and in 2020, the Steinberg/Lee/Dawkins administration created the first 
SGA Finance Videos, reflecting the office's continued growth in transparency and institutional 
responsibility. 
 
The three elected executive officers (colloquially known as the "Big 3") thus represent three 
distinct pillars of student governance: policy leadership and institutional representation 
(Student Body President), programming, identity advocacy, and student life (Student Body 
Vice President), and fiscal stewardship and accountability (Student Body Treasurer). The 

 Page 26 of 80 

Student Body Treasurer's title, however, has never been updated to match the naming 
conventions of the Student Body President and Student Body Vice President within the 
Constitution and Statutes, an inconsistency this amendment also seeks to address. More 
fundamentally, the current joint-ticket structure for the Vice President is an anomaly within 
FSU's own model, the Treasurer has always been elected independently, and the Vice 
President's role has grown to a scope and significance that warrants the same independent 
electoral mandate. This amendment would restore structural consistency among the Big 3 by 
ensuring that each elected executive officer derives authority directly from the student body, 
reflecting the distinct responsibilities each office has come to carry over more than seven 
decades of student self-governance at Florida State University. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

In the course of developing this amendment, the author engaged in outreach with members of 
the Student Senate and the broader student body to gauge sentiment regarding the 
independent election of the Student Body Vice President. Through one-on-one conversations 
and informal discussions among colleagues, a number of Senators expressed support for this 
type of legislation and, in many cases, had independently raised the idea themselves before 
formal drafting began. The consistency of this feedback across a wide cross-section of the 
Senate suggests that the current joint-ticket structure has become a point of growing concern 
among student legislators who observe its effects on governance firsthand. 

Several recurring themes emerged from these conversations. First, senators broadly 
recognized that the Student Body Vice President's role has evolved well beyond what a 
running-mate model can adequately reflect. The Vice President now oversees seven identity-
based Agencies, multiple Departments and Leadership Institutes, and the full scope of 
Executive Projects and student-facing programming, a portfolio that is operationally distinct 
from and no less consequential than that of the President. Senators expressed that an officer 
carrying this level of responsibility over the cultural, advocacy, and programmatic life of nearly 
45,000 students should derive their authority from an independent mandate of the student 
body, not from their selection by a single presidential candidate. 

Second, senators raised concerns that the joint-ticket structure effectively limits who is able to 
seek the Vice Presidency. Under the current system, a student who wishes to serve as Vice 
President must first be chosen by a presidential candidate as their running mate, restricting the 
pool of potential Vice Presidents to those within the personal and political network of whoever 
is running for President. Senators noted that this dynamic may exclude otherwise highly 
qualified candidates who could bring valuable experience and perspective to the office but who 
lack a preexisting relationship with a presidential contender. 

Third, and relatedly, senators observed that students themselves have expressed a desire for 
greater choice on the ballot. Under the current structure, voters select a ticket rather than 
independently evaluating candidates for each office. Informal feedback from the student body 
has reflected a sense of disconnect from the Vice Presidential selection, students often feel 
they are voting for a President and receiving a Vice President they may know little about, 
rather than making a deliberate, informed choice for each of the executive officers who will 

 Page 27 of 80 

represent them. Restoring the independent election of the Vice President would give every 
student a direct voice in choosing the officer responsible for the Agencies, Institutes, and 
programming that most immediately touch their campus experience. 

The breadth and consistency of this feedback, gathered organically through individual 
conversations rather than a single coordinated effort, demonstrates that this amendment 
reflects a genuine and widely held view within the Legislature that the time has come to align 
the Vice President's electoral structure with the independent scope the office has come to 
carry. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would give the student body more independent choice in their 
executive representation. It would create a separate election of the Student Body Vice 
President by a plurality vote of those voting. Additionally, the amendment changes references 
from “Student Body Treasurer” to “Treasurer” to make language more consistent in the 
Constitution overall in relation to executive positions.

Short Title: Amending the Senate Rules of Procedure to Establish Standing Committee Chair 
Liaison Assignments to Executive Branch Departments 

Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution amends Rule Two of the Senate Rules of Procedure to designate specific 
Standing Committee Chairs as liaisons to corresponding Executive Branch departments. It 
also preserves the Senate President’s authority to appoint additional liaisons to other 
Executive Branch departments as needed. The changes are intended to improve interbranch 
coordination and clarify liaison responsibilities. 

Background Information: 

The Student Senate relies on liaison positions to maintain consistent communication and 
collaboration with Executive Branch departments and campus partners. Currently, liaison 
assignments are largely discretionary, which can lead to uneven engagement and unclear 
lines of responsibility between key Senate committees and their most closely related Executive 
counterparts. 

This legislation formalizes a limited number of high-alignment liaison relationships—specifically 
between Judiciary, Internal Affairs, Finance, and Student Life and their respective Executive 
departments—while preserving the Senate President’s flexibility to assign additional liaisons 
where operationally necessary. By creating clearer structural expectations, the Senate can 
strengthen oversight, improve information flow, and support more coordinated Student 
Government operations. 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This legislation was developed through consultation with Senate President Holliday, and 
Student Body President Dale. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If enacted, this legislation will formally designate certain Standing Committee Chairs as 
liaisons to specified Executive Branch departments while preserving the Senate President’s 
authority to appoint additional liaisons to other Executive Branch departments as needed. The 

 Page 32 of 80 

amendment clarifies expectations for interbranch communication and accountability, improves 
structural consistency in Senate liaison assignments, and strengthens coordination between 
the Legislative and Executive Branches without altering the Senate President’s broader 
appointment powers or existing liaison reporting requirements.

Short Title: Amending Rule Ten, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Clarify Definitions and 
Streamline and Codify the Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This resolution updates Rule Ten of the Senate Rules of Procedure to clarify definitions of 
legislative instruments and establish a structured, transparent, and uniform amendment 
process. The changes align Senate procedural rules with recently adopted statutory standards, 
improve clarity for Senators and the public, and enhance efficiency and predictability during 
floor consideration of measures. 

Background Information: 
Rule Ten governs the submission, consideration, and amendment of measures before the 
Student Senate. Prior to this amendment, several key terms were either undefined or 
inconsistently applied, and procedures for submitting and considering amendments lacked 
sufficient structure. This resulted in confusion during debate, last-minute changes to 
legislation, and reduced transparency for both Senators and the public. Following the adoption 
of statutory reforms to the amendment process, it became necessary to revise Rule Ten to 
ensure consistency between the Senate Rules of Procedure and the Student Body Statutes, 
as well as to formally codify best practices that had developed informally over time. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with direct input from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate Leadership, 
and the outgoing Senate Officer Team.

Summary of Legislation: This legislation seeks to allocate $2,000 from the Senate Projects 
account to the Senior Class Council for the procurement and installation of communal seating 
as the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift. These funds will cover all costs associated with the 
purchase and shipping of high-quality couches to be permanently placed in the Oglesby 
Student Union terrace, providing a lasting enhancement to campus lounge spaces. By funding 
this initiative, the Senate will ensure a tangible contribution to the Florida State student 
experience.

Background Information:
The Class Councils are an executive entity of the FSU Student Government Association 
dedicated to fostering campus traditions and leaving a lasting impact on each graduating class. 
For the first time in years, the Senior Class Council is taking donations from Registered 
Student Organizations and the local community to furnish the Oglesby Student Union’s 
second-floor terrace. This legislation aims to allocate $2,000 from Senate Projects to procure 
and install communal seating for the student body to enjoy.

This bill was drafted with the co-sponsorship of Senate President Holliday and the Senior 
Class Council's leadership. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation:
If enacted, this legislation will officially transfer $2,000 from the Senate Projects account to the 
Senior Class Council to finalize the funding for the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift. This 
transfer will result in the permanent installation of communal seating on the Oglesby Student 
Union’s second-floor terrace, directly enhancing the quality of shared lounge spaces for all 
students. Beyond the physical beautification of the Union, this bill strengthens the collaborative 
relationship between the Student Senate and the Class Councils by supporting shared 
student-led initiatives. Ultimately, the project fosters a more visible and engaged on-campus 
presence for student government while providing a lasting benefit to the Florida State 
community.

Short Title: Amending Rule Thirteen of the Senate Rules of Procedure to Codify Disability 
Related Accommodations and Leaves of Absence 

Summary of Legislation: 
This legislation amends Rule Thirteen of the Student Senate Rules of Procedure to establish a 
formal process allowing Senators to request a temporary leave of absence during their term 
due to serious health conditions, family emergencies, or other significant circumstances. The 
amendment also clarifies that disability-related attendance exceptions may be approved by 
Senate leadership or the Rules Committee. The goal is to maintain accountability while 
providing reasonable flexibility for Senators facing circumstances that affect their ability to 
attend meetings. 

Background Information: 

The Student Senate maintains attendance requirements in order to ensure that Senators fulfill 
their responsibilities, maintain quorum, and effectively represent the student body. These 
expectations are essential for the orderly conduct of Senate business and for maintaining 
consistent representation of the student body. 

While the existing rules provide a structure for excused absences, they do not clearly establish 
a process for Senators who may need a temporary pause in participation due to significant 
personal circumstances. Situations such as serious health conditions, family emergencies, or 
other major disruptions may make it difficult for a Senator to maintain regular attendance for a 
limited period of time. 

Additionally, while the Senate has historically exercised discretion when evaluating attendance 
circumstances, the rules do not explicitly recognize that disability-related attendance 
exceptions may sometimes be appropriate. Clarifying this possibility ensures that Senate 
leadership has clear authority to make reasonable attendance determinations when necessary. 

Establishing a defined leave of absence process and clarifying the possibility of disability-
related attendance exceptions helps provide transparency and predictability for both Senators 
and Senate leadership. It also helps ensure that Senators facing temporary challenges are 
able to communicate openly with leadership while maintaining the overall functioning of the 
Senate. 

 Page 48 of 80 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Consultation occurred with current Student Senators and Senate leadership regarding the 
structure of Rule Thirteen and existing attendance practices. Outreach also included 
communication with the Director of the Office of Accessibility Services (OAS) to gather 
feedback regarding the inclusion of language recognizing disability-related attendance 
exceptions. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 

If enacted, this legislation would amend Rule Thirteen of the Student Senate Rules of 
Procedure to establish a formal process through which Senators may request a temporary 
leave of absence during their term for serious health conditions, family emergencies, or other 
significant circumstances. 

The legislation also explicitly states that disability-related attendance exceptions may be 
approved by the Student Senate President, Student Senate President Pro Tempore, and/or the 
Rules Committee. This clarification provides Senate leadership with the authority to make 
reasonable determinations regarding attendance when appropriate. 

During an approved leave of absence, the Senator would not accrue absences and would not 
be counted toward quorum. The Rules Committee would review leave requests and determine 
the conditions under which a Senator may return to active service.

Short Title: Restructuring the Executive for Visibility, Accountability, Modernization, and 
Performance (REVAMP) Act of 2026 

Summary of Legislation: 
This legislation would reform many processes for the appointment of officers under the Student 
Body Statutes, specifying exactly which offices in the Executive Branch require confirmation by 
the Student Senate. The bill discusses many ‘staff roles’ throughout the Executive Branch and 
clarifies their functions and appointment process. The bill also creates a new role of special 
advisor, an individual with an 8 week acting capacity to help assist the President on larger 
projects on a temporary basis. 

Background Information: 
The current appointment structure of the Executive Branch has had frictions between the 
Legislative and Executive arms of the SGA, which has caused issues relating to opposing 
memorandums, judicial filings, and disagreements about interpretation. To rectify this, the 
Legislative Branch has conferred with the Executive Branch to find a middle point that solves 
problems on all sides. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
Outreach has included the Senate President, the Chair and Vice Chair of Internal Affairs, 
Office of Attorney General and the President of the Student Government. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation would: specify the exact offices that need to be forwarded and confirmed by the 
Senate; allow for Executive appointment of staff roles; specifying promotion procedures; 
establish special advisors; create nonfeasance procedures; and correct many grammatical 
errors.
