Short Title: The Sustainability Education and Early Development (SEED) Act 

Summary of Legislation: 
This bill would provide $2,617.63 to the Childcare Development Center in order to fund 
numerous priorities for their outdoor classrooms. These priorities include mock gardens and 
infrastructure for students to grow various plants. 

Background Information: 
The Childcare Development Center is an organization that used to receive SGA funding, but 
was largely switched to COGS due to the majority of serviced students being Graduate 
students. However, the CDC still services children of undergraduate students, and the SGA 
has a vested interest in delivering the best outcomes for all students in the University, which 
includes the education of their dependent children which our institution serves. The CDC is 
requesting these allocations to ease their budgetary constraints, allowing for more resources to 
go back into teaching these students. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Childcare Development Center was the main outreach, requesting the individual expenses. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation would fund numerous requests by the Childcare Development Center, allowing 
for enhanced student outcomes in the fields of rural education and horticulture/agriculture 
introductions.

Short Title: Amending the Student Body Constitution, Article III, Section 2, to establish the 
sperate election of Student Body President and Student Body Vice President. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would eliminate the election of the Student Body President and 
Student Body Vice President as a ticket. Instead, students would elect each by a plurality vote. 
The constitutional amendment also clarifies language within the Constitution relating to the 
naming of the Student Body Treasurer, consistently referring to the office as “Treasurer” to 
mirror references made to “President” and “Vice President.” 

Background Information: 
Florida State University has one of the longest and richest traditions of student self-
governance in the state. Student government at FSU predates the university itself: in 1935, 
while the institution was still the Florida State College for Women, the College Government 
Association was established with executive, legislative, and judicial branches. When men were 
admitted in 1946 and the institution became Florida State University in 1947, the CGA split 
briefly into separate Men's and Women's Government Associations before merging in 1948, 
when Charles McMillan was elected the first Student Body President of Florida State. In 1949, 
the body was renamed the University Government Association, and the modern era of FSU 
student governance began, a lineage the SGA celebrated with its 75th anniversary reunion in 
September 2024. 
 
From the earliest days of coeducation, the Student Body President and Student Body Vice 
President have been the two foundational elected executive officers of the student body. The 
presidency has carried extraordinary institutional significance: the Student Body President 
administers and enforces all laws of the Student Body and holds voting seats on the FSU 
Board of Trustees, the Student Affairs Advisory Council, the Athletics Board, and the 
Foundation Board of Trustees. The office has produced a Florida Governor (Reubin Askew, 
the 1950 Student Body President, who later signed the landmark 1974 Activity & Service Fee 
law), and in recent years, four of the last five FSU Student Body Presidents have been elected 
Chair of the Florida Student Association, earning a seat on the Florida Board of Governors. 

 Page 3 of 24

The Student Body Vice President has similarly been an elected position since 1946, though its 
scope and responsibilities have evolved dramatically over the decades. In the early years of 
coeducation, men dominated the top two executive offices, it was not until 1957 that Jan 
Kaminis Platt became the first woman elected Vice President since the FSCW era. For much 
of SGA's history, the Vice President served primarily as a successor-in-waiting and general 
assistant to the President. Over time, however, the role has grown into the primary executive 
officer responsible for overseeing FSU's identity-based Agencies, the Asian American Student 
Union, Black Student Union, Hispanic/Latinx Student Union, Jewish Student Union, Pride 
Student Union, Veterans Student Union, and Women's Student Union, as well as the Bureaus, 
Leadership Institutes (including the Freshman Leadership Institute, founded in 2011, the 
Transfer Leadership Institute, and the Diversity and Inclusion Institute, developed in 2018), and 
the formulation and completion of Executive Projects. The Vice President's portfolio today 
encompasses the full breadth of SGA's student-facing programming, cultural advocacy, and 
leadership development operations, making the office substantively distinct from and 
complementary to the presidency in a way it was not in earlier decades. 
 
Notably, this joint-ticket structure has at times limited the pipeline between the two offices; 
when Stacey Pierre was elected Student Body President in 2018 after serving as Vice 
President, she was the first president in ten years to have previously held the vice presidency, 
suggesting that the running-mate model may discourage rather than encourage continuity of 
experienced executive leadership. 
 
The Student Body Treasurer represents a later but equally significant addition to the elected 
executive structure. The Treasurer's existence as an independently elected officer is 
inseparable from the passage of Chapter 74-312, Laws of Florida, in 1974, the Activity & 
Service Fee law that transferred authority over A&S fee allocation from university 
administrators to student governments. In 1974, Student Body President David Aronofsky, 
Vice President Jan Pietrzyk, and Senate President Doug Mannheimer became the first student 
leaders to set and allocate A&S fees, and in 1975, the first full A&S budget was established. 
This law transformed FSU's SGA from a purely advocacy-oriented body into a fiscal entity, one 
that today manages a budget of nearly $15.4 million. The need for an officer independently 
elected by and accountable to the full student body specifically for financial stewardship led to 
the creation of the Student Body Treasurer as a separately elected at-large position. Critically, 
the Treasurer has always run independently, not on a joint ticket with the President, giving the 
office its own electoral mandate as a fiscal check on executive spending. The Treasurer 
approves all activity and service fee expenditures and holds a constitutional place in the line of 
presidential succession. In 2019, the Pierre/Brown/Pimentel administration initiated the first 
official SGA Audit, and in 2020, the Steinberg/Lee/Dawkins administration created the first 
SGA Finance Videos, reflecting the office's continued growth in transparency and institutional 
responsibility. 
 
The three elected executive officers (colloquially known as the "Big 3") thus represent three 
distinct pillars of student governance: policy leadership and institutional representation 
(Student Body President), programming, identity advocacy, and student life (Student Body 
Vice President), and fiscal stewardship and accountability (Student Body Treasurer). The 

 Page 4 of 24

Student Body Treasurer's title, however, has never been updated to match the naming 
conventions of the Student Body President and Student Body Vice President within the 
Constitution and Statutes, an inconsistency this amendment also seeks to address. More 
fundamentally, the current joint-ticket structure for the Vice President is an anomaly within 
FSU's own model, the Treasurer has always been elected independently, and the Vice 
President's role has grown to a scope and significance that warrants the same independent 
electoral mandate. This amendment would restore structural consistency among the Big 3 by 
ensuring that each elected executive officer derives authority directly from the student body, 
reflecting the distinct responsibilities each office has come to carry over more than seven 
decades of student self-governance at Florida State University. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

In the course of developing this amendment, the author engaged in outreach with members of 
the Student Senate and the broader student body to gauge sentiment regarding the 
independent election of the Student Body Vice President. Through one-on-one conversations 
and informal discussions among colleagues, a number of Senators expressed support for this 
type of legislation and, in many cases, had independently raised the idea themselves before 
formal drafting began. The consistency of this feedback across a wide cross-section of the 
Senate suggests that the current joint-ticket structure has become a point of growing concern 
among student legislators who observe its effects on governance firsthand. 

Several recurring themes emerged from these conversations. First, senators broadly 
recognized that the Student Body Vice President's role has evolved well beyond what a 
running-mate model can adequately reflect. The Vice President now oversees seven identity-
based Agencies, multiple Departments and Leadership Institutes, and the full scope of 
Executive Projects and student-facing programming, a portfolio that is operationally distinct 
from and no less consequential than that of the President. Senators expressed that an officer 
carrying this level of responsibility over the cultural, advocacy, and programmatic life of nearly 
45,000 students should derive their authority from an independent mandate of the student 
body, not from their selection by a single presidential candidate. 

Second, senators raised concerns that the joint-ticket structure effectively limits who is able to 
seek the Vice Presidency. Under the current system, a student who wishes to serve as Vice 
President must first be chosen by a presidential candidate as their running mate, restricting the 
pool of potential Vice Presidents to those within the personal and political network of whoever 
is running for President. Senators noted that this dynamic may exclude otherwise highly 
qualified candidates who could bring valuable experience and perspective to the office but who 
lack a preexisting relationship with a presidential contender. 

Third, and relatedly, senators observed that students themselves have expressed a desire for 
greater choice on the ballot. Under the current structure, voters select a ticket rather than 
independently evaluating candidates for each office. Informal feedback from the student body 
has reflected a sense of disconnect from the Vice Presidential selection, students often feel 
they are voting for a President and receiving a Vice President they may know little about, 
rather than making a deliberate, informed choice for each of the executive officers who will 

 Page 5 of 24

represent them. Restoring the independent election of the Vice President would give every 
student a direct voice in choosing the officer responsible for the Agencies, Institutes, and 
programming that most immediately touch their campus experience. 

The breadth and consistency of this feedback, gathered organically through individual 
conversations rather than a single coordinated effort, demonstrates that this amendment 
reflects a genuine and widely held view within the Legislature that the time has come to align 
the Vice President's electoral structure with the independent scope the office has come to 
carry. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would give the student body more independent choice in their 
executive representation. It would create a separate election of the Student Body Vice 
President by a plurality vote of those voting. Additionally, the amendment changes references 
from “Student Body Treasurer” to “Treasurer” to make language more consistent in the 
Constitution overall in relation to executive positions.

Short Title: Allocating $2,000 from Senate Projects for the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift 

Summary of Legislation: This legislation seeks to allocate $2,000 from the Senate Projects 
account to the Senior Class Council for the procurement and installation of communal seating 
as the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift. These funds will cover all costs associated with the 
purchase and shipping of high-quality couches to be permanently placed in the Oglesby 
Student Union terrace, providing a lasting enhancement to campus lounge spaces. By funding 
this initiative, the Senate will ensure a tangible contribution to the Florida State student 
experience. 

Background Information: 
The Class Councils are an executive entity of the FSU Student Government Association 
dedicated to fostering campus traditions and leaving a lasting impact on each graduating class. 
For the first time in years, the Senior Class Council is taking donations from Registered 
Student Organizations and the local community to furnish the Oglesby Student Union’s 
second-floor terrace. This legislation aims to allocate $2,000 from Senate Projects to procure 
and install communal seating for the student body to enjoy. 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with the co-sponsorship of Senate President Holliday and the Senior 
Class Council's leadership. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If enacted, this legislation will officially transfer $2,000 from the Senate Projects account to the 
Senior Class Council to finalize the funding for the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift. This 
transfer will result in the permanent installation of communal seating on the Oglesby Student 
Union’s second-floor terrace, directly enhancing the quality of shared lounge spaces for all 
students. Beyond the physical beautification of the Union, this bill strengthens the collaborative 
relationship between the Student Senate and the Class Councils by supporting shared 
student-led initiatives. Ultimately, the project fosters a more visible and engaged on-campus 
presence for student government while providing a lasting benefit to the Florida State 
community.

Short Title: The Sustainability Education and Early Development (SEED) Act 

Summary of Legislation: 
This bill would provide $2,617.63 to the Childcare Development Center in order to fund 
numerous priorities for their outdoor classrooms. These priorities include mock gardens and 
infrastructure for students to grow various plants. 

Background Information: 
The Childcare Development Center is an organization that used to receive SGA funding, but 
was largely switched to COGS due to the majority of serviced students being Graduate 
students. However, the CDC still services children of undergraduate students, and the SGA 
has a vested interest in delivering the best outcomes for all students in the University, which 
includes the education of their dependent children which our institution serves. The CDC is 
requesting these allocations to ease their budgetary constraints, allowing for more resources to 
go back into teaching these students. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Childcare Development Center was the main outreach, requesting the individual expenses. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation would fund numerous requests by the Childcare Development Center, allowing 
for enhanced student outcomes in the fields of rural education and horticulture/agriculture 
introductions.

Short Title: Amending the Student Body Constitution, Article III, Section 2, to establish the 
sperate election of Student Body President and Student Body Vice President. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would eliminate the election of the Student Body President and 
Student Body Vice President as a ticket. Instead, students would elect each by a plurality vote. 
The constitutional amendment also clarifies language within the Constitution relating to the 
naming of the Student Body Treasurer, consistently referring to the office as “Treasurer” to 
mirror references made to “President” and “Vice President.” 

Background Information: 
Florida State University has one of the longest and richest traditions of student self-
governance in the state. Student government at FSU predates the university itself: in 1935, 
while the institution was still the Florida State College for Women, the College Government 
Association was established with executive, legislative, and judicial branches. When men were 
admitted in 1946 and the institution became Florida State University in 1947, the CGA split 
briefly into separate Men's and Women's Government Associations before merging in 1948, 
when Charles McMillan was elected the first Student Body President of Florida State. In 1949, 
the body was renamed the University Government Association, and the modern era of FSU 
student governance began, a lineage the SGA celebrated with its 75th anniversary reunion in 
September 2024. 
 
From the earliest days of coeducation, the Student Body President and Student Body Vice 
President have been the two foundational elected executive officers of the student body. The 
presidency has carried extraordinary institutional significance: the Student Body President 
administers and enforces all laws of the Student Body and holds voting seats on the FSU 
Board of Trustees, the Student Affairs Advisory Council, the Athletics Board, and the 
Foundation Board of Trustees. The office has produced a Florida Governor (Reubin Askew, 
the 1950 Student Body President, who later signed the landmark 1974 Activity & Service Fee 
law), and in recent years, four of the last five FSU Student Body Presidents have been elected 
Chair of the Florida Student Association, earning a seat on the Florida Board of Governors. 

 Page 5 of 26

The Student Body Vice President has similarly been an elected position since 1946, though its 
scope and responsibilities have evolved dramatically over the decades. In the early years of 
coeducation, men dominated the top two executive offices, it was not until 1957 that Jan 
Kaminis Platt became the first woman elected Vice President since the FSCW era. For much 
of SGA's history, the Vice President served primarily as a successor-in-waiting and general 
assistant to the President. Over time, however, the role has grown into the primary executive 
officer responsible for overseeing FSU's identity-based Agencies, the Asian American Student 
Union, Black Student Union, Hispanic/Latinx Student Union, Jewish Student Union, Pride 
Student Union, Veterans Student Union, and Women's Student Union, as well as the Bureaus, 
Leadership Institutes (including the Freshman Leadership Institute, founded in 2011, the 
Transfer Leadership Institute, and the Diversity and Inclusion Institute, developed in 2018), and 
the formulation and completion of Executive Projects. The Vice President's portfolio today 
encompasses the full breadth of SGA's student-facing programming, cultural advocacy, and 
leadership development operations, making the office substantively distinct from and 
complementary to the presidency in a way it was not in earlier decades. 
 
Notably, this joint-ticket structure has at times limited the pipeline between the two offices; 
when Stacey Pierre was elected Student Body President in 2018 after serving as Vice 
President, she was the first president in ten years to have previously held the vice presidency, 
suggesting that the running-mate model may discourage rather than encourage continuity of 
experienced executive leadership. 
 
The Student Body Treasurer represents a later but equally significant addition to the elected 
executive structure. The Treasurer's existence as an independently elected officer is 
inseparable from the passage of Chapter 74-312, Laws of Florida, in 1974, the Activity & 
Service Fee law that transferred authority over A&S fee allocation from university 
administrators to student governments. In 1974, Student Body President David Aronofsky, 
Vice President Jan Pietrzyk, and Senate President Doug Mannheimer became the first student 
leaders to set and allocate A&S fees, and in 1975, the first full A&S budget was established. 
This law transformed FSU's SGA from a purely advocacy-oriented body into a fiscal entity, one 
that today manages a budget of nearly $15.4 million. The need for an officer independently 
elected by and accountable to the full student body specifically for financial stewardship led to 
the creation of the Student Body Treasurer as a separately elected at-large position. Critically, 
the Treasurer has always run independently, not on a joint ticket with the President, giving the 
office its own electoral mandate as a fiscal check on executive spending. The Treasurer 
approves all activity and service fee expenditures and holds a constitutional place in the line of 
presidential succession. In 2019, the Pierre/Brown/Pimentel administration initiated the first 
official SGA Audit, and in 2020, the Steinberg/Lee/Dawkins administration created the first 
SGA Finance Videos, reflecting the office's continued growth in transparency and institutional 
responsibility. 
 
The three elected executive officers (colloquially known as the "Big 3") thus represent three 
distinct pillars of student governance: policy leadership and institutional representation 
(Student Body President), programming, identity advocacy, and student life (Student Body 
Vice President), and fiscal stewardship and accountability (Student Body Treasurer). The 

 Page 6 of 26

Student Body Treasurer's title, however, has never been updated to match the naming 
conventions of the Student Body President and Student Body Vice President within the 
Constitution and Statutes, an inconsistency this amendment also seeks to address. More 
fundamentally, the current joint-ticket structure for the Vice President is an anomaly within 
FSU's own model, the Treasurer has always been elected independently, and the Vice 
President's role has grown to a scope and significance that warrants the same independent 
electoral mandate. This amendment would restore structural consistency among the Big 3 by 
ensuring that each elected executive officer derives authority directly from the student body, 
reflecting the distinct responsibilities each office has come to carry over more than seven 
decades of student self-governance at Florida State University. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

In the course of developing this amendment, the author engaged in outreach with members of 
the Student Senate and the broader student body to gauge sentiment regarding the 
independent election of the Student Body Vice President. Through one-on-one conversations 
and informal discussions among colleagues, a number of Senators expressed support for this 
type of legislation and, in many cases, had independently raised the idea themselves before 
formal drafting began. The consistency of this feedback across a wide cross-section of the 
Senate suggests that the current joint-ticket structure has become a point of growing concern 
among student legislators who observe its effects on governance firsthand. 

Several recurring themes emerged from these conversations. First, senators broadly 
recognized that the Student Body Vice President's role has evolved well beyond what a 
running-mate model can adequately reflect. The Vice President now oversees seven identity-
based Agencies, multiple Departments and Leadership Institutes, and the full scope of 
Executive Projects and student-facing programming, a portfolio that is operationally distinct 
from and no less consequential than that of the President. Senators expressed that an officer 
carrying this level of responsibility over the cultural, advocacy, and programmatic life of nearly 
45,000 students should derive their authority from an independent mandate of the student 
body, not from their selection by a single presidential candidate. 

Second, senators raised concerns that the joint-ticket structure effectively limits who is able to 
seek the Vice Presidency. Under the current system, a student who wishes to serve as Vice 
President must first be chosen by a presidential candidate as their running mate, restricting the 
pool of potential Vice Presidents to those within the personal and political network of whoever 
is running for President. Senators noted that this dynamic may exclude otherwise highly 
qualified candidates who could bring valuable experience and perspective to the office but who 
lack a preexisting relationship with a presidential contender. 

Third, and relatedly, senators observed that students themselves have expressed a desire for 
greater choice on the ballot. Under the current structure, voters select a ticket rather than 
independently evaluating candidates for each office. Informal feedback from the student body 
has reflected a sense of disconnect from the Vice Presidential selection, students often feel 
they are voting for a President and receiving a Vice President they may know little about, 
rather than making a deliberate, informed choice for each of the executive officers who will 

 Page 7 of 26

represent them. Restoring the independent election of the Vice President would give every 
student a direct voice in choosing the officer responsible for the Agencies, Institutes, and 
programming that most immediately touch their campus experience. 

The breadth and consistency of this feedback, gathered organically through individual 
conversations rather than a single coordinated effort, demonstrates that this amendment 
reflects a genuine and widely held view within the Legislature that the time has come to align 
the Vice President's electoral structure with the independent scope the office has come to 
carry. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would give the student body more independent choice in their 
executive representation. It would create a separate election of the Student Body Vice 
President by a plurality vote of those voting. Additionally, the amendment changes references 
from “Student Body Treasurer” to “Treasurer” to make language more consistent in the 
Constitution overall in relation to executive positions.

Short Title: Allocating $2,000 from Senate Projects for the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift 

Summary of Legislation: This legislation seeks to allocate $2,000 from the Senate Projects 
account to the Senior Class Council for the procurement and installation of communal seating 
as the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift. These funds will cover all costs associated with the 
purchase and shipping of high-quality couches to be permanently placed in the Oglesby 
Student Union terrace, providing a lasting enhancement to campus lounge spaces. By funding 
this initiative, the Senate will ensure a tangible contribution to the Florida State student 
experience. 

Background Information: 
The Class Councils are an executive entity of the FSU Student Government Association 
dedicated to fostering campus traditions and leaving a lasting impact on each graduating class. 
For the first time in years, the Senior Class Council is taking donations from Registered 
Student Organizations and the local community to furnish the Oglesby Student Union’s 
second-floor terrace. This legislation aims to allocate $2,000 from Senate Projects to procure 
and install communal seating for the student body to enjoy. 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with the co-sponsorship of Senate President Holliday and the Senior 
Class Council's leadership. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If enacted, this legislation will officially transfer $2,000 from the Senate Projects account to the 
Senior Class Council to finalize the funding for the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift. This 
transfer will result in the permanent installation of communal seating on the Oglesby Student 
Union’s second-floor terrace, directly enhancing the quality of shared lounge spaces for all 
students. Beyond the physical beautification of the Union, this bill strengthens the collaborative 
relationship between the Student Senate and the Class Councils by supporting shared 
student-led initiatives. Ultimately, the project fosters a more visible and engaged on-campus 
presence for student government while providing a lasting benefit to the Florida State 
community.

Short Title: Amending the Student Body Constitution, Article III, Section 2, to establish the 
sperate election of Student Body President and Student Body Vice President. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would eliminate the election of the Student Body President and 
Student Body Vice President as a ticket. Instead, students would elect each by a plurality vote. 
The constitutional amendment also clarifies language within the Constitution relating to the 
naming of the Student Body Treasurer, consistently referring to the office as “Treasurer” to 
mirror references made to “President” and “Vice President.” 

Background Information: 
Florida State University has one of the longest and richest traditions of student self-
governance in the state. Student government at FSU predates the university itself: in 1935, 
while the institution was still the Florida State College for Women, the College Government 
Association was established with executive, legislative, and judicial branches. When men were 
admitted in 1946 and the institution became Florida State University in 1947, the CGA split 
briefly into separate Men's and Women's Government Associations before merging in 1948, 
when Charles McMillan was elected the first Student Body President of Florida State. In 1949, 
the body was renamed the University Government Association, and the modern era of FSU 
student governance began, a lineage the SGA celebrated with its 75th anniversary reunion in 
September 2024. 
 
From the earliest days of coeducation, the Student Body President and Student Body Vice 
President have been the two foundational elected executive officers of the student body. The 
presidency has carried extraordinary institutional significance: the Student Body President 
administers and enforces all laws of the Student Body and holds voting seats on the FSU 
Board of Trustees, the Student Affairs Advisory Council, the Athletics Board, and the 
Foundation Board of Trustees. The office has produced a Florida Governor (Reubin Askew, 
the 1950 Student Body President, who later signed the landmark 1974 Activity & Service Fee 
law), and in recent years, four of the last five FSU Student Body Presidents have been elected 
Chair of the Florida Student Association, earning a seat on the Florida Board of Governors. 

 Page 4 of 10

The Student Body Vice President has similarly been an elected position since 1946, though its 
scope and responsibilities have evolved dramatically over the decades. In the early years of 
coeducation, men dominated the top two executive offices, it was not until 1957 that Jan 
Kaminis Platt became the first woman elected Vice President since the FSCW era. For much 
of SGA's history, the Vice President served primarily as a successor-in-waiting and general 
assistant to the President. Over time, however, the role has grown into the primary executive 
officer responsible for overseeing FSU's identity-based Agencies, the Asian American Student 
Union, Black Student Union, Hispanic/Latinx Student Union, Jewish Student Union, Pride 
Student Union, Veterans Student Union, and Women's Student Union, as well as the Bureaus, 
Leadership Institutes (including the Freshman Leadership Institute, founded in 2011, the 
Transfer Leadership Institute, and the Diversity and Inclusion Institute, developed in 2018), and 
the formulation and completion of Executive Projects. The Vice President's portfolio today 
encompasses the full breadth of SGA's student-facing programming, cultural advocacy, and 
leadership development operations, making the office substantively distinct from and 
complementary to the presidency in a way it was not in earlier decades. 
 
Notably, this joint-ticket structure has at times limited the pipeline between the two offices; 
when Stacey Pierre was elected Student Body President in 2018 after serving as Vice 
President, she was the first president in ten years to have previously held the vice presidency, 
suggesting that the running-mate model may discourage rather than encourage continuity of 
experienced executive leadership. 
 
The Student Body Treasurer represents a later but equally significant addition to the elected 
executive structure. The Treasurer's existence as an independently elected officer is 
inseparable from the passage of Chapter 74-312, Laws of Florida, in 1974, the Activity & 
Service Fee law that transferred authority over A&S fee allocation from university 
administrators to student governments. In 1974, Student Body President David Aronofsky, 
Vice President Jan Pietrzyk, and Senate President Doug Mannheimer became the first student 
leaders to set and allocate A&S fees, and in 1975, the first full A&S budget was established. 
This law transformed FSU's SGA from a purely advocacy-oriented body into a fiscal entity, one 
that today manages a budget of nearly $15.4 million. The need for an officer independently 
elected by and accountable to the full student body specifically for financial stewardship led to 
the creation of the Student Body Treasurer as a separately elected at-large position. Critically, 
the Treasurer has always run independently, not on a joint ticket with the President, giving the 
office its own electoral mandate as a fiscal check on executive spending. The Treasurer 
approves all activity and service fee expenditures and holds a constitutional place in the line of 
presidential succession. In 2019, the Pierre/Brown/Pimentel administration initiated the first 
official SGA Audit, and in 2020, the Steinberg/Lee/Dawkins administration created the first 
SGA Finance Videos, reflecting the office's continued growth in transparency and institutional 
responsibility. 
 
The three elected executive officers (colloquially known as the "Big 3") thus represent three 
distinct pillars of student governance: policy leadership and institutional representation 
(Student Body President), programming, identity advocacy, and student life (Student Body 
Vice President), and fiscal stewardship and accountability (Student Body Treasurer). The 

 Page 5 of 10

Student Body Treasurer's title, however, has never been updated to match the naming 
conventions of the Student Body President and Student Body Vice President within the 
Constitution and Statutes, an inconsistency this amendment also seeks to address. More 
fundamentally, the current joint-ticket structure for the Vice President is an anomaly within 
FSU's own model, the Treasurer has always been elected independently, and the Vice 
President's role has grown to a scope and significance that warrants the same independent 
electoral mandate. This amendment would restore structural consistency among the Big 3 by 
ensuring that each elected executive officer derives authority directly from the student body, 
reflecting the distinct responsibilities each office has come to carry over more than seven 
decades of student self-governance at Florida State University. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

In the course of developing this amendment, the author engaged in outreach with members of 
the Student Senate and the broader student body to gauge sentiment regarding the 
independent election of the Student Body Vice President. Through one-on-one conversations 
and informal discussions among colleagues, a number of Senators expressed support for this 
type of legislation and, in many cases, had independently raised the idea themselves before 
formal drafting began. The consistency of this feedback across a wide cross-section of the 
Senate suggests that the current joint-ticket structure has become a point of growing concern 
among student legislators who observe its effects on governance firsthand. 

Several recurring themes emerged from these conversations. First, senators broadly 
recognized that the Student Body Vice President's role has evolved well beyond what a 
running-mate model can adequately reflect. The Vice President now oversees seven identity-
based Agencies, multiple Departments and Leadership Institutes, and the full scope of 
Executive Projects and student-facing programming, a portfolio that is operationally distinct 
from and no less consequential than that of the President. Senators expressed that an officer 
carrying this level of responsibility over the cultural, advocacy, and programmatic life of nearly 
45,000 students should derive their authority from an independent mandate of the student 
body, not from their selection by a single presidential candidate. 

Second, senators raised concerns that the joint-ticket structure effectively limits who is able to 
seek the Vice Presidency. Under the current system, a student who wishes to serve as Vice 
President must first be chosen by a presidential candidate as their running mate, restricting the 
pool of potential Vice Presidents to those within the personal and political network of whoever 
is running for President. Senators noted that this dynamic may exclude otherwise highly 
qualified candidates who could bring valuable experience and perspective to the office but who 
lack a preexisting relationship with a presidential contender. 

Third, and relatedly, senators observed that students themselves have expressed a desire for 
greater choice on the ballot. Under the current structure, voters select a ticket rather than 
independently evaluating candidates for each office. Informal feedback from the student body 
has reflected a sense of disconnect from the Vice Presidential selection, students often feel 
they are voting for a President and receiving a Vice President they may know little about, 
rather than making a deliberate, informed choice for each of the executive officers who will 

 Page 6 of 10

represent them. Restoring the independent election of the Vice President would give every 
student a direct voice in choosing the officer responsible for the Agencies, Institutes, and 
programming that most immediately touch their campus experience. 

The breadth and consistency of this feedback, gathered organically through individual 
conversations rather than a single coordinated effort, demonstrates that this amendment 
reflects a genuine and widely held view within the Legislature that the time has come to align 
the Vice President's electoral structure with the independent scope the office has come to 
carry. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would give the student body more independent choice in their 
executive representation. It would create a separate election of the Student Body Vice 
President by a plurality vote of those voting. Additionally, the amendment changes references 
from “Student Body Treasurer” to “Treasurer” to make language more consistent in the 
Constitution overall in relation to executive positions.

Short Title: Allocating $2,000 from Senate Projects for the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift 

Summary of Legislation: This legislation seeks to allocate $2,000 from the Senate Projects 
account to the Senior Class Council for the procurement and installation of communal seating 
as the Class of 2026 Senior Class Gift. These funds will cover all costs associated with the 
purchase and shipping of high-quality couches to be permanently placed in the Oglesby 
Student Union terrace, providing a lasting enhancement to campus lounge spaces. By funding 
this initiative, the Senate will ensure a tangible contribution to the Florida State student 
experience. 

Background Information: 
The Class Councils are an executive entity of the FSU Student Government Association 
dedicated to fostering campus traditions and leaving a lasting impact on each graduating class. 
For the first time in years, the Senior Class Council is taking donations from Registered 
Student Organizations and the local community to furnish the Oglesby Student Union’s 
second-floor terrace. This legislation aims to allocate $2,000 from Senate Projects to procure 
and install communal seating for the student body to enjoy. 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with the co-sponsorship of Senate President Holliday and the Senior 
Class Council's leadership.

Short Title: Amending the Senate Rules of Procedure to Establish Standing Committee Chair 
Liaison Assignments to Executive Branch Departments 

Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution amends Rule Two of the Senate Rules of Procedure to designate specific 
Standing Committee Chairs as liaisons to corresponding Executive Branch departments. It 
also preserves the Senate President’s authority to appoint additional liaisons to other 
Executive Branch departments as needed. The changes are intended to improve interbranch 
coordination and clarify liaison responsibilities. 

Background Information: 

The Student Senate relies on liaison positions to maintain consistent communication and 
collaboration with Executive Branch departments and campus partners. Currently, liaison 
assignments are largely discretionary, which can lead to uneven engagement and unclear 
lines of responsibility between key Senate committees and their most closely related Executive 
counterparts. 

This legislation formalizes a limited number of high-alignment liaison relationships—specifically 
between Judiciary, Internal Affairs, Finance, and Student Life and their respective Executive 
departments—while preserving the Senate President’s flexibility to assign additional liaisons 
where operationally necessary. By creating clearer structural expectations, the Senate can 
strengthen oversight, improve information flow, and support more coordinated Student 
Government operations. 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This legislation was developed through consultation with Senate President Holliday, and 
Student Body President Dale. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If enacted, this legislation will formally designate certain Standing Committee Chairs as 
liaisons to specified Executive Branch departments while preserving the Senate President’s 
authority to appoint additional liaisons to other Executive Branch departments as needed. The 

 Page 5 of 21

amendment clarifies expectations for interbranch communication and accountability, improves 
structural consistency in Senate liaison assignments, and strengthens coordination between 
the Legislative and Executive Branches without altering the Senate President’s broader 
appointment powers or existing liaison reporting requirements.

Short Title: Amending Rule Ten, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Clarify Definitions and 
Streamline and Codify the Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This resolution updates Rule Ten of the Senate Rules of Procedure to clarify definitions of 
legislative instruments and establish a structured, transparent, and uniform amendment 
process. The changes align Senate procedural rules with recently adopted statutory standards, 
improve clarity for Senators and the public, and enhance efficiency and predictability during 
floor consideration of measures. 

Background Information: 
Rule Ten governs the submission, consideration, and amendment of measures before the 
Student Senate. Prior to this amendment, several key terms were either undefined or 
inconsistently applied, and procedures for submitting and considering amendments lacked 
sufficient structure. This resulted in confusion during debate, last-minute changes to 
legislation, and reduced transparency for both Senators and the public. Following the adoption 
of statutory reforms to the amendment process, it became necessary to revise Rule Ten to 
ensure consistency between the Senate Rules of Procedure and the Student Body Statutes, 
as well as to formally codify best practices that had developed informally over time. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with direct input from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate Leadership, 
and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution clarifies the definitions of legislative instruments, including bills, resolutions, 
amendments, committee substitutes, and late-filed amendments. It codifies procedures for 
submitting amendments in advance of Senate meetings, establishes clear voting thresholds 
and debate procedures for late-filed amendments, and formalizes processes for committee 
substitutes, confirmations, and statements of dissent. Collectively, these changes improve 

 Page 9 of 21

legislative transparency, protect public notice, reduce administrative confusion, and ensure a 
more orderly and deliberative amendment process on the Senate floor.

Short Title: Amending Rule Thirteen of the Senate Rules of Procedure to Codify Disability 
Related Accommodations and Leaves of Absence 

Summary of Legislation: 
This legislation amends Rule Thirteen of the Student Senate Rules of Procedure to establish a 
formal process allowing Senators to request a temporary leave of absence during their term 
due to serious health conditions, family emergencies, or other significant circumstances. The 
amendment also clarifies that disability-related attendance exceptions may be approved by 
Senate leadership or the Rules Committee. The goal is to maintain accountability while 
providing reasonable flexibility for Senators facing circumstances that affect their ability to 
attend meetings. 

Background Information: 

The Student Senate maintains attendance requirements in order to ensure that Senators fulfill 
their responsibilities, maintain quorum, and effectively represent the student body. These 
expectations are essential for the orderly conduct of Senate business and for maintaining 
consistent representation of the student body. 

While the existing rules provide a structure for excused absences, they do not clearly establish 
a process for Senators who may need a temporary pause in participation due to significant 
personal circumstances. Situations such as serious health conditions, family emergencies, or 
other major disruptions may make it difficult for a Senator to maintain regular attendance for a 
limited period of time. 

Additionally, while the Senate has historically exercised discretion when evaluating attendance 
circumstances, the rules do not explicitly recognize that disability-related attendance 
exceptions may sometimes be appropriate. Clarifying this possibility ensures that Senate 
leadership has clear authority to make reasonable attendance determinations when necessary. 

Establishing a defined leave of absence process and clarifying the possibility of disability-
related attendance exceptions helps provide transparency and predictability for both Senators 
and Senate leadership. It also helps ensure that Senators facing temporary challenges are 
able to communicate openly with leadership while maintaining the overall functioning of the 
Senate. 

 Page 16 of 21

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Consultation occurred with current Student Senators and Senate leadership regarding the 
structure of Rule Thirteen and existing attendance practices. Outreach also included 
communication with the Director of the Office of Accessibility Services (OAS) to gather 
feedback regarding the inclusion of language recognizing disability-related attendance 
exceptions. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 

If enacted, this legislation would amend Rule Thirteen of the Student Senate Rules of 
Procedure to establish a formal process through which Senators may request a temporary 
leave of absence during their term for serious health conditions, family emergencies, or other 
significant circumstances. 

The legislation also explicitly states that disability-related attendance exceptions may be 
approved by the Student Senate President, Student Senate President Pro Tempore, and/or the 
Rules Committee. This clarification provides Senate leadership with the authority to make 
reasonable determinations regarding attendance when appropriate. 

During an approved leave of absence, the Senator would not accrue absences and would not 
be counted toward quorum. The Rules Committee would review leave requests and determine 
the conditions under which a Senator may return to active service.

Short Title: Amending the Student Body Constitution, Article III, Section 2, to establish the 
sperate election of Student Body President and Student Body Vice President. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would eliminate the election of the Student Body President and 
Student Body Vice President as a ticket. Instead, students would elect each by a plurality vote. 
The constitutional amendment also clarifies language within the Constitution relating to the 
naming of the Student Body Treasurer, consistently referring to the office as “Treasurer” to 
mirror references made to “President” and “Vice President.” 

Background Information: 
Florida State University has one of the longest and richest traditions of student self-
governance in the state. Student government at FSU predates the university itself: in 1935, 
while the institution was still the Florida State College for Women, the College Government 
Association was established with executive, legislative, and judicial branches. When men were 
admitted in 1946 and the institution became Florida State University in 1947, the CGA split 
briefly into separate Men's and Women's Government Associations before merging in 1948, 
when Charles McMillan was elected the first Student Body President of Florida State. In 1949, 
the body was renamed the University Government Association, and the modern era of FSU 
student governance began, a lineage the SGA celebrated with its 75th anniversary reunion in 
September 2024. 
 
From the earliest days of coeducation, the Student Body President and Student Body Vice 
President have been the two foundational elected executive officers of the student body. The 
presidency has carried extraordinary institutional significance: the Student Body President 
administers and enforces all laws of the Student Body and holds voting seats on the FSU 
Board of Trustees, the Student Affairs Advisory Council, the Athletics Board, and the 
Foundation Board of Trustees. The office has produced a Florida Governor (Reubin Askew, 
the 1950 Student Body President, who later signed the landmark 1974 Activity & Service Fee 
law), and in recent years, four of the last five FSU Student Body Presidents have been elected 
Chair of the Florida Student Association, earning a seat on the Florida Board of Governors. 

 Page 6 of 19

The Student Body Vice President has similarly been an elected position since 1946, though its 
scope and responsibilities have evolved dramatically over the decades. In the early years of 
coeducation, men dominated the top two executive offices, it was not until 1957 that Jan 
Kaminis Platt became the first woman elected Vice President since the FSCW era. For much 
of SGA's history, the Vice President served primarily as a successor-in-waiting and general 
assistant to the President. Over time, however, the role has grown into the primary executive 
officer responsible for overseeing FSU's identity-based Agencies, the Asian American Student 
Union, Black Student Union, Hispanic/Latinx Student Union, Jewish Student Union, Pride 
Student Union, Veterans Student Union, and Women's Student Union, as well as the Bureaus, 
Leadership Institutes (including the Freshman Leadership Institute, founded in 2011, the 
Transfer Leadership Institute, and the Diversity and Inclusion Institute, developed in 2018), and 
the formulation and completion of Executive Projects. The Vice President's portfolio today 
encompasses the full breadth of SGA's student-facing programming, cultural advocacy, and 
leadership development operations, making the office substantively distinct from and 
complementary to the presidency in a way it was not in earlier decades. 
 
Notably, this joint-ticket structure has at times limited the pipeline between the two offices; 
when Stacey Pierre was elected Student Body President in 2018 after serving as Vice 
President, she was the first president in ten years to have previously held the vice presidency, 
suggesting that the running-mate model may discourage rather than encourage continuity of 
experienced executive leadership. 
 
The Student Body Treasurer represents a later but equally significant addition to the elected 
executive structure. The Treasurer's existence as an independently elected officer is 
inseparable from the passage of Chapter 74-312, Laws of Florida, in 1974, the Activity & 
Service Fee law that transferred authority over A&S fee allocation from university 
administrators to student governments. In 1974, Student Body President David Aronofsky, 
Vice President Jan Pietrzyk, and Senate President Doug Mannheimer became the first student 
leaders to set and allocate A&S fees, and in 1975, the first full A&S budget was established. 
This law transformed FSU's SGA from a purely advocacy-oriented body into a fiscal entity, one 
that today manages a budget of nearly $15.4 million. The need for an officer independently 
elected by and accountable to the full student body specifically for financial stewardship led to 
the creation of the Student Body Treasurer as a separately elected at-large position. Critically, 
the Treasurer has always run independently, not on a joint ticket with the President, giving the 
office its own electoral mandate as a fiscal check on executive spending. The Treasurer 
approves all activity and service fee expenditures and holds a constitutional place in the line of 
presidential succession. In 2019, the Pierre/Brown/Pimentel administration initiated the first 
official SGA Audit, and in 2020, the Steinberg/Lee/Dawkins administration created the first 
SGA Finance Videos, reflecting the office's continued growth in transparency and institutional 
responsibility. 
 
The three elected executive officers (colloquially known as the "Big 3") thus represent three 
distinct pillars of student governance: policy leadership and institutional representation 
(Student Body President), programming, identity advocacy, and student life (Student Body 
Vice President), and fiscal stewardship and accountability (Student Body Treasurer). The 

 Page 7 of 19

Student Body Treasurer's title, however, has never been updated to match the naming 
conventions of the Student Body President and Student Body Vice President within the 
Constitution and Statutes, an inconsistency this amendment also seeks to address. More 
fundamentally, the current joint-ticket structure for the Vice President is an anomaly within 
FSU's own model, the Treasurer has always been elected independently, and the Vice 
President's role has grown to a scope and significance that warrants the same independent 
electoral mandate. This amendment would restore structural consistency among the Big 3 by 
ensuring that each elected executive officer derives authority directly from the student body, 
reflecting the distinct responsibilities each office has come to carry over more than seven 
decades of student self-governance at Florida State University. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

In the course of developing this amendment, the author engaged in outreach with members of 
the Student Senate and the broader student body to gauge sentiment regarding the 
independent election of the Student Body Vice President. Through one-on-one conversations 
and informal discussions among colleagues, a number of Senators expressed support for this 
type of legislation and, in many cases, had independently raised the idea themselves before 
formal drafting began. The consistency of this feedback across a wide cross-section of the 
Senate suggests that the current joint-ticket structure has become a point of growing concern 
among student legislators who observe its effects on governance firsthand. 

Several recurring themes emerged from these conversations. First, senators broadly 
recognized that the Student Body Vice President's role has evolved well beyond what a 
running-mate model can adequately reflect. The Vice President now oversees seven identity-
based Agencies, multiple Departments and Leadership Institutes, and the full scope of 
Executive Projects and student-facing programming, a portfolio that is operationally distinct 
from and no less consequential than that of the President. Senators expressed that an officer 
carrying this level of responsibility over the cultural, advocacy, and programmatic life of nearly 
45,000 students should derive their authority from an independent mandate of the student 
body, not from their selection by a single presidential candidate. 

Second, senators raised concerns that the joint-ticket structure effectively limits who is able to 
seek the Vice Presidency. Under the current system, a student who wishes to serve as Vice 
President must first be chosen by a presidential candidate as their running mate, restricting the 
pool of potential Vice Presidents to those within the personal and political network of whoever 
is running for President. Senators noted that this dynamic may exclude otherwise highly 
qualified candidates who could bring valuable experience and perspective to the office but who 
lack a preexisting relationship with a presidential contender. 

Third, and relatedly, senators observed that students themselves have expressed a desire for 
greater choice on the ballot. Under the current structure, voters select a ticket rather than 
independently evaluating candidates for each office. Informal feedback from the student body 
has reflected a sense of disconnect from the Vice Presidential selection, students often feel 
they are voting for a President and receiving a Vice President they may know little about, 
rather than making a deliberate, informed choice for each of the executive officers who will 

 Page 8 of 19

represent them. Restoring the independent election of the Vice President would give every 
student a direct voice in choosing the officer responsible for the Agencies, Institutes, and 
programming that most immediately touch their campus experience. 

The breadth and consistency of this feedback, gathered organically through individual 
conversations rather than a single coordinated effort, demonstrates that this amendment 
reflects a genuine and widely held view within the Legislature that the time has come to align 
the Vice President's electoral structure with the independent scope the office has come to 
carry. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would give the student body more independent choice in their 
executive representation. It would create a separate election of the Student Body Vice 
President by a plurality vote of those voting. Additionally, the amendment changes references 
from “Student Body Treasurer” to “Treasurer” to make language more consistent in the 
Constitution overall in relation to executive positions.

Short Title: Amending the Student Body Constitution, Article III, Section 2, to establish the 
sperate election of Student Body President and Student Body Vice President. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would eliminate the election of the Student Body President and 
Student Body Vice President as a ticket. Instead, students would elect each by a plurality vote. 
The constitutional amendment also clarifies language within the Constitution relating to the 
naming of the Student Body Treasurer, consistently referring to the office as “Treasurer” to 
mirror references made to “President” and “Vice President.” 

Background Information: 
Florida State University has one of the longest and richest traditions of student self-
governance in the state. Student government at FSU predates the university itself: in 1935, 
while the institution was still the Florida State College for Women, the College Government 
Association was established with executive, legislative, and judicial branches. When men were 
admitted in 1946 and the institution became Florida State University in 1947, the CGA split 
briefly into separate Men's and Women's Government Associations before merging in 1948, 
when Charles McMillan was elected the first Student Body President of Florida State. In 1949, 
the body was renamed the University Government Association, and the modern era of FSU 
student governance began, a lineage the SGA celebrated with its 75th anniversary reunion in 
September 2024. 
 
From the earliest days of coeducation, the Student Body President and Student Body Vice 
President have been the two foundational elected executive officers of the student body. The 
presidency has carried extraordinary institutional significance: the Student Body President 
administers and enforces all laws of the Student Body and holds voting seats on the FSU 
Board of Trustees, the Student Affairs Advisory Council, the Athletics Board, and the 
Foundation Board of Trustees. The office has produced a Florida Governor (Reubin Askew, 
the 1950 Student Body President, who later signed the landmark 1974 Activity & Service Fee 
law), and in recent years, four of the last five FSU Student Body Presidents have been elected 
Chair of the Florida Student Association, earning a seat on the Florida Board of Governors. 

 Page 6 of 15

The Student Body Vice President has similarly been an elected position since 1946, though its 
scope and responsibilities have evolved dramatically over the decades. In the early years of 
coeducation, men dominated the top two executive offices, it was not until 1957 that Jan 
Kaminis Platt became the first woman elected Vice President since the FSCW era. For much 
of SGA's history, the Vice President served primarily as a successor-in-waiting and general 
assistant to the President. Over time, however, the role has grown into the primary executive 
officer responsible for overseeing FSU's identity-based Agencies, the Asian American Student 
Union, Black Student Union, Hispanic/Latinx Student Union, Jewish Student Union, Pride 
Student Union, Veterans Student Union, and Women's Student Union, as well as the Bureaus, 
Leadership Institutes (including the Freshman Leadership Institute, founded in 2011, the 
Transfer Leadership Institute, and the Diversity and Inclusion Institute, developed in 2018), and 
the formulation and completion of Executive Projects. The Vice President's portfolio today 
encompasses the full breadth of SGA's student-facing programming, cultural advocacy, and 
leadership development operations, making the office substantively distinct from and 
complementary to the presidency in a way it was not in earlier decades. 
 
Notably, this joint-ticket structure has at times limited the pipeline between the two offices; 
when Stacey Pierre was elected Student Body President in 2018 after serving as Vice 
President, she was the first president in ten years to have previously held the vice presidency, 
suggesting that the running-mate model may discourage rather than encourage continuity of 
experienced executive leadership. 
 
The Student Body Treasurer represents a later but equally significant addition to the elected 
executive structure. The Treasurer's existence as an independently elected officer is 
inseparable from the passage of Chapter 74-312, Laws of Florida, in 1974, the Activity & 
Service Fee law that transferred authority over A&S fee allocation from university 
administrators to student governments. In 1974, Student Body President David Aronofsky, 
Vice President Jan Pietrzyk, and Senate President Doug Mannheimer became the first student 
leaders to set and allocate A&S fees, and in 1975, the first full A&S budget was established. 
This law transformed FSU's SGA from a purely advocacy-oriented body into a fiscal entity, one 
that today manages a budget of nearly $15.4 million. The need for an officer independently 
elected by and accountable to the full student body specifically for financial stewardship led to 
the creation of the Student Body Treasurer as a separately elected at-large position. Critically, 
the Treasurer has always run independently, not on a joint ticket with the President, giving the 
office its own electoral mandate as a fiscal check on executive spending. The Treasurer 
approves all activity and service fee expenditures and holds a constitutional place in the line of 
presidential succession. In 2019, the Pierre/Brown/Pimentel administration initiated the first 
official SGA Audit, and in 2020, the Steinberg/Lee/Dawkins administration created the first 
SGA Finance Videos, reflecting the office's continued growth in transparency and institutional 
responsibility. 
 
The three elected executive officers (colloquially known as the "Big 3") thus represent three 
distinct pillars of student governance: policy leadership and institutional representation 
(Student Body President), programming, identity advocacy, and student life (Student Body 
Vice President), and fiscal stewardship and accountability (Student Body Treasurer). The 

 Page 7 of 15

Student Body Treasurer's title, however, has never been updated to match the naming 
conventions of the Student Body President and Student Body Vice President within the 
Constitution and Statutes, an inconsistency this amendment also seeks to address. More 
fundamentally, the current joint-ticket structure for the Vice President is an anomaly within 
FSU's own model, the Treasurer has always been elected independently, and the Vice 
President's role has grown to a scope and significance that warrants the same independent 
electoral mandate. This amendment would restore structural consistency among the Big 3 by 
ensuring that each elected executive officer derives authority directly from the student body, 
reflecting the distinct responsibilities each office has come to carry over more than seven 
decades of student self-governance at Florida State University. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

In the course of developing this amendment, the author engaged in outreach with members of 
the Student Senate and the broader student body to gauge sentiment regarding the 
independent election of the Student Body Vice President. Through one-on-one conversations 
and informal discussions among colleagues, a number of Senators expressed support for this 
type of legislation and, in many cases, had independently raised the idea themselves before 
formal drafting began. The consistency of this feedback across a wide cross-section of the 
Senate suggests that the current joint-ticket structure has become a point of growing concern 
among student legislators who observe its effects on governance firsthand. 

Several recurring themes emerged from these conversations. First, senators broadly 
recognized that the Student Body Vice President's role has evolved well beyond what a 
running-mate model can adequately reflect. The Vice President now oversees seven identity-
based Agencies, multiple Departments and Leadership Institutes, and the full scope of 
Executive Projects and student-facing programming, a portfolio that is operationally distinct 
from and no less consequential than that of the President. Senators expressed that an officer 
carrying this level of responsibility over the cultural, advocacy, and programmatic life of nearly 
45,000 students should derive their authority from an independent mandate of the student 
body, not from their selection by a single presidential candidate. 

Second, senators raised concerns that the joint-ticket structure effectively limits who is able to 
seek the Vice Presidency. Under the current system, a student who wishes to serve as Vice 
President must first be chosen by a presidential candidate as their running mate, restricting the 
pool of potential Vice Presidents to those within the personal and political network of whoever 
is running for President. Senators noted that this dynamic may exclude otherwise highly 
qualified candidates who could bring valuable experience and perspective to the office but who 
lack a preexisting relationship with a presidential contender. 

Third, and relatedly, senators observed that students themselves have expressed a desire for 
greater choice on the ballot. Under the current structure, voters select a ticket rather than 
independently evaluating candidates for each office. Informal feedback from the student body 
has reflected a sense of disconnect from the Vice Presidential selection, students often feel 
they are voting for a President and receiving a Vice President they may know little about, 
rather than making a deliberate, informed choice for each of the executive officers who will 

 Page 8 of 15

represent them. Restoring the independent election of the Vice President would give every 
student a direct voice in choosing the officer responsible for the Agencies, Institutes, and 
programming that most immediately touch their campus experience. 

The breadth and consistency of this feedback, gathered organically through individual 
conversations rather than a single coordinated effort, demonstrates that this amendment 
reflects a genuine and widely held view within the Legislature that the time has come to align 
the Vice President's electoral structure with the independent scope the office has come to 
carry. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would give the student body more independent choice in their 
executive representation. It would create a separate election of the Student Body Vice 
President by a plurality vote of those voting. Additionally, the amendment changes references 
from “Student Body Treasurer” to “Treasurer” to make language more consistent in the 
Constitution overall in relation to executive positions.

This resolution would transfer a total of $2,500 from Executive Projects to the Development 
Fund.

This transfer was proposed by Student Body Treasurer Erica Wyatt in order to refill the 
Development Fund. This fund would help all Registered Student Organizations across our 
campus by providing support for programming, materials, and other initiatives.

Office of the Student Body Treasurer. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This would allow for the Office of the Treasury to continue to delegate the $300 development 
fund given to every RSO across our campus.
