Short Title: Amending the Student Body Constitution, Article III, Section 2, to establish the 
sperate election of Student Body President and Student Body Vice President. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would eliminate the election of the Student Body President and 
Student Body Vice President as a ticket. Instead, students would elect each by a plurality vote. 
The constitutional amendment also clarifies language within the Constitution relating to the 
naming of the Student Body Treasurer, consistently referring to the office as “Treasurer” to 
mirror references made to “President” and “Vice President.” 

Background Information: 
Florida State University has one of the longest and richest traditions of student self-
governance in the state. Student government at FSU predates the university itself: in 1935, 
while the institution was still the Florida State College for Women, the College Government 
Association was established with executive, legislative, and judicial branches. When men were 
admitted in 1946 and the institution became Florida State University in 1947, the CGA split 
briefly into separate Men's and Women's Government Associations before merging in 1948, 
when Charles McMillan was elected the first Student Body President of Florida State. In 1949, 
the body was renamed the University Government Association, and the modern era of FSU 
student governance began, a lineage the SGA celebrated with its 75th anniversary reunion in 
September 2024. 
 
From the earliest days of coeducation, the Student Body President and Student Body Vice 
President have been the two foundational elected executive officers of the student body. The 
presidency has carried extraordinary institutional significance: the Student Body President 
administers and enforces all laws of the Student Body and holds voting seats on the FSU 
Board of Trustees, the Student Affairs Advisory Council, the Athletics Board, and the 
Foundation Board of Trustees. The office has produced a Florida Governor (Reubin Askew, 
the 1950 Student Body President, who later signed the landmark 1974 Activity & Service Fee 
law), and in recent years, four of the last five FSU Student Body Presidents have been elected 
Chair of the Florida Student Association, earning a seat on the Florida Board of Governors. 

 Page 126 of 199 

The Student Body Vice President has similarly been an elected position since 1946, though its 
scope and responsibilities have evolved dramatically over the decades. In the early years of 
coeducation, men dominated the top two executive offices, it was not until 1957 that Jan 
Kaminis Platt became the first woman elected Vice President since the FSCW era. For much 
of SGA's history, the Vice President served primarily as a successor-in-waiting and general 
assistant to the President. Over time, however, the role has grown into the primary executive 
officer responsible for overseeing FSU's identity-based Agencies, the Asian American Student 
Union, Black Student Union, Hispanic/Latinx Student Union, Jewish Student Union, Pride 
Student Union, Veterans Student Union, and Women's Student Union, as well as the Bureaus, 
Leadership Institutes (including the Freshman Leadership Institute, founded in 2011, the 
Transfer Leadership Institute, and the Diversity and Inclusion Institute, developed in 2018), and 
the formulation and completion of Executive Projects. The Vice President's portfolio today 
encompasses the full breadth of SGA's student-facing programming, cultural advocacy, and 
leadership development operations, making the office substantively distinct from and 
complementary to the presidency in a way it was not in earlier decades. 
 
Notably, this joint-ticket structure has at times limited the pipeline between the two offices; 
when Stacey Pierre was elected Student Body President in 2018 after serving as Vice 
President, she was the first president in ten years to have previously held the vice presidency, 
suggesting that the running-mate model may discourage rather than encourage continuity of 
experienced executive leadership. 
 
The Student Body Treasurer represents a later but equally significant addition to the elected 
executive structure. The Treasurer's existence as an independently elected officer is 
inseparable from the passage of Chapter 74-312, Laws of Florida, in 1974, the Activity & 
Service Fee law that transferred authority over A&S fee allocation from university 
administrators to student governments. In 1974, Student Body President David Aronofsky, 
Vice President Jan Pietrzyk, and Senate President Doug Mannheimer became the first student 
leaders to set and allocate A&S fees, and in 1975, the first full A&S budget was established. 
This law transformed FSU's SGA from a purely advocacy-oriented body into a fiscal entity, one 
that today manages a budget of nearly $15.4 million. The need for an officer independently 
elected by and accountable to the full student body specifically for financial stewardship led to 
the creation of the Student Body Treasurer as a separately elected at-large position. Critically, 
the Treasurer has always run independently, not on a joint ticket with the President, giving the 
office its own electoral mandate as a fiscal check on executive spending. The Treasurer 
approves all activity and service fee expenditures and holds a constitutional place in the line of 
presidential succession. In 2019, the Pierre/Brown/Pimentel administration initiated the first 
official SGA Audit, and in 2020, the Steinberg/Lee/Dawkins administration created the first 
SGA Finance Videos, reflecting the office's continued growth in transparency and institutional 
responsibility. 
 
The three elected executive officers (colloquially known as the "Big 3") thus represent three 
distinct pillars of student governance: policy leadership and institutional representation 
(Student Body President), programming, identity advocacy, and student life (Student Body 
Vice President), and fiscal stewardship and accountability (Student Body Treasurer). The 

 Page 127 of 199 

Student Body Treasurer's title, however, has never been updated to match the naming 
conventions of the Student Body President and Student Body Vice President within the 
Constitution and Statutes, an inconsistency this amendment also seeks to address. More 
fundamentally, the current joint-ticket structure for the Vice President is an anomaly within 
FSU's own model, the Treasurer has always been elected independently, and the Vice 
President's role has grown to a scope and significance that warrants the same independent 
electoral mandate. This amendment would restore structural consistency among the Big 3 by 
ensuring that each elected executive officer derives authority directly from the student body, 
reflecting the distinct responsibilities each office has come to carry over more than seven 
decades of student self-governance at Florida State University. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

In the course of developing this amendment, the author engaged in outreach with members of 
the Student Senate and the broader student body to gauge sentiment regarding the 
independent election of the Student Body Vice President. Through one-on-one conversations 
and informal discussions among colleagues, a number of Senators expressed support for this 
type of legislation and, in many cases, had independently raised the idea themselves before 
formal drafting began. The consistency of this feedback across a wide cross-section of the 
Senate suggests that the current joint-ticket structure has become a point of growing concern 
among student legislators who observe its effects on governance firsthand. 

Several recurring themes emerged from these conversations. First, senators broadly 
recognized that the Student Body Vice President's role has evolved well beyond what a 
running-mate model can adequately reflect. The Vice President now oversees seven identity-
based Agencies, multiple Departments and Leadership Institutes, and the full scope of 
Executive Projects and student-facing programming, a portfolio that is operationally distinct 
from and no less consequential than that of the President. Senators expressed that an officer 
carrying this level of responsibility over the cultural, advocacy, and programmatic life of nearly 
45,000 students should derive their authority from an independent mandate of the student 
body, not from their selection by a single presidential candidate. 

Second, senators raised concerns that the joint-ticket structure effectively limits who is able to 
seek the Vice Presidency. Under the current system, a student who wishes to serve as Vice 
President must first be chosen by a presidential candidate as their running mate, restricting the 
pool of potential Vice Presidents to those within the personal and political network of whoever 
is running for President. Senators noted that this dynamic may exclude otherwise highly 
qualified candidates who could bring valuable experience and perspective to the office but who 
lack a preexisting relationship with a presidential contender. 

Third, and relatedly, senators observed that students themselves have expressed a desire for 
greater choice on the ballot. Under the current structure, voters select a ticket rather than 
independently evaluating candidates for each office. Informal feedback from the student body 
has reflected a sense of disconnect from the Vice Presidential selection, students often feel 
they are voting for a President and receiving a Vice President they may know little about, 
rather than making a deliberate, informed choice for each of the executive officers who will 

 Page 128 of 199 

represent them. Restoring the independent election of the Vice President would give every 
student a direct voice in choosing the officer responsible for the Agencies, Institutes, and 
programming that most immediately touch their campus experience. 

The breadth and consistency of this feedback, gathered organically through individual 
conversations rather than a single coordinated effort, demonstrates that this amendment 
reflects a genuine and widely held view within the Legislature that the time has come to align 
the Vice President's electoral structure with the independent scope the office has come to 
carry. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This constitutional amendment would give the student body more independent choice in their 
executive representation. It would create a separate election of the Student Body Vice 
President by a plurality vote of those voting. Additionally, the amendment changes references 
from “Student Body Treasurer” to “Treasurer” to make language more consistent in the 
Constitution overall in relation to executive positions.

Short Title: Amending Chapter 401, Student Body Statutes, to Streamline and Codify the 
Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This bill amends Chapter 401 of the Student Body Statutes to establish a clear, structured, and 
transparent process for submitting and considering amendments to legislation. The proposed 
changes enhance legislative efficiency, promote informed deliberation, and ensure meaningful 
public notice and participation throughout the amendment process. 

Background Information: 
Prior to this amendment, the Student Body Statutes lacked a formalized process for submitting 
amendments to measures outside of standing committee proceedings. As a result, 
amendments were frequently introduced orally and in large batches on the Senate floor, often 
without sufficient notice to Senators or the public. 
 
This practice created confusion during debate, administrative inefficiencies, and uncertainty 
regarding the substance of legislation under consideration. In some cases, measures were 
materially altered from their publicly noticed descriptions, undermining transparency and public 
trust in the legislative process. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with input comment from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate 
Leadership, and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This bill establishes a standardized amendment submission process, including the creation of 
an amendment submission form and a forty-eight (48) hour deadline for amendments prior to a 
bill’s second reading. It increases procedural safeguards for late-filed amendments by raising 
voting thresholds and authorizing recesses for review. 

 Page 135 of 199 

Additionally, the legislation requires amendments that materially alter a measure’s publicly 
noticed purpose or description to be clearly identified as such, thereby strengthening 
transparency, preserving public notice, and improving the overall integrity of the legislative 
process.

Short Title: Amending Rule Ten, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Clarify Definitions and 
Streamline and Codify the Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This resolution updates Rule Ten of the Senate Rules of Procedure to clarify definitions of 
legislative instruments and establish a structured, transparent, and uniform amendment 
process. The changes align Senate procedural rules with recently adopted statutory standards, 
improve clarity for Senators and the public, and enhance efficiency and predictability during 
floor consideration of measures. 

Background Information: 
Rule Ten governs the submission, consideration, and amendment of measures before the 
Student Senate. Prior to this amendment, several key terms were either undefined or 
inconsistently applied, and procedures for submitting and considering amendments lacked 
sufficient structure. This resulted in confusion during debate, last-minute changes to 
legislation, and reduced transparency for both Senators and the public. Following the adoption 
of statutory reforms to the amendment process, it became necessary to revise Rule Ten to 
ensure consistency between the Senate Rules of Procedure and the Student Body Statutes, 
as well as to formally codify best practices that had developed informally over time. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with direct input from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate Leadership, 
and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution clarifies the definitions of legislative instruments, including bills, resolutions, 
amendments, committee substitutes, and late-filed amendments. It codifies procedures for 
submitting amendments in advance of Senate meetings, establishes clear voting thresholds 
and debate procedures for late-filed amendments, and formalizes processes for committee 
substitutes, confirmations, and statements of dissent. Collectively, these changes improve 

 Page 137 of 199 

legislative transparency, protect public notice, reduce administrative confusion, and ensure a 
more orderly and deliberative amendment process on the Senate floor.

displacement for the citizens of Ukraine. The conflict has been determined, per the

recognition of Ukraine's efforts to keep its integrity as a nation and to realize recognition as an 
important step towards moving for peace.

scale invasion on February 24, 2022. This proclamation serves to address the need brought up 
by students who sought out recognition from student government of the nation's struggle for 
sovereignty abroad. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Florida State University Students. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation:

campus for the purpose of moving towards peace and security.

Short Title: Amending the Senate Rules of Procedure to Establish Standing Committee Chair

Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution amends Rule Two of the Senate Rules of Procedure to designate specific 
Standing Committee Chairs as liaisons to corresponding Executive Branch departments. It 
also preserves the Senate President’s authority to appoint additional liaisons to other 
Executive Branch departments as needed. The changes are intended to improve interbranch 
coordination and clarify liaison responsibilities. 

Background Information: 

The Student Senate relies on liaison positions to maintain consistent communication and 
collaboration with Executive Branch departments and campus partners. Currently, liaison 
assignments are largely discretionary, which can lead to uneven engagement and unclear 
lines of responsibility between key Senate committees and their most closely related Executive 
counterparts. 

This legislation formalizes a limited number of high-alignment liaison relationships—specifically 
between Judiciary, Internal Affairs, Finance, and Student Life and their respective Executive 
departments—while preserving the Senate President’s flexibility to assign additional liaisons 
where operationally necessary. By creating clearer structural expectations, the Senate can 
strengthen oversight, improve information flow, and support more coordinated Student 
Government operations. 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This legislation was developed through consultation with Senate President Holliday, and 
Student Body President Dale. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If enacted, this legislation will formally designate certain Standing Committee Chairs as 
liaisons to specified Executive Branch departments while preserving the Senate President’s 
authority to appoint additional liaisons to other Executive Branch departments as needed. The

structural consistency in Senate liaison assignments, and strengthens coordination between 
the Legislative and Executive Branches without altering the Senate President’s broader

Short Title: Amending Senate Rule of Procedure to Exclude Religious Holy Days from 
Absence Penalties 

Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution amends Senate Rule of Procedure 13.4 to clarify that absences taken in 
observance of a religious holy day, as recognized under Rule 13.9(b)(4), shall not constitute a 
half absence. While religious holy days are currently classified as excused absences, they still 
result in a half-absence penalty under existing language. This amendment ensures that the 
Senate Rules of Procedure and Student Body Statutes § 206.1, which states that Student 
Government Officers shall not be penalized for observing a holy day. 

Background Information: 
Under current Senate Rules of Procedure, excused absences result in a half absence being 
assessed to the Senator. Rule 13.9(b)(4) explicitly includes religious holy days as a valid 
excused absence reason. However, Student Body Statues § 206.1 provides that Student 
Government Officers shall not be penalized for choosing to observe a holy day. This creates a 
procedural inconsistency in which religious observance is recognized as excused yet still 
carries a penalty. As members of the Student Senate represent a diverse student body with a 
variety of religious backgrounds and obligations, it is important that Senate policies allow 
inclusivity and statutory compliance. This legislation is presented to ensure the consistency 
between both governing documents. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

In drafting this resolution, consultation occurred with student leaders representing faith-based 
organizations at Florida State University. Sam Nunnally, Director of the Catholic Student 
Union, expressed support for ensuring that students are not placed in a position where they 
must choose between their religious observances and their civic responsibilities within Student 
Government. Rameen Ahmad, President of the Muslim Student Union, also voiced support for 
the amendment and affirmed the importance of protecting religious holy day observances from 
penalty within Senate attendance policy. Sela Teplin, Director of the Jewish Student Union, 
also voiced support for the amendment and affirmed the importance of protecting religious holy 
day observances from penalty within Senate attendance policy. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 

 Page 151 of 199 

This resolution would amend Senate Rule of Procedure 13.4 to explicitly state that an excused 
absence taken pursuant to Rule (13.9)(b)(4) for observance of a religious holy day shall not 
constitute a half absence. Religious holy day observances would therefore not count toward 
the maximum number of excused absences permitted per term.

Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution amends Rule 10 and Rule 8 of the Senate Rules of Procedure to more clearly 
define the various forms of legislation considered by the Senate, resolutions, allocation 
resolutions, and proclamations. It distinguishes proclamations as ceremonial recognitions 
separate from policy-oriented resolutions and aligns Senate Rules with updates made to 
Student Body Statutes Chapter 401. The legislation also updates submission deadlines to be 
consistent with current Senate practices. 

Background Information: 
Rule 10 of the Senate Rules of Procedure currently governs the forms of legislation considered 
by the 78th Student Senate at Florida State University. However, recent updates to Student 
Body Statutes Chapter 401, “Forms of Legislation,” have created inconsistencies between 
statutory language and the Senate’s internal rules. In particular, proclamations—while regularly 
utilized for ceremonial recognition—are not clearly distinguished from resolutions within the 
Rules of Procedure. To promote consistency, transparency, and orderly legislative practice, 
the Rules of Procedure must be updated to align with statutory definitions and clearly delineate 
each recognized form of Senate action.

Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution establishes a three-hour maximum committee meeting duration, with meetings 
adjourning no later than 11:30 PM unless extended by a majority vote. This guideline is 
intended to support effective student leadership within committee operations. 

Background Information: 

Members of the Student Senate serve as full-time students balancing academic, professional, 
and personal responsibilities in addition to their legislative service. Committee meetings that 
extend late into the evening may reduce productivity, weaken the quality of deliberation, and 
contribute to unnecessary fatigue. Effective committee operations depend upon focused 
discussion, structured agendas, and responsible use of time. Establishing a clear committee 
adjournment time would encourage efficient agenda planning while reinforcing the Senate’s 
commitment to effective governance. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
The proposed legislation would formally establish a recommended committee adjournment 
guideline for regular meetings. While committees would retain flexibility to extend meetings by 
vote when necessary, this resolution promotes efficiency, intentional leadership, and improved 
meeting practices within the 78th Student Senate.

Short Title: Specifying Florida Statute 1004.26 in Chapter 405: Impeachment And Removal 
From Office 

Summary of Legislation: 

This bill would amend the Student Body Statues Chapter 405, “Impeachment And Removal 
From Office”. This bill clarifies the jurisdiction and procedures for impeachment, suspension, 
removal, resignation, and appeal of Student Government officers and guarantees officers the 
right to appeal disciplinary actions to the Vice President of Student Affairs or a designated 
senior administrator pursuant to Florida Statute 1004.26(4)(d). 

Background Information: 
This bill was requested to be adopted by the FSU General Council as it not a SGA policy, but a 
State of Florida Law. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

The FSU General Council, Senate President Holliday, Student Governance & Advocacy 
Advising Staff. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 

This provision establishes a formal right of appeal for any elected or appointed Student 
Government officer who has been disciplined, suspended, or removed from office. It allows the 
officer to directly appeal the decision to the Vice President of Student Affairs or another 
designated senior university administrator pursuant to Florida Statute 1004.26(4)(d). The 
legislation further clarifies that exercising this right to appeal, and any resulting administrative 
decision, does not serve as a condition precedent to or override the authority of any Student 
Government judicial or student panel proceedings, thereby preserving institutional due process 
while maintaining student governance autonomy.1004.26(4)(d).

sections.text:
76th 
 Calendar: March 4, 2026 
 Location: Courtroom A121, College of Law Advocacy Center 
 Time: 8:00 AM 
 Submit Public Comment Here 

Ordes and Motions 
• SC-26-SP-02 

Briefs 

 Page 1 of 28
 IN THE STUDENT BODY SUPREME COURT 
 OF FLORIDA STATE UNIVERSITY 

RILEY PERANTONI, 

 Petitioner, 

v. 

CARSON DALE, in his official capacity as Student Body President, 

 Respondent. 

 / 

 COMPLAINT FOR CONSTITUTIONAL AND STATUTORY VIOLATIONS 

 The Petitioner, RILEY PERANTONI, a Student Senator, hereby files this 

Complaint against Respondent, CARSON DALE, and in support thereof, states 

as follows: 

 JURISDICTION 

1. This is an action for declaratory and injunctive relief, and for the issuance of 

 extraordinary writs, arising from violations of the Student Body Constitution 

 and Student Body Statutes. This Court has original jurisdiction pursuant to 

 Article IV, Sections 3.3(a) and (b) of the Student Body Constitution, which 

 vests the Court with authority over "cases and controversies involving 

 questions of the constitutionality of actions by student governing groups" 

 and "violations of the Student Body Constitution and Statutes." 

2. Jurisdiction is further invoked under Article III, Section 6 and Article II, 

 Section 6(1)(b), which provide that executive policies, such as the contested 

 1 

 Page 2 of 28
 Executive Orders (#80-06, #80-07, #80-09, #80-10, and #80-11), are subject 

 to judicial review by the Student Supreme Court in the same manner as 

 legislation. This controversy involves the interpretation of the "advice and 

 consent" powers under Article II, Section 5(1)(d) and Article III, Section 3(2), 

 and specific statutory violations including, but not limited to, SBS § 301.4. 

3. Because the Respondent is a Student Body Officer, this Court is empowered

 under Article IV, Section 3.3(d) to issue writs of mandamus, prohibition, and 

 quo warranto, or such other writs necessary and proper to the complete 

 exercise of its jurisdiction. This matter is ripe for adjudication as it presents 

 the specific "litigation" regarding statutory violations contemplated by this 

 Court in Advisory Opinion 2025-03.

 PARTIES AND STANDING 

4. Petitioner, RILEY PERANTONI, is a student at Florida State University and

 a duly elected Student Senator currently serving in the 78th Student

 Senate. At all times material to this action, Petitioner has been acting in

 their official capacity as a member of the Legislative Branch.

5. Respondent, CARSON DALE, is the Student Body President. Respondent is

 the officer responsible for issuing the challenged Executive Orders and is

 the appointing authority under Article III of the Student Body Constitution.

6. Petitioner has standing to bring this action because the Respondent's

 conduct has resulted in a concrete and particularized injury-in-fact to the

 Petitioner’s constitutionally mandated duties. Pursuant to Article II, Section

 5(1)(d) of the Student Body Constitution, the Petitioner possesses a non-

 2 

 Page 3 of 28
 discretionary constitutional right and duty to "Consider appointments of the 

 Student Body President... by a majority vote." This 'Advice and Consent' 

 power is not a mere privilege or post-hoc formality; it is a mandatory 

 constitutional check and a condition precedent to the lawful exercise of 

 executive authority. The Respondent's failure to present these nominees 

 constitutes a structural injury to the Senate’s institutional integrity. When 

 the Executive Branch unilaterally fills offices, it engages in constitutional 

 aggrandizement, stripping the Petitioner of their non-discretionary oversight 

 role and nullifying their individual voting power. 

7. By issuing Executive Orders #80-06, #80-07, #80-09, #80-10, and #80-11

 and seating individuals in Executive Department roles without seeking

 Senate confirmation, the Respondent has nullified the Petitioner’s individual

 voting power. This bypass of the "advice and consent" process constitutes a

 "power-grab" that prevents the Petitioner from exercising the legislative

 check-and-balance mandated by the Constitution.

8. Furthermore, Petitioner maintains standing as a representative of the

 Student Body. Pursuant to the Mission Statement in Article I, Section 3, the

 Student Government Association exists to provide students with

 "representation, services and advocacy." The Student Body exercises this

 right to representation through the Senate’s oversight of the Executive

 Branch.

9. When the Respondent bypasses the confirmation process, he creates a

 representational void where executive officers operate without the "lawful

 consent of the governed" as expressed through their elected representatives.

 3 

 Page 4 of 28
 This constitutes an injury to the Petitioner’s ability to provide the 

 "representation and advocacy" they are sworn to uphold. 

10. The injury to the Petitioner is actual and ongoing. The Petitioner is

 currently unable to perform their constitutionally required role in the

 appointment process for over a dozen executive positions currently filled by

 the Respondent’s unilateral action. This injury is direct, ongoing, and

 unique to the Petitioner's status as a Senator. It is not a generalized

 grievance, as the Petitioner is one of the few individuals specifically

 empowered by the Constitution to rectify this breach through a vote—a vote

 that the Respondent has unilaterally withheld.

11. This injury to the Petitioner’s legislative authority is directly traceable to the

 Respondent’s issuance of the challenged Executive Orders and is

 redressable by this Court through the exercise of its authority under Article

 IV, Section 3.3(d) to declare such appointments void and compel

 constitutional compliance.

12. Petitioner further asserts that the Respondent's actions violate the

 Separation of Powers doctrine. By merging the power of appointment (Art.

 III) with the power of confirmation (Art. II), the Respondent has engaged in

 structural encroachment that is alien to the Student Body Constitution. 

 This attempt to exercise a consolidated authority—whereby the Executive 

 Branch bypasses the Senate’s non-discretionary oversight—seeks to replace 

 the "Advice and Consent" process with executive fiat. Such a model renders 

 the Senate’s constitutional role inchoate and is destructive to the "checks 

 and balances" system intended by the framers of the Student Body Statutes. 

 4 

 Page 5 of 28
 GENERAL ALLEGATIONS 

13. The Student Body Constitution and the Student Body Statutes establish a

 mandatory, exhaustive framework for the confirmation of executive

 appointees.

14. Pursuant to Article II, Section 5(1)(d) of the Student Body Constitution, the

 Student Senate is required to consider "appointments of the Student Body

 President... by a majority vote for other appointments."

15. This constitutional mandate is codified and expanded upon in Student

 Body Statute § 201, which states: "Appointments of the Student Body

 President shall require... a majority vote for all other appointments except

 for Supreme Court Justices... under any circumstances." (Emphasis added).

16. Further, SBS § 301.4(c) explicitly defines the scope of the Cabinet, stating

 that "Additional internal department roles... shall be created... subject to

 approval from the Student Body President and Student Senate" and that "All

 roles within Executive Departments shall compose the Executive Cabinet."

17. On December 12, 2025, this Court issued a non-binding Advisory Opinion

 2025-03, clarifying that "The President may not fill Cabinet positions

 without Senate confirmation."

18. Notwithstanding these requirements, the Respondent has established a

 pattern of seating individuals in executive roles via Executive Order without

 seeking the "advice and consent" of the Student Senate.

19. On September 3, 2025, Respondent issued Executive Order #80-07,

 appointing Adriana Diaz (Graphic Design Director), Alyson Mizanin (Social

 Media Director), Carson Mann (Programming Coordinator), and London

 5 

 Page 6 of 28
 Jackoboice (Media & Content Director) to positions within Executive 

 Departments. 

20. On October 2, 2025, Respondent issued Executive Order #80-09,

 appointing eight additional individuals—including Jessica Weinberg, Patrick

 Ball, Charlotte Brown, Kaylee Vasquez, Natalie Gonzalez, Emily Dorman,

 Malek Mani, and Angelina Kennedy—to "positions within various Executive

 Departments.”

21. On November 13, 2025, Respondent issued Executive Order #80-10,

 appointing Claudia Urday as "Deputy Solicitor General" within the

 Department of Legal Affairs.

22. On December 4, 2025, Respondent issued Executive Order #80-11,

 appointing several individuals to roles that did not previously exist within

 the statutory structure of the Executive Branch. Pursuant to SBS § 301.4(c),

 the creation of "additional internal department roles" is explicitly subject to

 "approval from the... Student Senate." No such approval was sought or

 granted prior to these appointments.

23. The appointments in EO #80-11 included Ian Seibert, Isabella LoBianco,

 Jack Rowan, and Nicolas Valenzuela. Notably, Mr. Rowan was named to a

 dual-role capacity as "Senior Counselor to the Student Body President and

 Attorney General."

24. At the time of this appointment, and continuing through the date of this

 filing, Mr. Rowan serves in a major elected position, as a Representative of

 the College of Law, in the Congress of Graduate Students. This dual-service

 creates a structural conflict between the Congress of Graduate Students

 6 

 Page 7 of 28
 and the Executive Branch, further complicating the lack of Senate oversight 

 through the "advice and consent" process. 

25. The Petitioner has identified an undocumented and unilateral promotion of

 Logan Rubenstein to the title of "Deputy Attorney General".

26. Mr. Rubenstein previously served in the confirmed role of Legislative Affairs

 Coordinator; however, he has repeatedly identified himself as "Deputy

 Attorney General" for the official record during convened meetings of the

 77th and 78th Student Senate.

27. There is a total absence of any notification, Executive Order, or Forwarding

 Letter memorializing this change in role or elevation in authority.

28. Unlike other challenged roles, the "Deputy Attorney General" position

 appears neither in the Department of Legal Affairs structure in Student

 Body Statutes nor in Respondent’s own unratified Executive Order #80-06.

29. On February 6, 2026, following the issuance of Senate President

 Memorandum #78-001 ("Notice of Non-Compliance"), the Respondent

 transmitted a Forwarding Letter to the Student Senate.

30. Notably, this letter only included the name of Nicolas Valenzuela for the

 position of Secretary of Campus Life. The Respondent’s decision to forward

 Mr. Valenzuela—and only Mr. Valenzuela—serves as an admission of the

 Respondent's knowledge that these positions are subject to Senate

 confirmation.

31. Despite this admission, the Respondent has failed to forward the names of

 the remaining appointees listed in EO #80-07, #80-09, #80-10, and #80-11,

 including those in newly created roles that have not been authorized by the

 7 

 Page 8 of 28
 Student Senate. 

32. Under SBS § 301.4(b)(4)(C), "Acting" capacity is limited to six (6) weeks. For

 the individuals in EO #80-11, this authority expired on or about January

 15, 2026. Aside from Mr. Valenzuela, all other "Acting" appointees continue

 to hold office in violation of this temporal limit.

33. Pursuant to SBS § 202.4, Senate confirmation is a "condition precedent" to

 the performance of any duties. The individuals named in Paragraphs 19-23

 continue to perform official duties and utilize SGA resources without having

 satisfied this condition.

34. Specific to the appointments in EO #80-11, the Respondent failed to

 comply with the mandatory Candidate Search requirements of Executive

 Branch Policy EXEC-2024-02, Section 3. Specifically:

 (a) “No position requiring Senate confirmation may be filled until it has been

 advertised properly."

 (b) “All positions must be advertised for at least one week on the SGA

 Website."

 (c) Unlike the appointments in EOs #80-07, #80-09, and #80-10, the roles

 in EO #80-11 were never publicly advertised, depriving the student body

 of the "fair and open" process mandated by Article I, Section 5(7) of the

 Student Body Constitution.

35. Specific to the appointments in EO #80-11, the Respondent failed to

 conduct the Candidate Screening Process required by EXEC-2024-02,

 Section 4, which mandates that the Chief of Staff "shall interview all

 candidates." Because no application process or public notice existed for the

 8 

 Page 9 of 28
 EO #80-11 positions, no competitive screening or standardized interviews 

 occurred, rendering these appointments statutorily defective from their 

 inception. 

 COUNT I : SYSTEMIC VIOLATION OF ARTICLE II 

36. Petitioner incorporates by reference the allegations contained in Paragraphs

 1 through 35 as if fully set forth herein.

37. The Student Body Constitution, under Article II, Section 5(1)(d), grants the

 Student Senate the express power to "[c]onsider appointments of the

 Student Body President... by a majority vote for other appointments."

38. This constitutional mandate is further strengthened by SBS § 201, which

 provides that "Appointments of the Student Body President shall require... a

 majority vote for all other appointments... under any circumstances."

39. Under the standard of Plain Meaning and the precedent of State v. Bodden,

 877 So. 2d 680 (Fla. 2004), when the language of a governing document is

 clear and unambiguous, the Court must give effect to that language as

 written. The phrase "all other appointments" contains no qualifying

 language and admits no exceptions for "staff" or "administrative" roles.

40. By seating individuals in the roles listed in EO #80-07, #80-09, #80-10,

 and #80-11 without seeking a majority vote, the Respondent has effectively

 written a "staff exception" into the Constitution that does not exist. The

 Student Body Constitution is a document of enumerated powers. Where the

 text is silent regarding a “staff exception,” no such power exists. The

 Respondent cannot find in the margins of the Constitution a power that the

 9 

 Page 10 of 28
 Student Body did not explicitly grant. 

41. This Court must apply the Canon against Surplusage, which dictates that a 

 text must be interpreted so that no word or phrase is rendered meaningless. 

 If the Respondent is permitted to unilaterally designate appointees as "staff" 

 to bypass the Senate, the constitutional requirement for "other 

 appointments" in Article II is rendered a functional nullity. To hold otherwise 

 would be to suggest the Framers included the "Advice and Consent" clause 

 as mere "constitutional window-dressing"—a conclusion forbidden by the 

 rules of construction.

42. Furthermore, the Respondent’s actions violate the Separation of Powers and 

 the principle against Constitutional Encroachment. As established in Chiles 

 v. United Faculty of Florida, 615 So. 2d 671 (Fla. 1993), one branch of 

 government may not "encroach upon the powers of another." By merging the 

 power of appointment with the power of confirmation, the Respondent has 

 usurped the Senate's constitutionally mandated checking function.

43. Finally, pursuant to SBS § 202.4, "Duties, rights, and responsibilities, shall 

 vest upon confirmation by the Student Senate and upon taking the oath of 

 office." Because no confirmation has occurred for the appointments in the 

 challenged Executive Orders, no legal authority has vested in these 

 individuals. Their current exercise of executive power is therefore ultra vires. 

 Any official actions or exercise of policy by these unconfirmed individuals is 

 legally void and constitutes a breach of the public trust as defined in the 

 Preamble of the Student Body Constitution.

45. Pursuant to Student Body Statute § 301.4(c), the creation of "additional

 internal department roles" is explicitly "subject to approval from the Student

 Body President and Student Senate". Furthermore, this statute mandates

 that "all roles within Executive Departments shall compose the Executive

 Cabinet," thereby establishing that no "staff" loophole exists for roles created

 within these departments.

46. On December 4, 2025, the Respondent issued Executive Order #80-11,

 which created and purportedly filled several roles that did not previously

 exist within the statutory structure of the Executive Branch or the ratified

 Executive Cabinet Structure (EXEC-2024-01), including "Senior Counselor

 to the Student Body President," "Senior Advisor and Special Projects

 Coordinator," and "Community Affairs Coordinator".

47. Because these positions were created without the mandatory approval of

 the Student Senate required by SBS § 301.4(c), these offices are legally non-

 existent. Consequently, the appointments of Ian Seibert, Isabella LoBianco,

 and Jack Rowan to these unauthorized positions are void ab initio.

48. Further, Executive Branch Policy EXEC-2024-02, Section 3 stipulates that

 "no position requiring Student Senate confirmation may be filled until the

 position has been advertised properly". Proper advertisement requires that

 positions be posted for "at least one week on the SGA Website".

 and public notices from November 20, 2025, through December 4, 2025,

 reveals a total absence of the mandatory notice for the positions established

 in EO #80-11. This failure to provide public notice constitutes a fatal

 procedural defect that renders the subsequent appointments statutorily

 invalid.

 Screening Process," requiring that the Chief of Staff or a designee "shall

 interview all candidates" using a "standardized and professional form".

51. Because the roles in EO #80-11 were never advertised and no application

 process was opened to the Student Body, no competitive screening or

 standardized interviews occurred. The Respondent’s unilateral selection

 process bypassed these mandatory statutory safeguards, depriving qualified

 students of the opportunity to apply for and serve in these roles.

52. These statutory failures are not purely technical; they constitute a per se

 violation of Article I, Section 5(7) of the Student Body Constitution, which

 mandates that the Student Government Association develop policies in a

 "fair and open manner". The search and screening requirements of the

 Student Body Statutes are the functional mechanisms that give the "Fair

 and Open" clause its meaning. By subverting these statutes, the

 Respondent has necessarily violated the constitutional rights of the Student

 Body to open and equitable access to government service.

 Body President (for Secretaries) or the Secretary and Student Body

 President (for Directors and Coordinators) may designate an acting officer,

 who may serve for no more than six (6) weeks without Senate confirmation".

 ensure that temporary appointments do not subvert the Student Senate’s

55. On December 4, 2025, the Respondent issued Executive Order #80-11,

 appointing Ian Seibert, Isabella LoBianco, and Jack Rowan to "Acting"

 these individuals expired exactly six (6) calendar weeks later, on January

56. As of January 16, 2026, the authority of these individuals ceased by

 operation of law. Because no formal nominations were forwarded to the

 Senate by the expiration of this term, Ian Seibert, Isabella LoBianco, and

 Jack Rowan were stripped of their official status and returned to the status

 of private citizens.

 January 15, 2026, these individuals have persisted in a systemic

 usurpation of office. It is a brazen and ongoing impersonation of government

 student-funded office space, and, most critically, exercise “Significant

 administrative or clerical. While the Student Body Constitution and Statutes

 require confirmation for all executive appointments without exception, the

 judicial thresholds for "significant authority." See Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S.

 the Department of Legal Affairs. In this capacity, he has actively assisted in

 independent to effectively represent the interests of graduate students.

 Florida jurisprudence, a person is prohibited from holding two offices where

 the duties conflict or where the independence of one is compromised by the

 other (Gryzik v. State, 380 So. 2d 1102). A legislator cannot impartially serve

 counselor for the Executive Branch.

 Executive Branch. Under the principle of Omnia Praesumuntur Contra

 Short Title: Funding support for the 2026 LINC Graduate Student Conference 

 Summary of Legislation: This legislation authorizes funding support for the 2026 Literatures 
 and Linguistics Interdisciplinary Conference (LINC) at Florida State University. The requested 
 funds will help cover keynote expenses, conference materials, and food for presenters and 
 attendees. The bill aims to support interdisciplinary graduate student research, collaboration, 
 and professional development. 

 Background Information: The Literatures and Linguistics Interdisciplinary Conference (LINC) 
 is an annual, graduate-student-led conference hosted by the Department of Modern Languages 
 and Linguistics at Florida State University. The conference brings together undergraduate 
 students, graduate students, and independent scholars from institutions across the United

Short Title: Amending Cogs Code, Chapter 204.4 to establish procedure in the event of a 
tie in Deputy elections.

Summary of Legislation: This bill would amend Chapter 204, COGS Code, to establish 
procedure in the event of a tie in Deputy elections. The bill makes the presiding officer 
of the contested position the tie breaker in the event of a second tie. The bill provides 
that after a first round of voting that results in a tie, the candidates will be given 1 
minute to address the Congress if they choose, followed by an immediate second round 
of voting. The presiding officer will cast his vote only after the second round of votes 
and only if that second round comes to a second tie.

Background Information: During the 33rd COGS November 2025 election for Deputy 
Speaker of Judicial Affairs, there were two candidates for the position. The election 
went through three rounds of voting. If the third round had yielded another tie, we 
were planning on resorting to flipping a coin to resolve the tie. The goal of this bill is 
avoiding the awkwardness of endless ties and revotes. Setting the presiding deputy as 
the tie breaking vote ensures no election goes beyond two rounds of voting. The bill 
seeks to keep the presiding deputy separate from debate to ensure fairness to the 
candidates. The presiding deputy will cast their vote after the votes are recounted and 
discretely, away from the Congress to provide anonymity to the Speaker.

Effect of Proposed Legislation: This legislation, if passed, would change the current 
method of handling ties in deputy elections from an endless series of voting and 
possibly a coin flip to only two sets of voting. This ensures efficiency and fairness in the 
deputy election process.

Short Title: 2026-2027 Congress of Graduate Students (COGS) Annual Budget 

Summary of Legislation: This legislation adopts the Fiscal Year (FY) 2026-2027 Activity and 
Service (A&S) budget for the Congress of Graduate Students. The bill appropriates 
$1,396,738.91 in A&S funds to graduate student organizations, university entities, and COGS-
administered programs in accordance with the COGS Administrative Code. The legislation also 
adopts the associated proviso language governing use of these funds. 

Background Information: Each fiscal year, COGS is responsible for reviewing and adopting 
the A&S fee budget that supports graduate student organizations, programming, and services 
at Florida State University. The FY 2026-2027 budget was developed through the COGS budget 
process in coordination with student organizations, university partners, and the Budget 
Committee, consistent with Chapter 105 of the COGS Administrative Code. This legislation is 
presented to formally authorize the allocation of A&S funds for the upcoming fiscal year and to 
establish the binding proviso language governing their use. Adoption of this budget ensures 
continued financial support for graduate student programming, conference grants, professional 
development, and key university services that directly impact the graduate student body. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: If enacted, this legislation will formally approve and implement 
the FY 2026–2027 COGS A&S budget totaling $1,396,738.91. The bill will authorize distribution 
of funds to the listed graduate student organizations, university entities, and COGS-administered 
programs and will make the accompanying proviso language binding for the fiscal year. This 
action enables funded programs and services to operate beginning July 1, 2026.

 Senate Proclamation #: 007 
 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Collantes 
 Co-sponsor(s): Rodriguez 

Short Title: Recognizing Ukraine's Noble Efforts to Resist Putin's Invasion 

Summary of Legislation: 
The ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine has caused widespread destruction and 
displacement for the citizens of Ukraine. The conflict has been determined, per the 
International Criminal Court, to involve war crimes on part of Putin's military strategy. This 
conflict has consisted of attacks on cultural, economic, political, educational institutions that 
make up the foundation of a Ukrainian nation. This proclamation serves to advocate for the 
recognition of Ukraine's efforts to keep its integrity as a nation and to realize recognition as an 
important step towards moving for peace. 
 
Background Information: 
This piece of legislation was considered because of the 4-year anniversary since Russia's full-
scale invasion on February 24, 2022. This proclamation serves to address the need brought up 
by students who sought out recognition from student government of the nation's struggle for 
sovereignty abroad. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Florida State University Students. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
To fully recognize an ongoing conflict that impacts students here on Florida State University's 
campus for the purpose of moving towards peace and security. 

Attachment(s): 
 • Attachment #1: Proclamation Recognizing Ukraine 

 Page 2 of 7

 Senate Proclamation #: 003 
 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Collantes 
 Co-Sponsor(s): Rodriguez 
 
 A PROCLAMATION 
 Recognizing Ukraine's Noble Efforts to Resist Putin's Invasion 

 1 WHEREAS, On February 24th, 2022, Ukraine was subjected to a full-scale Russian military invasion. 
 2 The invasion marked an escalation towards force that has since caused extensive destruction and 
 3 displacement for the citizens of Ukraine. 

 4 WHEREAS, Russia controls a significant portion of Ukraine, such as the Luhansk and Donetsk region. 
 5 According to the Public International Law & Public Group, Atlantic Council, and the U.S. 
 6 Department of State, citizens within these regions are facing intense surveillance, cultural erasure, 
 7 displacement, and the exploitation of local resources; and 

 8 WHEREAS, These acts of warfare include 500,000-600,000 Ukrainian military casualties, infrastructure 
 9 instability, economic collapse, and the erosion of an independent Ukrainian culture; and 

10 WHEREAS, Putin's military strategy has drawn the ire of the International Criminal Court as they 
11 determine his acts to be war crimes that include the destruction of critical infrastructure, targeting of 
12 civilians, abduction of children, and the violation of a ceasefire in May 2025 that resulted in 
13 unnecessary civilian deaths; and 

14 WHEREAS, The invasion of Ukraine violates the sovereign, self-determinate, and autonomous ideals 
15 that maintain international order; and 

16 WHEREAS, Ukraine has responded to this violation by executing military operations for the purpose of 
17 protecting their territorial integrity and national identity, reaching out to the international community 
18 for support; and 

19 WHEREAS, Ukrainian human rights advocate, Oleksandra Matviichuk, has been welcomed on campus 
20 to speak on the injustices and human right violations that characterize Putin's military strategy. She 
21 is part of the broader movement to realize Ukraine's efforts to resist occupation to secure human 
22 rights for its civilians at a time of warfare; and 

 Page 1 of 2 

 Page 3 of 7
 
23 WHEREAS, Florida State University is the home of an international community that includes both 
24 Ukrainian and Russian students; and 

25 WHEREAS, Florida State University is beholden to promoting an environment that acknowledges the 
26 hardships of international conflict for the betterment of fostering a genuine connection to our 
27 international community; and 

28 WHEREAS, Florida State University can act as a voice for Ukrainian and Russian students who share 
29 and advocate a vision for peace abroad; and 

30 NOW THEREFORE BE IT PROCLAIMED by the 78th Student Senate at Florida State University 
31 that: we recognize the dedicated efforts on part of the Ukrainian citizenry and military to fight 
32 against a regime that violates human rights in favor of power. 

33 BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED that: Both Russian and Ukrainian students are beholden to a future 
34 that holds their intentional relationship in harmony rather conflict. 

35 BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED that: Florida State University recognizes the catastrophe of warfare 
36 and seek to support its end for the betterment of both Ukraine and Russian nations.

 DONE AND ADOPTED by the 78th Student Senate at Florida State University this DAY of MONTH, 
 YEAR.

Short Title: A proclamation encouraging the Student Senate to donate professional clothing to 
the 2026 Spring Cleaning With Meaning Clothing Drive organized by the Career Center 
 
Summary of Legislation: This proclamation encourages the Student Senate to donate 
professional clothing to the 2026 Spring Cleaning With Meaning Clothing Drive organized by 
the Career Center, running from March 2nd to April 3rd, 2026. This resolution sets a goal of 
acquiring 100 items from senators and officers throughout the duration of the drive. 
 
Background Information: The Professional Clothing Closet provides professional attire at no 
cost to all part-time and full-time students at Florida State University. Access to professional 
clothing is essential for students participating in interviews, internships, networking events, and 
other career related opportunities. The Spring Cleaning With Meaning Clothing Drive supports 
the Professional Clothing Closet by increasing available inventory and ensuring access to 
professional resources for students across campus. 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: Senate President Holliday, Heather Lazar, Stormy 
McGivern 
 
Effect of Proposed Legislation: If enacted, this proclamation would formally encourage 
Student Senate members to participate in the 2026 Spring Cleaning With Meaning Clothing 
Drive by donating professional clothing. While non-binding, this action promotes engagement 
and reinforces the Student Senate’s commitment to professional development and equity by 
helping expand access to career ready resources for the student body. 
 
Attachment(s):

 2 Florida State University students to participate confidently in interviews, internships, networking 
 3 events, and career-related opportunities; and 
 
 4 WHEREAS, Florida State University Career Center’s Professional Clothing Closet provides 
 5 professional clothing at no cost to all part-time and full-time students, helping to reduce financial 
 6 barriers and promote equitable access to career resources; and 
 
 7 WHEREAS, the 2026 Spring Cleaning With Meaning Clothing Drive, hosted by the Career Center from 
 8 March 2nd through April 3rd, 2026, seeks to expand the inventory of the Professional Clothing 
 9 Closet through community ; and 
 
10 WHEREAS, the Student Senate has a longstanding commitment to supporting initiatives that advance 
11 professional development, equity, and student opportunity across campus; 

12 NOW THEREFORE BE IT PROCLAIMED by the 78th Student Senate at Florida State University 
13 that: the student senate formally encourages its members to donate gently used professional

15 hundred (100) items;

Short Title: Amending Chapter 401, Student Body Statutes, to Streamline and Codify the 
Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This bill amends Chapter 401 of the Student Body Statutes to establish a clear, structured, and 
transparent process for submitting and considering amendments to legislation. The proposed 
changes enhance legislative efficiency, promote informed deliberation, and ensure meaningful 
public notice and participation throughout the amendment process. 

Background Information: 
Prior to this amendment, the Student Body Statutes lacked a formalized process for submitting 
amendments to measures outside of standing committee proceedings. As a result, 
amendments were frequently introduced orally and in large batches on the Senate floor, often 
without sufficient notice to Senators or the public. 
 
This practice created confusion during debate, administrative inefficiencies, and uncertainty 
regarding the substance of legislation under consideration. In some cases, measures were 
materially altered from their publicly noticed descriptions, undermining transparency and public 
trust in the legislative process. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with input comment from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate 
Leadership, and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This bill establishes a standardized amendment submission process, including the creation of 
an amendment submission form and a forty-eight (48) hour deadline for amendments prior to a 
bill’s second reading. It increases procedural safeguards for late-filed amendments by raising 
voting thresholds and authorizing recesses for review. 

 Page 12 of 38

Additionally, the legislation requires amendments that materially alter a measure’s publicly 
noticed purpose or description to be clearly identified as such, thereby strengthening 
transparency, preserving public notice, and improving the overall integrity of the legislative 
process.

Short Title: Amending Rule Ten, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Clarify Definitions and 
Streamline and Codify the Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This resolution updates Rule Ten of the Senate Rules of Procedure to clarify definitions of 
legislative instruments and establish a structured, transparent, and uniform amendment 
process. The changes align Senate procedural rules with recently adopted statutory standards, 
improve clarity for Senators and the public, and enhance efficiency and predictability during 
floor consideration of measures. 

Background Information: 
Rule Ten governs the submission, consideration, and amendment of measures before the 
Student Senate. Prior to this amendment, several key terms were either undefined or 
inconsistently applied, and procedures for submitting and considering amendments lacked 
sufficient structure. This resulted in confusion during debate, last-minute changes to 
legislation, and reduced transparency for both Senators and the public. Following the adoption 
of statutory reforms to the amendment process, it became necessary to revise Rule Ten to 
ensure consistency between the Senate Rules of Procedure and the Student Body Statutes, 
as well as to formally codify best practices that had developed informally over time. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with direct input from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate Leadership, 
and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution clarifies the definitions of legislative instruments, including bills, resolutions, 
amendments, committee substitutes, and late-filed amendments. It codifies procedures for 
submitting amendments in advance of Senate meetings, establishes clear voting thresholds 
and debate procedures for late-filed amendments, and formalizes processes for committee 
substitutes, confirmations, and statements of dissent. Collectively, these changes improve 

 Page 14 of 38

legislative transparency, protect public notice, reduce administrative confusion, and ensure a 
more orderly and deliberative amendment process on the Senate floor.

Summary of Legislation:

displacement for the citizens of Ukraine. The conflict has been determined, per the 
International Criminal Court, to involve war crimes on part of Putin's military strategy. This 
conflict has consisted of attacks on cultural, economic, political, educational institutions that 
make up the foundation of a Ukrainian nation. This proclamation serves to advocate for the 
recognition of Ukraine's efforts to keep its integrity as a nation and to realize recognition as an 
important step towards moving for peace. 
 
Background Information: 
This piece of legislation was considered because of the 4-year anniversary since Russia's full-
scale invasion on February 24, 2022. This proclamation serves to address the need brought up 
by students who sought out recognition from student government of the nation's struggle for 
sovereignty abroad. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Florida State University Students. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation:

campus for the purpose of moving towards peace and security.

Short Title: Amending the Senate Rules of Procedure to Establish Standing Committee Chair 
Liaison Assignments to Executive Branch Departments 

Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution amends Rule Two of the Senate Rules of Procedure to designate specific 
Standing Committee Chairs as liaisons to corresponding Executive Branch departments. It 
also preserves the Senate President’s authority to appoint additional liaisons to other 
Executive Branch departments as needed. The changes are intended to improve interbranch 
coordination and clarify liaison responsibilities. 

Background Information: 

The Student Senate relies on liaison positions to maintain consistent communication and 
collaboration with Executive Branch departments and campus partners. Currently, liaison 
assignments are largely discretionary, which can lead to uneven engagement and unclear 
lines of responsibility between key Senate committees and their most closely related Executive 
counterparts. 

This legislation formalizes a limited number of high-alignment liaison relationships—specifically 
between Judiciary, Internal Affairs, Finance, and Student Life and their respective Executive 
departments—while preserving the Senate President’s flexibility to assign additional liaisons 
where operationally necessary. By creating clearer structural expectations, the Senate can 
strengthen oversight, improve information flow, and support more coordinated Student 
Government operations. 

Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This legislation was developed through consultation with Senate President Holliday, and 
Student Body President Dale. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If enacted, this legislation will formally designate certain Standing Committee Chairs as 
liaisons to specified Executive Branch departments while preserving the Senate President’s 
authority to appoint additional liaisons to other Executive Branch departments as needed. The 

 Page 24 of 38

amendment clarifies expectations for interbranch communication and accountability, improves 
structural consistency in Senate liaison assignments, and strengthens coordination between 
the Legislative and Executive Branches without altering the Senate President’s broader 
appointment powers or existing liaison reporting requirements.

Short Title: Amending Senate Rule of Procedure to Exclude Religious Holy Days from 
Absence Penalties 

Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution amends Senate Rule of Procedure 13.4 to clarify that absences taken in 
observance of a religious holy day, as recognized under Rule 13.9(b)(4), shall not constitute a 
half absence. While religious holy days are currently classified as excused absences, they still 
result in a half-absence penalty under existing language. This amendment ensures that the 
Senate Rules of Procedure and Student Body Statutes § 206.1, which states that Student 
Government Officers shall not be penalized for observing a holy day. 

Background Information: 
Under current Senate Rules of Procedure, excused absences result in a half absence being 
assessed to the Senator. Rule 13.9(b)(4) explicitly includes religious holy days as a valid 
excused absence reason. However, Student Body Statues § 206.1 provides that Student 
Government Officers shall not be penalized for choosing to observe a holy day. This creates a 
procedural inconsistency in which religious observance is recognized as excused yet still 
carries a penalty. As members of the Student Senate represent a diverse student body with a 
variety of religious backgrounds and obligations, it is important that Senate policies allow 
inclusivity and statutory compliance. This legislation is presented to ensure the consistency 
between both governing documents. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

In drafting this resolution, consultation occurred with student leaders representing faith-based 
organizations at Florida State University. Sam Nunnally, Director of the Catholic Student 
Union, expressed support for ensuring that students are not placed in a position where they 
must choose between their religious observances and their civic responsibilities within Student 
Government. Rameen Ahmad, President of the Muslim Student Union, also voiced support for 
the amendment and affirmed the importance of protecting religious holy day observances from 
penalty within Senate attendance policy. Sela Teplin, Director of the Jewish Student Union, 
also voiced support for the amendment and affirmed the importance of protecting religious holy 
day observances from penalty within Senate attendance policy. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 

 Page 28 of 38

This resolution would amend Senate Rule of Procedure 13.4 to explicitly state that an excused 
absence taken pursuant to Rule (13.9)(b)(4) for observance of a religious holy day shall not 
constitute a half absence. Religious holy day observances would therefore not count toward 
the maximum number of excused absences permitted per term.

Short Title: Clarifying Forms of Legislation and Amending Rule 10 and Rule 8 of the Senate 
Rules of Procedure 

Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution amends Rule 10 and Rule 8 of the Senate Rules of Procedure to more clearly 
define the various forms of legislation considered by the Senate, resolutions, allocation 
resolutions, and proclamations. It distinguishes proclamations as ceremonial recognitions 
separate from policy-oriented resolutions and aligns Senate Rules with updates made to 
Student Body Statutes Chapter 401. The legislation also updates submission deadlines to be 
consistent with current Senate practices. 

Background Information: 
Rule 10 of the Senate Rules of Procedure currently governs the forms of legislation considered 
by the 78th Student Senate at Florida State University. However, recent updates to Student 
Body Statutes Chapter 401, “Forms of Legislation,” have created inconsistencies between 
statutory language and the Senate’s internal rules. In particular, proclamations—while regularly 
utilized for ceremonial recognition—are not clearly distinguished from resolutions within the 
Rules of Procedure. To promote consistency, transparency, and orderly legislative practice, 
the Rules of Procedure must be updated to align with statutory definitions and clearly delineate 
each recognized form of Senate action. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

(List the individuals, groups, and entities consulted during the drafting and development 
process. This includes fellow and former Senators, students, University administrators, faculty 
members, professional staff, Student Organizations (RSOs), SGA officers, and any relevant 
outside organizations or community partners who influenced the text or intent of this 
legislation.) 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
The legislation expands and clarify the definition of a “Resolution” to specify that it is a formal 
statement or amendment of Senate policy or intent, while separately defining an “Allocation 

 Page 32 of 38

Resolution” as a funding-specific measure approving recommendations from authorized 
boards or allocating or transferring Student Government funds as permitted by statute. The 
legislation formally establishes “Proclamation” as a distinct form of legislation used for 
ceremonial recognition of individuals, groups, events, or causes. The filing deadlines in Rule 8 
are modified to explicitly include proclamations and to update submission deadlines to current 
practice. Overall, the legislation ensures consistency between the Senate Rules of Procedure 
and Student Body Statutes Chapter 401, promotes transparency in legislative categorization, 
and clarifies procedural treatment of all recognized forms of Senate action.

Short Title: Adding the Finance Vice Chair into the Annual Budget Committee 

Summary of Legislation: 

This bill will guarantee the Student Senate Finance Vice Chair is also bound to be a member of 
the Annual Budget Committee in correlation to the large role the Finance Vice Chair already 
serves in establishing and planning the Annual Budget Process. 

Background Information: 
Amongst the many responsibilities the Vice Chair has in ensuring the Annual Budgeting 
Process for the Student Government Association. Representing the Student Senate as a 
member of the Budget Committee is not included. With the amount of work and responsibility 
that the Finance Vice Chair does, it is deemed appropriate for the position to be included in the 
actual process by default. This will raise the committee membership to twenty members all 
selected from different represented bodies of the Student Government Association, while 
keeping quorum rules the same, in a combined effort to allow students appointed to the 
committee academic and professional flexibility with less of a threat of missing quorum while 
allowing the Student Senate Vice Chair of Finance to partake in the annual budget process. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
The Student Senate Vice Chair of Finance will now serve annually in the budgeting process as 
a member of the Budget Committee.

Short Title: Amending Chapter 422, Section 2.a to increase the minimum allocation to the 
Campus Advancement and Development Fund. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This bill would increase the minimum allocation of the CAD fund from .25% of our yearly 
budget to .50%. 

Background Information: 
The CAD fund has been established to provide for larger Senate funding projects and for 
potential budgetary shortfalls. To establish the fund as able to finance larger projects in the 
future, the cap should be raised to allow for faster growth of the account and better potential 
for Senate usage. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Senators listed as co-sponsors. Chairman of the Finance and Budget Committee. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation would increase the minimum allocation from .25% to .50%, allowing the CAD 
fund to grow faster, allowing for quicker and larger Senate projects to be funded.

Short Title: Amending Chapter 401, Student Body Statutes, to Streamline and Codify the 
Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This bill amends Chapter 401 of the Student Body Statutes to establish a clear, structured, and 
transparent process for submitting and considering amendments to legislation. The proposed 
changes enhance legislative efficiency, promote informed deliberation, and ensure meaningful 
public notice and participation throughout the amendment process. 

Background Information: 
Prior to this amendment, the Student Body Statutes lacked a formalized process for submitting 
amendments to measures outside of standing committee proceedings. As a result, 
amendments were frequently introduced orally and in large batches on the Senate floor, often 
without sufficient notice to Senators or the public. 
 
This practice created confusion during debate, administrative inefficiencies, and uncertainty 
regarding the substance of legislation under consideration. In some cases, measures were 
materially altered from their publicly noticed descriptions, undermining transparency and public 
trust in the legislative process. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with input comment from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate 
Leadership, and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This bill establishes a standardized amendment submission process, including the creation of 
an amendment submission form and a forty-eight (48) hour deadline for amendments prior to a 
bill’s second reading. It increases procedural safeguards for late-filed amendments by raising 
voting thresholds and authorizing recesses for review. 

 Page 8 of 12

Additionally, the legislation requires amendments that materially alter a measure’s publicly 
noticed purpose or description to be clearly identified as such, thereby strengthening 
transparency, preserving public notice, and improving the overall integrity of the legislative 
process.

Summary of Legislation: 

This bill will guarantee the Student Senate Finance Vice Chair is also bound to be a member of 
the Annual Budget Committee in correlation to the large role the Finance Vice Chair already 
serves in establishing and planning the Annual Budget Process. 

Background Information: 
Amongst the many responsibilities the Vice Chair has in ensuring the Annual Budgeting 
Process for the Student Government Association. Representing the Student Senate as a 
member of the Budget Committee is not included. With the amount of work and responsibility 
that the Finance Vice Chair does, it is deemed appropriate for the position to be included in the 
actual process by default. This will raise the committee membership to twenty members all 
selected from different represented bodies of the Student Government Association, while 
keeping quorum rules the same, in a combined effort to allow students appointed to the 
committee academic and professional flexibility with less of a threat of missing quorum while 
allowing the Student Senate Vice Chair of Finance to partake in the annual budget process.

The Student Senate Vice Chair of Finance will now serve annually in the budgeting process as 
a member of the Budget Committee.

Short Title: Improved Infrastructure Near DeGraff Hall 

Summary of Legislation: 
This Proclamation aims to bring awareness to the current lack of infrastructure near DeGraff 
Hall. Specifically, this looks at a lack of crosswalk on the intersection of Dewey Street and W 
Virginia Street, a lack of a walkway from this area to the DeGraff Tunnel, and better 
maintenance for the gravel lots in this area. It also refers to contacts that will be contacted in 
the future to facilitate the construction of this infrastructure, namely the City of Tallahassee and 
Transportation and Parking Services. 

Background Information: 
There are currently 3 different apartments on W Virginia Street, and by the Fall there will be 4. 
In the future, there have been discussions of further construction and off-campus student 
housing in this area. Currently, the only method these students have to access campus without 
crossing Tennessee Street is going through the DeGraff tunnel, which is inaccessible without 
jaywalking due to a lack of a crosswalk on W Virginia St; this street sees speeds of 25 mph or 
higher, so this is a large pedestrian risk that needs to be addressed. In addition, the area 
around DeGraff Hall is not well-maintained, as a lack of a sidewalk is forcing pedestrians to 
walk across the grass and parking lots, leading to the grass dying and further pedestrian risk 
as they navigate around vehicles. Finally, the gravel lots near DeGraff Hall have been known 
to cause damage to cars, as there are severe potholes and a lack of maintenance. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
So far I have been in preliminary talks with FSU Maintenance and TAPS contacts regarding 
the crosswalk specifically. The OGA Director has also been contacted to try to find a contact 
for the City of Tallahassee regarding future resolutions. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
To bring awareness to changes the Senate wishes to see as further construction and off-
campus student housing is developed in this area. In addition, bringing awareness to potential 
pedestrian safety risks in the area that need to be resolved.
