Short Title: Amending Rule Ten, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Clarify Definitions and 
Streamline and Codify the Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This resolution updates Rule Ten of the Senate Rules of Procedure to clarify definitions of 
legislative instruments and establish a structured, transparent, and uniform amendment 
process. The changes align Senate procedural rules with recently adopted statutory standards, 
improve clarity for Senators and the public, and enhance efficiency and predictability during 
floor consideration of measures. 

Background Information: 
Rule Ten governs the submission, consideration, and amendment of measures before the 
Student Senate. Prior to this amendment, several key terms were either undefined or 
inconsistently applied, and procedures for submitting and considering amendments lacked 
sufficient structure. This resulted in confusion during debate, last-minute changes to 
legislation, and reduced transparency for both Senators and the public. Following the adoption 
of statutory reforms to the amendment process, it became necessary to revise Rule Ten to 
ensure consistency between the Senate Rules of Procedure and the Student Body Statutes, 
as well as to formally codify best practices that had developed informally over time. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with direct input from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate Leadership, 
and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution clarifies the definitions of legislative instruments, including bills, resolutions, 
amendments, committee substitutes, and late-filed amendments. It codifies procedures for 
submitting amendments in advance of Senate meetings, establishes clear voting thresholds 
and debate procedures for late-filed amendments, and formalizes processes for committee 
substitutes, confirmations, and statements of dissent. Collectively, these changes improve 

 Page 12 of 21

legislative transparency, protect public notice, reduce administrative confusion, and ensure a 
more orderly and deliberative amendment process on the Senate floor.

 A RESOLUTION 
 Amending Rule Ten, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Clarify Definitions and Streamline and 
 Codify the Amendment Process 

 1 WHEREAS, Rule Ten of the Senate Rules of Procedure governs the submission, consideration, and 
 2 amendment of measures before the Student Senate; and 

 3 WHEREAS, clear definitions and consistent procedures are essential to ensuring transparency, 
 4 efficiency, and fairness in the legislative process; and 

 5 WHEREAS, prior versions of Rule Ten lacked comprehensive definitions for certain legislative 
 6 instruments and did not fully codify procedures for submitting and considering amendments; and 

 7 WHEREAS, the absence of structured amendment procedures has led to confusion during Senate 
 8 debate, last-minute substantive changes to legislation, and reduced clarity for Senators and 
 9 members of the public; and 

10 WHEREAS, it is necessary to amend Rule Ten to align the Senate Rules of Procedure with those 
11 statutory reforms and to codify best practices for legislative consideration and debate; 

12 NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED by the 78th Student Senate at Florida State University that: 
13 Rule 10 of the Senate Rules of Procedure entitled “Submission and Consideration of Measures” is 
14 hereby amended and shall read as follows: 

15 RULE TEN - Submission And Consideration Of Measures 

16 1. Definitions: 

17 a. A "Constitutional Amendment" shall be any measure proposing a change, deletion or 
18 addition to the Student Body Constitution. 

19 b. A "Bill" shall be any measure proposing an amendment to the Student Body Statutes or 
20 any measure appropriating money.

21 c. A "Resolution" shall be any measure which is not a bill, constitutional amendment, 
22 nomination, confirmation, or statement of dissent. 

23 d. A "Proclamation" shall be defined as a formal public declaration or official announcement 
24 issued by the Senate to recognize a specific individual, group, event, or cause. 

25 e. An "Amendment" shall be defined as a written document proposing a change to a pending 
26 measure, including a Bill, Resolution, Proclamation, Constitutional Amendment, or 
27 Committee Substitute, that has been submitted at least forty-eight (48) hours prior to the 
28 Senate meeting to be published along with the Senate Calendar. 

29 f. A "Nomination" shall be the name of any person who has been forwarded to fill a vacant 
30 position in Student Government that requires confirmation by the Senate. 

31 g. “Confirmation” shall be defined as the approval of a nomination by the Senate, in which 
32 case the nominee shall then immediately assume office. 

33 h. “Statement of Dissent” shall be defined as a written explanation expressing disagreement 
34 with any motion, action, or measure made the Senate. 

35 i. A "Committee Substitute" (CS) shall be defined as any measure that has been amended 
36 in a standing committee and reported favorably, effectively replacing the original text of 
37 the measure for consideration by the full Senate. 

38 j. A "Late Filed Amendment" shall be defined as an amendment submitted on the prescribed 
39 form after the forty-eight (48) hour submission deadline but prior to the Call to Order of the 
40 Senate meeting, which requires a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the Senate to be considered 
41 during that meeting. 

42 k. A "Friendly Amendment" shall be defined as a proposed amendment that is accepted by 
43 the primary sponsor of the measure and receives no objections from the Senate, allowing 
44 for its immediate adoption without debate. 

45 2. Any bill, or resolution, or amendment filed on time shall be drawn up by the Senate Staff and 
46 distributed to members of the Senate via email and/or packets. 

47 3. Any bills affecting Student Government funds which are restrictive shall state all restrictions, 
48 earmarks, stipulations and provisions as part of the proviso of the bill. 

49 4. All appropriations bills must be accompanied by an information form detailing the need for the 
50 money, the specific uses for the money, and alternative methods of funding which have been 
51 investigated. 

52 5. All bills, constitutional amendments, and resolutions shall include a purpose and description 
53 section detailing a statement of legislative intent. No bill shall be placed on second reading without 
54 a statement of legislative intent. 

55 6. All constitutional amendments, bills, and resolutions shall be submitted on the appropriate forms 
56 as designated by the Student Senate President. 

57 7. Any measure being brought before the Senate for the first time shall be placed on first reading, 
58 unless otherwise moved. 

59 8. Any measure reported out of committee(s) shall be placed on second reading to be heard by the 
60 full Senate at the next meeting. If a measure is amended in committee, the Chair or Vice Chair 
61 must submit the amended legislation using the prescribed Amendment Form directly following the 
62 adjournment of the committee meeting pursuant to Chapter 401 of the Student Body Statutes.

 63 a. Upon submission, the measure shall be designated as a Committee Substitute (CS) on 
 64 the Senate Calendar. 

 65 9. All nominees to Student Government offices requiring Senate confirmation shall have their 
 66 completed applications forwarded to the appropriate Senate committee for consideration. The 
 67 committee shall interview and question the nominee and then vote on whether to forward or deny

 69 called to the floor of the Senate at its next meeting. The structure of debate for Senate 
 70 confirmations shall be as follows: 

 71 a. Nominees shall be allowed to give an opening statement lasting no longer than five (5) 
 72 minutes, with their remaining time being allocated to their closing. 

 73 b. Nominees may be questioned by any Senator on matters of their experience, 
 74 qualifications, and goals for the respective position. 

 75 c. Upon passage of a motion to enter debate by majority vote, Senators may speak freely as 
 76 to the qualifications of any candidate. Nominees shall be permitted to remain in the Senate

 79 nominee shall have the time remaining from their opening statement to give a closing

 86 Senate Parliamentarian, and the Program Director of Student Governance and Advocacy and

 91 1. Upon the passage of such a motion, the Student Senate President may order a

102 1. Debate on the amendment shall not address the merits of the original measure, 
103 unless it is pertinent to the merits of the amendment. Additionally, questions and

120 b. The Student Senate President Pro Tempore shall act as the Vice Chair of a committee of 
121 the whole, unless they choose to relinquish their position. 

122 c. When the Senate reconvenes, any senator may move to accept the decision of the 
123 committee as the decision of the whole. 

124 d. Should the Senate enter a committee of the whole, only members of the original committee 
125 who were on the prevailing side of a motion may move for a reconsideration of the vote 
126 on the said motion. 

127 14. Any senator may, during New Business, move to add a Statement of Dissent into the record. 

128 a. The statement must solely address a singular action, motion, or measure made during 
129 that meeting. 

130 b. There may only be one statement submitted per any action, motion, or measure per 
131 Senator. 

132 c. Senators who did not make the action, motion, or measure on the floor may cosign the 
133 Statement with the consent of the Senator who made the action, motion, or measure. 

134 d. The statement must be submitted to Senate Staff within two (2) school days following the 
135 meeting of the senate when the action, motion, or measure was made. 

136 15. A resolution recognizing all Florida State University students that have deceased shall be heard 
137 on the floor of the Senate during the meeting prior to the last Senate meeting of the session, or 
138 “Sine Die.” 

139 a. The list of students will be provided by the SGA Director. 

140 b. This resolution shall be proposed and advertised one (1) week prior to it being heard. 

141 c. This resolution shall be referred to the Student Life Committee after its first reading and 
142 shall be reported out of the committee in one (1) week. 

143 d. No other resolutions recognizing students that have passed shall be considered unless 
144 this rule is waived by two-thirds (2/3) vote of the Senate.

Short Title: Recognizing Ukraine's Noble Efforts to Resist Putin's Invasion 

Summary of Legislation: 
The ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine has caused widespread destruction and 
displacement for the citizens of Ukraine. The conflict has been determined, per the 
International Criminal Court, to involve war crimes on part of Putin's military strategy. This 
conflict has consisted of attacks on cultural, economic, political, educational institutions that 
make up the foundation of a Ukrainian nation. This proclamation serves to advocate for the 
recognition of Ukraine's efforts to keep its integrity as a nation and to realize recognition as an 
important step towards moving for peace. 
 
Background Information: 
This piece of legislation was considered because of the 4-year anniversary since Russia's full-
scale invasion on February 24, 2022. This proclamation serves to address the need brought up 
by students who sought out recognition from student government of the nation's struggle for 
sovereignty abroad. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Florida State University Students. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
To fully recognize an ongoing conflict that impacts students here on Florida State University's 
campus for the purpose of moving towards peace and security.

 A PROCLAMATION 
 Recognizing Ukraine's Noble Efforts to Resist Putin's Invasion 

 1 WHEREAS, On February 24th, 2022, Ukraine was subjected to a full-scale Russian military invasion. 
 2 The invasion marked an escalation towards force that has since caused extensive destruction and 
 3 displacement for the citizens of Ukraine. 

 4 WHEREAS, Russia controls a significant portion of Ukraine, such as the Luhansk and Donetsk region. 
 5 According to the Public International Law & Public Group, Atlantic Council, and the U.S. 
 6 Department of State, citizens within these regions are facing intense surveillance, cultural erasure, 
 7 displacement, and the exploitation of local resources; and 

 8 WHEREAS, These acts of warfare include 500,000-600,000 Ukrainian military casualties, infrastructure 
 9 instability, economic collapse, and the erosion of an independent Ukrainian culture; and 

10 WHEREAS, Putin's military strategy has drawn the ire of the International Criminal Court as they 
11 determine his acts to be war crimes that include the destruction of critical infrastructure, targeting of 
12 civilians, abduction of children, and the violation of a ceasefire in May 2025 that resulted in 
13 unnecessary civilian deaths; and 

14 WHEREAS, The invasion of Ukraine violates the sovereign, self-determinate, and autonomous ideals 
15 that maintain international order; and 

16 WHEREAS, Ukraine has responded to this violation by executing military operations for the purpose of 
17 protecting their territorial integrity and national identity, reaching out to the international community 
18 for support; and 

19 WHEREAS, Ukrainian human rights advocate, Oleksandra Matviichuk, has been welcomed on campus 
20 to speak on the injustices and human right violations that characterize Putin's military strategy. She 
21 is part of the broader movement to realize Ukraine's efforts to resist occupation to secure human 
22 rights for its civilians at a time of warfare; and

23 WHEREAS, Florida State University is the home of an international community that includes both 
24 Ukrainian and Russian students; and 

25 WHEREAS, Florida State University is beholden to promoting an environment that acknowledges the 
26 hardships of international conflict for the betterment of fostering a genuine connection to our 
27 international community; and 

28 WHEREAS, Florida State University can act as a voice for Ukrainian and Russian students who share 
29 and advocate a vision for peace abroad; and 

30 NOW THEREFORE BE IT PROCLAIMED by the 78th Student Senate at Florida State University 
31 that: we recognize the dedicated efforts on part of the Ukrainian citizenry and military to fight 
32 against a regime that violates human rights in favor of power. 

33 BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED that: Both Russian and Ukrainian students are beholden to a future 
34 that holds their intentional relationship in harmony rather conflict. 

35 BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED that: Florida State University recognizes the catastrophe of warfare 
36 and seek to support its end for the betterment of both Ukraine and Russian nations.

 Senate Bill/Resolution/Proclamation/PCA #: 007 
 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Nucatola

Short Title: Adding the Finance Vice Chair into the Annual Budget Committee 

Summary of Legislation: 

This bill will guarantee the Student Senate Finance Vice Chair is also bound to be a member of 
the Annual Budget Committee in correlation to the large role the Finance Vice Chair already 
serves in establishing and planning the Annual Budget Process. 

Background Information: 
Amongst the many responsibilities the Vice Chair has in ensuring the Annual Budgeting 
Process for the Student Government Association. Representing the Student Senate as a 
member of the Budget Committee is not included. With the amount of work and responsibility 
that the Finance Vice Chair does, it is deemed appropriate for the position to be included in the 
actual process by default. This will raise the committee membership to twenty members all 
selected from different represented bodies of the Student Government Association, while 
keeping quorum rules the same, in a combined effort to allow students appointed to the 
committee academic and professional flexibility with less of a threat of missing quorum while 
allowing the Student Senate Vice Chair of Finance to partake in the annual budget process. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
The Student Senate Vice Chair of Finance will now serve annually in the budgeting process as 
a member of the Budget Committee.

Short Title: Amending Chapter 201 of the COGS Code to Allow At-Large Representatives 
to Redesignate to College-Specific Seats. 

Summary of Legislation: This bill would amend Chapter 201 of the COGS Code to allow 
existing COGS representatives to reclassify from an at-large seat to a college-specific 
seat. After representatives are given notice of a vacancy, any representative sitting in 
an at-large may write to the Deputy Speaker of Judicial Affairs announcing their 
intention to redesignate, which will then be voted on by the Internal Affairs committee 

Background Information: Our goal is to have an active Congress, with as many avenues 
for participation as possible. There have been instances in which there is a vacancy in a 
college-specific seat, but there is a current COGS representative who is from that 
college but sitting in a at-large seat. This legislation will allow those individuals to 
redesignate their seat, thus opening an at-large seat which may be filled by any 
graduate student from any college. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: By allowing at-large representatives to redesignate to 
college-specific seats, there will be more opportunities to allow graduate students to 
participate in the Congress. This will promote the goal of an active Congress by 
providing an open seat which may be filled by any eligible graduate student.

Short Title: Amending Cogs Code, Chapter 204.4 to establish procedure in the event of a 
tie in Deputy elections. 

Summary of Legislation: This bill would amend Chapter 204, COGS Code, to establish 
procedure in the event of a tie in Deputy elections. The bill makes the presiding officer 
of the contested position the tie breaker in the event of a second tie. The bill provides 
that after a first round of voting that results in a tie, the candidates will be given 1 
minute to address the Congress if they choose, followed by an immediate second round 
of voting. The presiding officer will cast his vote only after the second round of votes 
and only if that second round comes to a second tie. 

Background Information: During the 33rd COGS November 2025 election for Deputy 
Speaker of Judicial Affairs, there were two candidates for the position. The election 
went through three rounds of voting. If the third round had yielded another tie, we 
were planning on resorting to flipping a coin to resolve the tie. The goal of this bill is 
avoiding the awkwardness of endless ties and revotes. Setting the presiding deputy as 
the tie breaking vote ensures no election goes beyond two rounds of voting. The bill 
seeks to keep the presiding deputy separate from debate to ensure fairness to the 
candidates. The presiding deputy will cast their vote after the votes are recounted and 
discretely, away from the Congress to provide anonymity to the Speaker. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: This legislation, if passed, would change the current 
method of handling ties in deputy elections from an endless series of voting and 
possibly a coin flip to only two sets of voting. This ensures efficiency and fairness in the 
deputy election process.

Short Title: Amending Chapter 401, Student Body Statutes, to Streamline and Codify the 
Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This bill amends Chapter 401 of the Student Body Statutes to establish a clear, structured, and 
transparent process for submitting and considering amendments to legislation. The proposed 
changes enhance legislative efficiency, promote informed deliberation, and ensure meaningful 
public notice and participation throughout the amendment process. 

Background Information: 
Prior to this amendment, the Student Body Statutes lacked a formalized process for submitting 
amendments to measures outside of standing committee proceedings. As a result, 
amendments were frequently introduced orally and in large batches on the Senate floor, often 
without sufficient notice to Senators or the public. 
 
This practice created confusion during debate, administrative inefficiencies, and uncertainty 
regarding the substance of legislation under consideration. In some cases, measures were 
materially altered from their publicly noticed descriptions, undermining transparency and public 
trust in the legislative process. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with input comment from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate 
Leadership, and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This bill establishes a standardized amendment submission process, including the creation of 
an amendment submission form and a forty-eight (48) hour deadline for amendments prior to a 
bill’s second reading. It increases procedural safeguards for late-filed amendments by raising 
voting thresholds and authorizing recesses for review. 

 Page 7 of 11

Additionally, the legislation requires amendments that materially alter a measure’s publicly 
noticed purpose or description to be clearly identified as such, thereby strengthening 
transparency, preserving public notice, and improving the overall integrity of the legislative 
process.

Short Title: Adding the Finance Vice Chair into the Annual Budget Committee 

Summary of Legislation: 

This bill will guarantee the Student Senate Finance Vice Chair is also bound to be a member of 
the Annual Budget Committee in correlation to the large role the Finance Vice Chair already 
serves in establishing and planning the Annual Budget Process. 

Background Information: 
Amongst the many responsibilities the Vice Chair has in ensuring the Annual Budgeting 
Process for the Student Government Association. Representing the Student Senate as a 
member of the Budget Committee is not included. With the amount of work and responsibility 
that the Finance Vice Chair does, it is deemed appropriate for the position to be included in the 
actual process by default. This will raise the committee membership to twenty members all 
selected from different represented bodies of the Student Government Association, while 
keeping quorum rules the same, in a combined effort to allow students appointed to the 
committee academic and professional flexibility with less of a threat of missing quorum while 
allowing the Student Senate Vice Chair of Finance to partake in the annual budget process. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
The Student Senate Vice Chair of Finance will now serve annually in the budgeting process as 
a member of the Budget Committee.

Short Title: Recognizing the Holy Month of Ramadan 

Summary of Legislation: 
This proclamation formally recognizes the holy month of Ramadan and honors its significance 
to Muslim students, faculty, staff, and community members at Florida State University. It 
acknowledges Ramadan as a time of reflection, service, self-discipline, and community, and 
affirms the Student Senate’s commitment to inclusion and cultural awareness. 

Background Information: 
Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar and is observed by Muslims as a period of 
fasting from dawn to sunset, prayer, self-reflection, and community service. Members of the 
Florida State University community observe Ramadan through charity, devotion, and 
mindfulness while balancing academic and professional responsibilities. Recognizing 
Ramadan promotes cultural understanding, religious diversity, and supports an inclusive 
campus community aligned with the values of Florida State University. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This proclamation was informed by conversations with Muslim students and members of the 
Florida State University community, including the Muslim Student Union (MSU) and the Arab 
Student Union (ASU). Additional consideration was given to the principles of inclusion, 
diversity, and religious accommodation within the Student Government Association. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If enacted, this proclamation will formally recognize the holy month of Ramadan within the 
Student Senate record, affirm support for Muslim members of the FSU community, and 
encourage awareness, respect, and inclusivity across campus.

Short Title: A Proclamation to Honor the 100th Black History Month and Illuminate Black 
Student Leadership 

Summary of Legislation: 
This proclamation aims to honor the 100th Black History Month by recognizing the month’s 
history and illuminating the deep importance of black student leadership at Florida State 
University. 

Background Information: 
Across campus and within the FSU Student Government Association, Black History has 
permeated the lives of those who identity as Black in a meaningful and positive way. During 
the month of February, it is imperative to reflect on Black History and its impact on students. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Currently working across campus. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
Honor and celebrate Black History Month and recognize Black Student Leadership.

 A PROCLAMATION 
 To Honor the 100th Black History Month and Illuminate Black Student Leadership 

 1 WHEREAS, In 1915, the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History (ASNLH) was founded to 
 2 research, teach, and preserve Black History; and 

 3 WHEREAS, One hundred years ago, in 1926, Negro History Week commenced in 1926 when it was 
 4 established by Dr. Carter G. Woodson; and 

 5 WHEREAS, In 1937, the founder of Daytona Beach, Florida’s Bethune Cookman University, Dr. Mary 
 6 McLeod Bethune urged Woodson to develop the Negro History Bulletin to distribute Black history as 
 7 lesson plans and history articles; and 

 8 WHEREAS, In 1976, only fifty years ago, the grassroots movement led by Black educators and 
 9 scholars to form Black History month led to its establishment under President Ford’s 
10 administration,; and 

11 WHEREAS, 78th Student Senate Chair of Judiciary, Leila Jackson, states, “We are charged with 
12 standing firm upon the shoulders of our ancestors, who are named and not, for their sacrifice 
13 toward the greater freedom we as life-long learners and transformational leaders work daily to 
14 realize as members of the Black race.”; and 

15 WHEREAS, 78th Student Senator, Vanessa Aihe, states, “Black History Month, especially serving as a 
16 senator, is a reminder that the leadership qualities, skills, and characteristics I’ve cultivated are not 
17 extraordinary—they are historical. As a student and senator, it reminds me that advocacy and 
18 public service are more important than ever: our voices matter, and our imagination is the only limit 
19 to what we can achieve as a collective.”; and 

20 WHEREAS, 78th Student Senator, Ianko Abreu-Diaz, states “Afro Latino resembles two things. the 
21 ability to represent two distinct cultures and background united with one mutual identity. being a 
22 senator has allowed me the opportunity to represent the beautiful morals and teachings of black 
23 history and the Latino culture that has formed me into the person that I am today.”; and 

 Page 1 of 2

24 WHEREAS, 78th Student Senator, Calleigh Bellmany, states, “Being a Black senator means honoring 
25 where I come from while staying true to my identity during the decision making process. Black 
26 History Month reminds me how vital it is to lead with strength and faith—because, as Dr. King once 
27 said, ‘faith is taking the first step even when you don’t see the whole staircase.”; and 

28 WHEREAS, 78th Student Senator, Destinee Britto states, “Black history is not just something we honor 
29 in the past, it’s something we continue to write every day through resilience, leadership, and the

31 WHEREAS, 78th Student Senator, Nikole Ramirez, resonates with the quote, ““In this truth, in this faith,

 Resolution #: 007 
 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Bigenho

Short Title: Amending Rule Ten, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Clarify Definitions and 
Streamline and Codify the Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This resolution updates Rule Ten of the Senate Rules of Procedure to clarify definitions of 
legislative instruments and establish a structured, transparent, and uniform amendment 
process. The changes align Senate procedural rules with recently adopted statutory standards, 
improve clarity for Senators and the public, and enhance efficiency and predictability during 
floor consideration of measures. 

Background Information: 
Rule Ten governs the submission, consideration, and amendment of measures before the 
Student Senate. Prior to this amendment, several key terms were either undefined or 
inconsistently applied, and procedures for submitting and considering amendments lacked 
sufficient structure. This resulted in confusion during debate, last-minute changes to 
legislation, and reduced transparency for both Senators and the public. Following the adoption 
of statutory reforms to the amendment process, it became necessary to revise Rule Ten to 
ensure consistency between the Senate Rules of Procedure and the Student Body Statutes, 
as well as to formally codify best practices that had developed informally over time. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with direct input from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate Leadership, 
and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution clarifies the definitions of legislative instruments, including bills, resolutions, 
amendments, committee substitutes, and late-filed amendments. It codifies procedures for 
submitting amendments in advance of Senate meetings, establishes clear voting thresholds 
and debate procedures for late-filed amendments, and formalizes processes for committee 
substitutes, confirmations, and statements of dissent. Collectively, these changes improve 

 Page 3 of 9

legislative transparency, protect public notice, reduce administrative confusion, and ensure a 
more orderly and deliberative amendment process on the Senate floor.

 Senate PCA #: 001 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Jackson

Short Title: A Proposed Constitutional Amendment Clarifying the Appointment Powers of the Student 
Body President. 

Summary of Legislation: 
The proposed amendment clarifies the appointment powers of the Student Body President (SBP) by 
reinforcing the status quo envisioned by Senate Bills 76-038 and 77-028. Namely, that the SBP appoints 
all non-elected major officers (except those offices which the Constitution vests appointment authority in 
another officer/entity), with Senate confirmation, and that the President appoints all non-major, non-
elected, officers without the need for Senate confirmation. It further provides a statement of intent and 
title for the Spring 2026 ballot. 

Background Information: 
Over the course of the 76th and 77th Student Senates, several bills passed that had the cumulative effect 
of removing the need for Senate confirmation from many non-major offices within SGA.1 The Senate 
passed these bills after careful consideration regarding the scale of the confirmation process and after 
years of confirmation backlogs leaving numerous administrations unable to begin executing their priorities 
until mid-fall, at best. Bill 77-028 passed unanimously, and Bill 76-038 passed with only one vote against. 
 
As a result, the Executive Branch has relied on Chapter 301, Student Body Statutes, and has appointed 
large swaths of the Executive Branch without seeking Senate confirmation. All Cabinet secretaries were 
put forward for Senate confirmation and were confirmed. 
 
On December 12, 2025, the Student Supreme Court issued an advisory opinion related to the 
appointment powers of the Student Body President. In it, the Court stated that appointees to the Cabinet 
must be forwarded to the Senate for confirmation.2 The Court did not opine on what the Cabinet is 
comprised of.3 Out of an abundance of caution, the Office of the Attorney General has recommended a 
constitutional amendment that clarifies the Student Body President’s appointment power by reinforcing 
the appointment structure previously adopted by the Student Senate. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
 
1 See, e.g., Bill 76-038, FSU Stud. Sen. (codified as Chp. 304, SBS) (replacing the appointments process with an 
authorization for the Executive Branch to adopt policies regulating the appointment process); s. 2, Bill 77-028, FSU 
Stud. Sen. (codified as Chp. 301, SBS) (creating the current Executive Department structure, requiring department 
secretaries to be confirmed by the Senate, and authorizing directors and coordinators to be appointed by each 
secretary without Senate confirmation). 
2 Concerning Presidential Appointment Powers, Advisory Opinion 2025-03 at 2–3 (Fla. St. Student Sup. Ct. 2025). 
3 Id. at 2. 

 Page 2 of 5

The proposed amendment was drafted in collaboration with the Office of the Attorney General. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
Section 1 repeals Article II, Section 5(1)(d), of the Florida State University Student Body Constitution. 
This paragraph repeats rules set forth in Section 2 of the amendment, as well as Article IV, Section 5 
(setting a two-thirds vote for Supreme Court justices), and Article V, Section 7 (setting a two-thirds vote 
for appointments to vacant elected offices). 
 
Section 2 amends Article III, Section 3(2), of the Florida State University Student Body Constitution to 
clarify the appointment powers of the Student Body President. All major, non-elected, officers shall be 
appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, unless otherwise specified by the Constitution.4 
All non-major, non-elected, officers shall be appointed by the Student Body President, without Senate 
confirmation, except that the power to appoint such officers may be vested in other officers by law.5 
Finally, the amendment protects other places in the Constitution that vests appointment powers in other 
places.6 
 
Section 3 sets a title for the ballot measure, sets a statement of intent, and details that ratification occurs 
upon two-thirds vote of the Student Body and approval by the Vice President for Student Affairs.7 
 
If the amendment is proposed by three-fourths vote of the Senate, the amendment must be delivered to 
the Supervisor of Elections by the Senate President.8 The Supervisor shall submit the amendment to the 
Student Supreme Court for review within seven days of passage through the Senate.9 The amendment 
will also be noticed to the public prior to the vote.

Supervisor of Elections as the appointer of the Deputy Supervisor of Elections. 
5 For example, Chp. 301, SBS, allows cabinet secretaries to appoint directors and coordinators in their department. 
Another example would be allowing agencies to appoint any position that isn’t Director, Assistant Director, or 
Treasurer. 
6 The method of appointment for Senate officers is determined by statute. FLA. ST. U. STUDENT BODY CONST. art. II, 
§ 2(3). The Constitution designates the Chief Justice as the appointer of Election Commissioners. Id. art. IV, § 
8(1)(c). 
7 The precedents of Spring 2025 are clear that constitutional amendments go to the ballot prior to being presented 
to the Vice President for Student Affairs (VPSA) for approval as an amendment is only in the proper posture to take 
effect when it has already been approved by the Student Body. Cf. Concerning the Approval and Publ’g Procs. for 
Proposed Amends. to Appear on the Election Ballot, Advisory Opinion 2025-01 at 3, 6 (Fla. St. Student Sup. Ct.

(clarifying that the VPSA must approve constitutional amendments “before they are officially adopted by SGA.”). In 
Spring 2025, the amendments proposed by the Constitutional Revision Commission were placed on the general

Short Title: A Proposed Constitutional Amendment Clarifying the Appointment Powers of the Student 
Body President. 

Summary of Legislation: 
The proposed amendment clarifies the appointment powers of the Student Body President (SBP) by 
reinforcing the status quo envisioned by Senate Bills 76-038 and 77-028. Namely, that the SBP appoints 
all non-elected major officers (except those offices which the Constitution vests appointment authority in 
another officer/entity), with Senate confirmation, and that the President appoints all non-major, non-
elected, officers without the need for Senate confirmation. It further provides a statement of intent and 
title for the Spring 2026 ballot. 

Background Information: 
Over the course of the 76th and 77th Student Senates, several bills passed that had the cumulative effect 
of removing the need for Senate confirmation from many non-major offices within SGA.1 The Senate 
passed these bills after careful consideration regarding the scale of the confirmation process and after 
years of confirmation backlogs leaving numerous administrations unable to begin executing their priorities 
until mid-fall, at best. Bill 77-028 passed unanimously, and Bill 76-038 passed with only one vote against. 
 
As a result, the Executive Branch has relied on Chapter 301, Student Body Statutes, and has appointed 
large swaths of the Executive Branch without seeking Senate confirmation. All Cabinet secretaries were 
put forward for Senate confirmation and were confirmed. 
 
On December 12, 2025, the Student Supreme Court issued an advisory opinion related to the 
appointment powers of the Student Body President. In it, the Court stated that appointees to the Cabinet 
must be forwarded to the Senate for confirmation.2 The Court did not opine on what the Cabinet is 
comprised of.3 Out of an abundance of caution, the Office of the Attorney General has recommended a 
constitutional amendment that clarifies the Student Body President’s appointment power by reinforcing 
the appointment structure previously adopted by the Student Senate. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
 
1 See, e.g., Bill 76-038, FSU Stud. Sen. (codified as Chp. 304, SBS) (replacing the appointments process with an 
authorization for the Executive Branch to adopt policies regulating the appointment process); s. 2, Bill 77-028, FSU 
Stud. Sen. (codified as Chp. 301, SBS) (creating the current Executive Department structure, requiring department 
secretaries to be confirmed by the Senate, and authorizing directors and coordinators to be appointed by each 
secretary without Senate confirmation). 
2 Concerning Presidential Appointment Powers, Advisory Opinion 2025-03 at 2–3 (Fla. St. Student Sup. Ct. 2025). 
3 Id. at 2. 

 Page 4 of 20 

The proposed amendment was drafted in collaboration with the Office of the Attorney General. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
Section 1 repeals Article II, Section 5(1)(d), of the Florida State University Student Body Constitution. 
This paragraph repeats rules set forth in Section 2 of the amendment, as well as Article IV, Section 5 
(setting a two-thirds vote for Supreme Court justices), and Article V, Section 7 (setting a two-thirds vote 
for appointments to vacant elected offices). 
 
Section 2 amends Article III, Section 3(2), of the Florida State University Student Body Constitution to 
clarify the appointment powers of the Student Body President. All major, non-elected, officers shall be 
appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, unless otherwise specified by the Constitution.4 
All non-major, non-elected, officers shall be appointed by the Student Body President, without Senate 
confirmation, except that the power to appoint such officers may be vested in other officers by law.5 
Finally, the amendment protects other places in the Constitution that vests appointment powers in other 
places.6 
 
Section 3 sets a title for the ballot measure, sets a statement of intent, and details that ratification occurs 
upon two-thirds vote of the Student Body and approval by the Vice President for Student Affairs.7 
 
If the amendment is proposed by three-fourths vote of the Senate, the amendment must be delivered to 
the Supervisor of Elections by the Senate President.8 The Supervisor shall submit the amendment to the 
Student Supreme Court for review within seven days of passage through the Senate.9 The amendment 
will also be noticed to the public prior to the vote. 

Attachment(s):

4 FLA. ST. U. STUDENT BODY CONST. art. IV, §§ 3(1)(c), 8(1)(a) (designating the Chief Justice as the appointer of the 
Clerk of the Court and, with Senate confirmation, the Supervisor of Elections); id. art. IV, §§ 8(1)(b) (designating the 
Supervisor of Elections as the appointer of the Deputy Supervisor of Elections. 
5 For example, Chp. 301, SBS, allows cabinet secretaries to appoint directors and coordinators in their department. 
Another example would be allowing agencies to appoint any position that isn’t Director, Assistant Director, or 
Treasurer. 
6 The method of appointment for Senate officers is determined by statute. FLA. ST. U. STUDENT BODY CONST. art. II, 
§ 2(3). The Constitution designates the Chief Justice as the appointer of Election Commissioners. Id. art. IV, § 
8(1)(c). 
7 The precedents of Spring 2025 are clear that constitutional amendments go to the ballot prior to being presented 
to the Vice President for Student Affairs (VPSA) for approval as an amendment is only in the proper posture to take 
effect when it has already been approved by the Student Body. Cf. Concerning the Approval and Publ’g Procs. for 
Proposed Amends. to Appear on the Election Ballot, Advisory Opinion 2025-01 at 3, 6 (Fla. St. Student Sup. Ct. 
2025) (“[art. VI, §1] says nothing about SGA officials or school administrators needing to approve the proposals.”) 
(clarifying that the VPSA must approve constitutional amendments “before they are officially adopted by SGA.”). In 
Spring 2025, the amendments proposed by the Constitutional Revision Commission were placed on the general 
election ballot and were presented to the VPSA after the amendments were passed.

ensure that the amendment meets all constitutional requirements, which includes judicial review and notice).

MEMORANDUM #78-001

TO:
Carson Dale, Student Body President
Madeleine Siegel, Student Body Attorney General
Andrew Barrineau, Student Supreme Court Chief Justice

RE: Notice of Non-Compliance - Unauthorized Executive Appointees

This Memorandum serves as formal notice regarding the presence of unauthorized appointees currently
operating within the Executive Branch. The Office of the Senate President issues this notice in good faith, with
the express intent of offering an administrative remedy to restore constitutional order. This notice addresses
several distinct categories of non-compliance discovered during a review of recent Executive Orders and
outlines the necessary steps to regularize the Executive Branch.

It is our preference to rectify these statutory defects collaboratively, thereby avoiding the necessity of further
litigation, Quo Warranto proceedings, or direct intervention by the Judicial Branch.

I. AUTHORITY OF NOTICE

Following the issuance of Advisory Opinion 2025-03, the Student Supreme Court has definitively
ruled that "The President may not fill Cabinet positions without Senate confirmation". The Court
affirmed that Article II, Section 5.1(d) of the Constitution provides "two exclusive avenues" for
appointments: either a two-thirds vote or a majority vote, and that bypassing the Senate is
unconstitutional.

A review of recent Executive Orders reveals a systematic violation of this ruling, relying on the false
premise that "departmental" or "staff" roles are exempt from confirmation. This premise is explicitly
refuted by the Student Body Statutes:

 1. Article III, Section 5 of the Student Body Constitution states that membership of the Cabinet
 "shall be determined by Statutes".
 2.Chapter 301.4(C) of the Student Body Statutes unequivocally states: "Additional internal
 department roles may be created by the Secretary or Director, subject to approval from the
 Student Body President and Student Senate.”
 3.Recent Executive Orders (specifically #80-07, #80-09, and #80-11) explicitly appoint
 individuals to "positions within various Executive Departments".

Therefore, under the combined authority of the Student Body Constitution and Chapter 301.4(C),
every individual listed in these orders is a member of the Executive Cabinet.

 Page 8 of 20February, 6th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-001

Because these individuals were not submitted for confirmation, they have failed to meet the
condition precedent for office holding required by Chapter 202(4), which states that "duties, rights,
and responsibilities, shall vest [only] upon confirmation by the Student Senate and upon taking the
oath of office". Consequently, these appointees possess no legal authority to act, spend funds, or
execute the laws of the Student Body.

To mitigate liability and prevent the further unauthorized exercise of power, the Senate is issuing
the following directives effective immediately.

II. NOTICE OF SUSPENSION OF EXPIRED "ACTING" APPOINTEES (EO #80-11)

The individuals listed in Executive Order #80-11 (dated December 4, 2025) are hereby noticed as
holding no legal authority to perform official duties effective immediately. Pursuant to SBS
§301.4(b)(4)(C), the authority of an acting officer is strictly limited to a duration of six (6) weeks.
As Executive Order #80-11 was promulgated on December 4, 2025, the statutory window for
acting capacity closed on January 15, 2026. Because no Forwarding Letters were submitted to the
Senate for these individuals, their legal standing terminated by operation of law on that date.
Consequently, any actions taken by these individuals between January 15 and the present are
voidable as they were performed without constitutional or statutory authority.

Appointees Affected:
 Ian Seibert (Community Affairs Coordinator) 
 Isabella LoBianco (Senior Advisor and Special Projects Coordinator) 
 Jack Rowan (Senior Counselor to the Student Body President and Attorney General)1
 Nicolas Valenzuela (Acting Secretary for the Department of Campus Life)

Pursuant to SBS §202.4, §202.3, and §301.4, these individuals shall not produce work product,
authorize expenditures, represent the Student Government Association, or act in any official
capacity. As per SBS §202.4, all duties, rights, and responsibilities of office vest only upon Senate
confirmation and the subsequent administration of the oath of office.

1 The Senate formally notices that Mr. Jack Rowan’s appointment is constitutionally void ab initio under Article V,
Section 4, which explicitly forbids holding “two major offices... concurrently” by retaining his seat as a COGS
Representative (a constitutionally enumerated Major Office) while attempting to serve as Senior Counselor in the
Executive Office of the President (a Major Office per SBS §100.5(c)(5)).

 Page 9 of 20February, 6th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-001

III. NOTICE OF INVALID APPOINTMENTS AND INVALIDITY OF EO #80-06

The Office of the Senate President has identified individuals holding titles that have not been
established by the Student Body Statutes nor authorized by a Senate Resolution. Under Article III,
Section 5 of the Constitution, the membership of the Cabinet "shall be determined by Statutes". As
these positions do not exist in law, no individual can validly be appointed to fill them.

 Executive Order #80-10 appoints Ms. Urday to the position of "Deputy Solicitor General". In 
 Student Body Statutes, no such office exists. While this title appears in the proposed text of
 Executive Order #80-06, that order is legally void and failed to create the position.2
 The Senate understands that Mr. Rubenstein is currently operating3 under the title of "Deputy
 Attorney General", a promotion from his previous confirmed role as Legislative Affairs
 Coordinator. The Senate has received no notification, Executive Order, or Forwarding Letter
 regarding this change. Unlike the position above, the "Deputy Attorney General" role does not
 appear in the Statutes nor in the unratified Executive Order #80-06.

Because these offices have not been created by Bill or Resolution, these appointments are
effectively void ab initio. The Senate cannot confirm individuals to positions that do not legally
exist. Therefore, the Senate considers these individuals inactive in these specific capacities:

 1.These individuals must immediately return to their previously confirmed roles (if applicable) or
 vacate the unauthorized positions.
 2.If the Executive Branch wishes to establish these roles, a Bill must be passed to add the position
 to the Statutes, or a Resolution must be passed authorizing the creation of the role.4
 3.Only after the position is legally created can a nominee be forwarded for confirmation.

We request immediate clarification on the status of these individuals (whether they are acting,
appointed, confirmed, or are pending confirmation) and confirmation that they have ceased
operating under these unauthorized titles.

2 Executive Order #80-06 explicitly states: "Senate shall adopt this Executive Policy pursuant to Title IV, § 421, upon
which this Executive Policy document shall become effective". No Resolution or Bill was ever introduced or passed to
ratify this order. Consequently, the "Executive Branch Policy" and all positions created solely within it (including
Deputy Solicitor General) never legally came into existence.
3 The Senate notes that Mr. Rubenstein has identified himself numerous times as “Deputy Attorney General” for the
official record at convened meetings of the 77th and 78th Student Senate.
4 SBS Chapter 301.4(C) states: "Additional internal department roles may be created by the Secretary or Director,
subject to approval from the Student Body President and Student Senate..."
 Page 10 of 20February, 6th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-001

IV. NOTICE REGARDING UNCONFIRMED APPOINTEES (EO #80-09 & #80-07)

The Senate has identified approximately twelve (12) individuals currently serving in Executive
Department roles who were appointed solely via Executive Order. This violation concerns
individuals appointed under the following orders: Executive Order #80-07 and Executive Order
#80-09.

These appointments suffer from two distinct legal defects that render the appointees unable to
validly hold office:

 1.Under Advisory Opinion 2025-03, the Supreme Court ruled that "The President may not fill
 Cabinet positions without Senate confirmation". As Chapter 301.4(C) defines "All roles within
 Executive Departments" as members of the Executive Cabinet, the President’s attempt to install
 these officers unilaterally via Executive Order violates Article II, Section 5.1(d) of the
 Constitution.
 2.Many of the specific titles held by these appointees (e.g., Civic Engagement Coordinator,
 Social Media Director) do not exist in the Student Body Statutes. They appear to be defined
 only within the "Executive Branch Policy" attached to Executive Order #80-06. As established
 in Section III, Executive Order #80-06 was never ratified by the Senate as required by its own
 text. Therefore, strictly speaking, these specific offices do not legally exist. The President
 cannot appoint individuals to positions created by an unratified policy.

The Office of the Senate President recognizes that these positions are intended to serve vital
functions for the Student Body. We desire a cooperative solution to legitimize the Executive Branch
structure. 

The Senate is willing to immediately take up a Resolution to:
 1.Officially adopt a finalized updated list of Executive Branch departmental positions.
 2.Ratify the "Executive Branch Policy" originally proposed in EO #80-06, thereby curing one of
 the statutory defects.

However, this legislative cooperation is contingent upon the following:
 Ratifying the positions does not automatically ratify the people. Once the Resolution is passed
 and the positions legally exist and are correctly advertised to the public, the Executive Branch
 must immediately submit a Forwarding Letter containing the names of the individuals up for
 Senate confirmation.

 Page 11 of 20February, 6th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-001

V. REQUESTS FOR REMEDY & PATH FORWARD

To restore the constitutional order of the Student Government Association and avoid further
conflict, the Senate requests the following immediate actions:

 1.As described in Section II: The Senate notes that the "six-week acting capacity" for the
 individuals listed in Executive Order #80-11 (Ian Seibert, Isabella LoBianco, Jack Rowan,
 Nicolas Valenzuela) expired on January 15, 2026.
 a.These individuals must immediately suspend all official duties. To reinstate them, the
 Executive Branch must first cure the initial procedural defect by properly noticing
 applications for these positions on the SGA website for the mandated period, as this public
 advertisement was not performed prior to their initial appointment.
 b.Mr. Jack Rowan cannot be validly forwarded for confirmation while he continues to hold a
 second major position with his legislative seat as a Representative of the College of Law in
 the Congress of Graduate Students.
 2.As described in Section III: The positions of "Deputy Solicitor General" (Ms. Claudia Urday)
 and "Deputy Attorney General" (Mr. Logan Rubenstein) are law enforcement roles that enforce
 the Student Body Statutes. As such, it is our request they be established by Statute, not merely
 by Executive policy.
 a.These individuals must return to their previously confirmed roles or vacate their current
 unauthorized titles immediately.
 b.The Senate views the creation of these roles as a high priority. We are ready to fast-track a
 Bill to formally add these positions to the Department of Legal Affairs statute. Once the
 positions are legally created, you may immediately forward these nominees for
 confirmation.
 3.As described Section IV: Regarding the twelve (12) individuals appointed via EO #80-07 and
 EO #80-09 (e.g., Social Media Director, Grants Coordinator):
 a.The Senate is prepared to immediately take up the necessary legislative action to ratify the
 "Executive Branch Policy" proposed in EO #80-06. We are willing to pass a Resolution
 adopting an updated position list, thereby curing the statutory defect for these titles.
 b.In exchange for this legislative fix, we request a Forwarding Letter for all twelve individuals
 following the adoption of EO #80-06.
 4.To better facilitate all of the above steps in this process, we request the submission of a
 complete roster of the Executive Branch. Please list every current member, their official title,
 and their appointment status (e.g., "Confirmed," "Acting," or "Appointed via EO").

 Page 12 of 20February, 6th, 2026
MEMORANDUM #78-001

VI. CONCLUSION

The Student Senate recognizes the ambition and dedication of the Executive Branch in serving the
student body. We understand that the administrative hurdles of governance can often feel
burdensome, and we appreciate the President's desire to staff these departments quickly to deliver
results for the students of Florida State University and to set up statutory precedent for future
administrations to come.

The Office of the Senate President remains committed to meeting with the Executive Branch as
many times as needed during this process. Our goal is to ensure that your administration's priorities
are heard, understood, and represented, so that the Executive Branch is able to faithfully serve the
student body within the framework of our statutes.

It is the position of the Office of the Senate President that true "faithful service" requires adherence
to the law. We are open to future dialogue about reforming the confirmation process to allow for
greater flexibility, but we cannot ignore the current rules while those discussions occur. As the
Supreme Court noted, protecting these processes "protects the separation of powers". We must
ensure that every officer of this government holds their title not by decree, but by the lawful
consent of the governed.

We are a student government of laws, and we must adhere to the Constitution as it stands today.

Furthermore, we must ensure that the Student Body is actually aware of these opportunities. In the
case of recent appointments, positions were created and filled without providing the student body
their legal opportunity to apply. To ensure equity, every vacancy must be properly noticed to the
public as required by Statute. We cannot fast-track appointments at the expense of fair competition
and open access to student government. 

We look forward to receiving the forwarded nominations and the updated roster so that we may
move past these procedural defects and return to our mission of representing the student body.

 Alexia Holliday
 78th Student Senate President

Short Title: Commending Seminoles Engaged in Politics during FSU Day at the Capitol. 

Summary of Legislation: This proclamation formally recognizes Seminoles Engaged in 
Politics for their organization and execution during the Florida State University Day at the 
Capitol. It commends participating students for their sustained preparation, civic engagement, 
and professional representation of the FSU student body through advocacy and dialogue with 
state officials. 

Background Information: 
Seminoles Engaged in Politics is a Florida State University student organization dedicated to 
civic engagement, political education, and student advocacy. In preparation for the FSU Day at 
the Capitol, members of the Seminoles Engaged in Politics cohort participated in a lobbying 
workshop and later attended a total of 102 meetings across the cohort during the Day at the 
Capitol. The Day at the Capitol provided students with a direct opportunity to observe and 
participate in the legislative process while advocating on issues relevant to college students, 
higher education, and the broader community. Through meetings at the Florida State Capitol, 
participating students represented the interests of Florida State University with professionalism 
and intentionality. This proclamation is presented to recognize the depth of leadership 
development, and commitment to civic responsibility demonstrated by students in the 
Seminoles Engaged in Politics cohort and the Florida State Office of Governmental Affairs. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

Adrion Milton, Natalie Gonzalez, Director and Deputy Director of the Office of Governmental 
Affairs. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This proclamation formally recognizes the Office of Governmental Affairs and the Seminoles 
Engaged in Politics cohort for their leadership, preparation, and representation of Florida State 
University during the Day at the Capitol. It affirms the Student Senate’s support for student 
civic engagement initiatives and acknowledges the importance of student involvement in the 
democratic process.

State University students. This bill is presented to ensure consistency between the Student 
Body Statutes and the program’s existing structure, mission, and operations. By formally 
defining SEP within Chapter 301, the amendment provides clarity for future students, 
administrators, and Student Government leadership regarding the program’s purpose, 
oversight, and selection process.

Politics Program without altering its operational authority or mission. If enacted, it will ensure 
accuracy, clarity, and continuity within the Student Body Statutes regarding the program’s 
name, purpose, and placement under the Office of Governmental Affairs.

Short Title: Amending Chapter 401, Student Body Statutes, to Streamline and Codify the 
Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This bill amends Chapter 401 of the Student Body Statutes to establish a clear, structured, and 
transparent process for submitting and considering amendments to legislation. The proposed 
changes enhance legislative efficiency, promote informed deliberation, and ensure meaningful 
public notice and participation throughout the amendment process. 

Background Information: 
Prior to this amendment, the Student Body Statutes lacked a formalized process for submitting 
amendments to measures outside of standing committee proceedings. As a result, 
amendments were frequently introduced orally and in large batches on the Senate floor, often 
without sufficient notice to Senators or the public. 
 
This practice created confusion during debate, administrative inefficiencies, and uncertainty 
regarding the substance of legislation under consideration. In some cases, measures were 
materially altered from their publicly noticed descriptions, undermining transparency and public 
trust in the legislative process. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with input comment from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate 
Leadership, and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This bill establishes a standardized amendment submission process, including the creation of 
an amendment submission form and a forty-eight (48) hour deadline for amendments prior to a 
bill’s second reading. It increases procedural safeguards for late-filed amendments by raising 
voting thresholds and authorizing recesses for review. 

 Page 8 of 16

Additionally, the legislation requires amendments that materially alter a measure’s publicly 
noticed purpose or description to be clearly identified as such, thereby strengthening 
transparency, preserving public notice, and improving the overall integrity of the legislative 
process.

Short Title: A Proposed Constitutional Amendment Clarifying the Appointment Powers of the Student 
Body President. 

Summary of Legislation: 
The proposed amendment clarifies the appointment powers of the Student Body President (SBP) by 
reinforcing the status quo envisioned by Senate Bills 76-038 and 77-028. Namely, that the SBP appoints 
all non-elected major officers (except those offices which the Constitution vests appointment authority in 
another officer/entity), with Senate confirmation, and that the President appoints all non-major, non-
elected, officers without the need for Senate confirmation. It further provides a statement of intent and 
title for the Spring 2026 ballot. 

Background Information: 
Over the course of the 76th and 77th Student Senates, several bills passed that had the cumulative effect 
of removing the need for Senate confirmation from many non-major offices within SGA.1 The Senate 
passed these bills after careful consideration regarding the scale of the confirmation process and after 
years of confirmation backlogs leaving numerous administrations unable to begin executing their priorities 
until mid-fall, at best. Bill 77-028 passed unanimously, and Bill 76-038 passed with only one vote against. 
 
As a result, the Executive Branch has relied on Chapter 301, Student Body Statutes, and has appointed 
large swaths of the Executive Branch without seeking Senate confirmation. All Cabinet secretaries were 
put forward for Senate confirmation and were confirmed. 
 
On December 12, 2025, the Student Supreme Court issued an advisory opinion related to the 
appointment powers of the Student Body President. In it, the Court stated that appointees to the Cabinet 
must be forwarded to the Senate for confirmation.2 The Court did not opine on what the Cabinet is 
comprised of.3 Out of an abundance of caution, the Office of the Attorney General has recommended a 
constitutional amendment that clarifies the Student Body President’s appointment power by reinforcing 
the appointment structure previously adopted by the Student Senate. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
 
1 See, e.g., Bill 76-038, FSU Stud. Sen. (codified as Chp. 304, SBS) (replacing the appointments process with an 
authorization for the Executive Branch to adopt policies regulating the appointment process); s. 2, Bill 77-028, FSU 
Stud. Sen. (codified as Chp. 301, SBS) (creating the current Executive Department structure, requiring department 
secretaries to be confirmed by the Senate, and authorizing directors and coordinators to be appointed by each 
secretary without Senate confirmation). 
2 Concerning Presidential Appointment Powers, Advisory Opinion 2025-03 at 2–3 (Fla. St. Student Sup. Ct. 2025). 
3 Id. at 2. 

 Page 10 of 16

The proposed amendment was drafted in collaboration with the Office of the Attorney General. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
Section 1 repeals Article II, Section 5(1)(d), of the Florida State University Student Body Constitution. 
This paragraph repeats rules set forth in Section 2 of the amendment, as well as Article IV, Section 5 
(setting a two-thirds vote for Supreme Court justices), and Article V, Section 7 (setting a two-thirds vote 
for appointments to vacant elected offices). 
 
Section 2 amends Article III, Section 3(2), of the Florida State University Student Body Constitution to 
clarify the appointment powers of the Student Body President. All major, non-elected, officers shall be 
appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, unless otherwise specified by the Constitution.4 
All non-major, non-elected, officers shall be appointed by the Student Body President, without Senate 
confirmation, except that the power to appoint such officers may be vested in other officers by law.5 
Finally, the amendment protects other places in the Constitution that vests appointment powers in other 
places.6 
 
Section 3 sets a title for the ballot measure, sets a statement of intent, and details that ratification occurs 
upon two-thirds vote of the Student Body and approval by the Vice President for Student Affairs.7 
 
If the amendment is proposed by three-fourths vote of the Senate, the amendment must be delivered to 
the Supervisor of Elections by the Senate President.8 The Supervisor shall submit the amendment to the 
Student Supreme Court for review within seven days of passage through the Senate.9 The amendment 
will also be noticed to the public prior to the vote.

 Workshop on Redesignation of At-Large Representatives

Lead Representatives: Chair Rowan and Deputy Speaker Lananae 

 Representatives will discuss whether COGS should adopt an amendment to 
the COGS Code that allows At-Large representatives to be redesignated as 
representatives within their college if a vacancy in the college exists. 

Options 

 1. Recommend a policy allowing At-Large representatives to be redesignated as 
 representatives within their college and designate one-to-two members of the 
 Committee to draft a bill amending COGS Code in a manner determined by 
 the Committee. 
 a. Potential methods: 
 i. Simple application & Assembly vote. 
 ii. Full re-petitioning. 
 iii. Requiring a petition with a lower number of signatures. 
 2. Recommend against changing the Code to allow At-Large representatives to 
 be redesignated as representatives within their college. 
 3. Committee discretion. 

 Page 6 of 7
 COGS Internal Affairs Committee 

 Action Item #3 

 Workshop on Organizations Engaging in Fundraising 

Lead Representatives: Speaker Medarev, Deputy Speaker Serrone. 

 Representatives will discuss whether COGS should adopt an amendment to 
the COGS Code allowing organizations receiving COGS funds to fundraise, 
particularly when such fundraising is for a charitable cause. Currently, organizations 
cannot use COGS funds solely for fundraising but are allowed to use COGS funds to 
events where there is a fundraising aspect. However, any funds raised at such event 
must be paid back to COGS until the amount of COGS funds used towards the event 
is paid back. 

Options 

 1. Recommend a policy allowing organizations to fundraise using COGS funds 
 without having to pay money back to COGS and designate one-to-two members 
 of the Committee to draft a bill amending Chapter 303, COGS Code, in a 
 manner determined by the Committee. 
 i. Consideration: Orgs fundraising for self vs. for charitable cause. 
 ii. Consideration: Non-profits that may exist as external arms for 
 the organization. 
 2. Recommend against changing the Code to allow organizations to fundraise 
 using COGS funds without having to pay money back to COGS. 
 3. Committee discretion.

 78th STUDENT SENATE 
 Legislation Cover Sheet 
 
 Resolution #: 007 
 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Bigenho 
 Co-sponsor(s): 

Short Title: Amending Rule Ten, Senate Rules of Procedure, to Clarify Definitions and 
Streamline and Codify the Amendment Process 

Summary of Legislation: 

This resolution updates Rule Ten of the Senate Rules of Procedure to clarify definitions of 
legislative instruments and establish a structured, transparent, and uniform amendment 
process. The changes align Senate procedural rules with recently adopted statutory standards, 
improve clarity for Senators and the public, and enhance efficiency and predictability during 
floor consideration of measures. 

Background Information: 
Rule Ten governs the submission, consideration, and amendment of measures before the 
Student Senate. Prior to this amendment, several key terms were either undefined or 
inconsistently applied, and procedures for submitting and considering amendments lacked 
sufficient structure. This resulted in confusion during debate, last-minute changes to 
legislation, and reduced transparency for both Senators and the public. Following the adoption 
of statutory reforms to the amendment process, it became necessary to revise Rule Ten to 
ensure consistency between the Senate Rules of Procedure and the Student Body Statutes, 
as well as to formally codify best practices that had developed informally over time. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 

This bill was drafted with direct input from the Senate Rules Committee, Senate Leadership, 
and the outgoing Senate Officer Team. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This resolution clarifies the definitions of legislative instruments, including bills, resolutions, 
amendments, committee substitutes, and late-filed amendments. It codifies procedures for 
submitting amendments in advance of Senate meetings, establishes clear voting thresholds 
and debate procedures for late-filed amendments, and formalizes processes for committee 
substitutes, confirmations, and statements of dissent. Collectively, these changes improve 

 Page 3 of 13

legislative transparency, protect public notice, reduce administrative confusion, and ensure a 
more orderly and deliberative amendment process on the Senate floor.

 Senate PCA #: 001 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Jackson

Short Title: A Proposed Constitutional Amendment Clarifying the Appointment Powers of the Student 
Body President. 

Summary of Legislation: 
The proposed amendment clarifies the appointment powers of the Student Body President (SBP) by 
reinforcing the status quo envisioned by Senate Bills 76-038 and 77-028. Namely, that the SBP appoints 
all non-elected major officers (except those offices which the Constitution vests appointment authority in 
another officer/entity), with Senate confirmation, and that the President appoints all non-major, non-
elected, officers without the need for Senate confirmation. It further provides a statement of intent and 
title for the Spring 2026 ballot. 

Background Information: 
Over the course of the 76th and 77th Student Senates, several bills passed that had the cumulative effect 
of removing the need for Senate confirmation from many non-major offices within SGA.1 The Senate 
passed these bills after careful consideration regarding the scale of the confirmation process and after 
years of confirmation backlogs leaving numerous administrations unable to begin executing their priorities 
until mid-fall, at best. Bill 77-028 passed unanimously, and Bill 76-038 passed with only one vote against. 
 
As a result, the Executive Branch has relied on Chapter 301, Student Body Statutes, and has appointed 
large swaths of the Executive Branch without seeking Senate confirmation. All Cabinet secretaries were 
put forward for Senate confirmation and were confirmed. 
 
On December 12, 2025, the Student Supreme Court issued an advisory opinion related to the 
appointment powers of the Student Body President. In it, the Court stated that appointees to the Cabinet 
must be forwarded to the Senate for confirmation.2 The Court did not opine on what the Cabinet is 
comprised of.3 Out of an abundance of caution, the Office of the Attorney General has recommended a 
constitutional amendment that clarifies the Student Body President’s appointment power by reinforcing 
the appointment structure previously adopted by the Student Senate. 
 
Legislative Outreach and Consultation: 
 
1 See, e.g., Bill 76-038, FSU Stud. Sen. (codified as Chp. 304, SBS) (replacing the appointments process with an 
authorization for the Executive Branch to adopt policies regulating the appointment process); s. 2, Bill 77-028, FSU 
Stud. Sen. (codified as Chp. 301, SBS) (creating the current Executive Department structure, requiring department 
secretaries to be confirmed by the Senate, and authorizing directors and coordinators to be appointed by each 
secretary without Senate confirmation). 
2 Concerning Presidential Appointment Powers, Advisory Opinion 2025-03 at 2–3 (Fla. St. Student Sup. Ct. 2025). 
3 Id. at 2. 

 Page 10 of 13

The proposed amendment was drafted in collaboration with the Office of the Attorney General. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
Section 1 repeals Article II, Section 5(1)(d), of the Florida State University Student Body Constitution. 
This paragraph repeats rules set forth in Section 2 of the amendment, as well as Article IV, Section 5 
(setting a two-thirds vote for Supreme Court justices), and Article V, Section 7 (setting a two-thirds vote 
for appointments to vacant elected offices). 
 
Section 2 amends Article III, Section 3(2), of the Florida State University Student Body Constitution to 
clarify the appointment powers of the Student Body President. All major, non-elected, officers shall be 
appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, unless otherwise specified by the Constitution.4 
All non-major, non-elected, officers shall be appointed by the Student Body President, without Senate 
confirmation, except that the power to appoint such officers may be vested in other officers by law.5 
Finally, the amendment protects other places in the Constitution that vests appointment powers in other 
places.6 
 
Section 3 sets a title for the ballot measure, sets a statement of intent, and details that ratification occurs 
upon two-thirds vote of the Student Body and approval by the Vice President for Student Affairs.7 
 
If the amendment is proposed by three-fourths vote of the Senate, the amendment must be delivered to 
the Supervisor of Elections by the Senate President.8 The Supervisor shall submit the amendment to the 
Student Supreme Court for review within seven days of passage through the Senate.9 The amendment 
will also be noticed to the public prior to the vote.

 78th STUDENT SENATE 
 Legislation Cover Sheet 
 
 Senate Bill #: 001 
 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Perantoni 
 Co-sponsor(s): 

Short Title: Amending Chapter 701, 708, and 710 of the Student Body Statutes to provide 
definitions, codify practices, and create enforcement. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This bill amends Chapter 701 to add definitions for the terms “Fraudulent,” “Defamatory,” and 
“Officer” as used in the Student Body Statutes. This bill amends Chapter 708 to codify a 
requirement that parties send a list of specified volunteers and officers to the Supervisor of 
Elections. This bill amends Chapter 710 to create enforcement mechanisms against a violation 
of the amended section of Chapter 708. 

Background Information: 
The first portion of this legislation is needed in light of the recent case “Ojha v. ForwardFSU,” 
where the court was asked to identify a definition of officer, currently undefined in our student 
body statutes, especially as it relates to holding parties accountable for their officer’s official 
actions. The next part of this legislation acts as a means to codify the existing practice of 
candidates and political parties sending in lists of their volunteers and officers, allowing the 
party to clearly identify who is acting in an official capacity of the party and who is acting 
merely as a campaign volunteer. Finally, the last amendment will create an enforcement 
mechanism of the campaign volunteer submissions as a matter of election violations. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
The effects of this proposed legislation will allow for our key terms surrounding most severe 
violations to have official definitional language, allowing for superior enforcement, easier court 
cases, and proper due process for students to review permitted and non-permitted conduct. 
The volunteer list will codify a standing practice, and allow for the Supervisor of Elections to 
enforce the requirement for a political party to submit their volunteers/officers, in order to make 
it clear who has the authority to act as an official agent of the party.
