63 who are academic Juniors or Seniors shall be the only students eligible to vote for 
64 candidates seeking the offices in the Senior Class Council. All students registered for 
65 classes during the election may vote for candidates for campus-wide elected offices, 
66 as well as for Constitutional Amendments and Referenda. 

67 l. General Election: Elections held for the purpose of determining the candidate who 
68 shall assume office. There shall be two General Elections per year, one in the fall 
69 semester and the other in the spring semester. 

70 m. Special Election: Any election held at any time other than a General Election for any 
71 purpose. 

72 n. Division: Academic colleges and schools as reported by the Office of Institutional 
73 Research. 

74 o. Certificate of Election: A document certifying that a candidate has been duly elected. 

75 p. Final Expense Statement: A document listing all financial expenditures or 
76 contributions in regard to fees and/or donations during the election cycle. All receipts 
77 of expenditures, all bank statements and their proper relatives, deposit slips, and 
78 other documentation recording expenses and donations received are part of the 
79 Final Expense Statement. The following shall also be considered part of the Final 
80 Expense Statement: 

81 1. A statement of the cumulative campaign expenditures based on the fair 
82 market value, signed by the candidates and/or party chairman. 

83 2. An itemized list of all expenses. 

84 3. An itemized report containing the full name of each person who has made 
85 one or more contributions in any form to the campaign. 

86 4. Campaign Contribution Statement, a copy of all account statements, check 
87 stubs, deposit slips, and any other financial documents shall be submitted 
88 on the first Monday of campaigning by 12:00 p.m. as well as in the 
89 candidate or party’s final expense statement. 

90 5. Each political party shall include a Financial Recap Summary of all funds 
91 collected throughout the academic year preceding the election. This 
92 summary must detail the source, amount, and date of all income received, 
93 including but not limited to donations, dues, merchandise sales, and 
94 fundraising activities. It must be attached to the Final Expense Statement 
95 submission and posted publicly. Additionally, the summary must be 
96 formatted according to templates issued by the Supervisor of Elections and 
97 verified against any previously reported Campaign Contribution Statements. 

 Page 5 of 15 
 98 q. Complete Final Expense Statement: A Final Expense Statement if it is free of any 
 99 false statements, a complete and accurate campaign contribution list, and all receipts 
100 are legible and can be understood by the Office of Elections. 

101 r. Incomplete Final Expense Statement: A statement that is missing receipts for 
102 expenses, having an incomplete campaign contribution statement, or containing 
103 receipts that are illegible or unintelligible. 

104 s. Fraudulent Final Expense Statement is defined as a statement that is intentionally 
105 misleading which includes false payment forms and receipts, as well as intentionally 
106 lying about the usage of donations, party dues, and/or other party or individual funds. 
107 Fraudulent Final Expense Statements also include the mislabeling of where 
108 donations originate. 

109 t. Unofficial Election Results: Election results that have not officially been verified by 
110 the Supervisor of Elections as outlined by Chapter 713 and 714 of the Student Body 
111 Election Code. 

112 u. Official Election Results: All votes of an election that have been verified by the 
113 Supervisor of Elections as outlined by Chapter 713 and 714 of the Student Body 
114 Election Code. 

115 v. Final Election Results: The election results after all final expense statements have 
116 been approved and there are not outstanding appeals and/or alleged violations. 

117 w. Campaign Contribution Statement: A copy of bank account statements, check stubs, 
118 deposit slips, receipts of both campaign expenses and campaign materials, up to the 
119 date of submission and any other financial documents which shall be submitted by 
120 12:00 p.m. on the first Monday of campaigning and in the candidate or party’s final 
121 expense statement. This shall be submitted on a form prescribed by the Supervisor 
122 of Elections. 

123 x. Election Cycle: When Title VII goes into effect for an election. The Election Cycle 
124 begins when Candidacy Declaration opens and ends the first Friday following an 
125 election. 

126 y. Advertisement: Notice or announcement in a public medium promoting a candidate 
127 of a political party in which a monetary transaction is made or considered a 
128 campaign material. 

129 1. Non-candidate or non-dues paying political party members’ posts shall not 
130 be considered advertisements. 

131 z. False or Malicious Charges: Allegations that knowingly, deliberately or recklessly 
132 mislead, or attempt to mislead a student regarding alleged violations of the Student 
133 Body Election Code. 

134 aa. Fair Market Value: The retail (non-discounted) value of a single item, including 
135 applicable taxes. 

 Page 6 of 15 
136 1. All items posted prior to the beginning of campaigning that do not constitute 
137 as campaign material shall not constitute a campaign expense. 

138 2. Discounted items that are available to all persons and parties at the time of 
139 purchase shall be exempted from fair market value criterion. 

140 bb. Ranked Choice Voting: A voting method in which voters rank candidates in order of 
141 preference. If a candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, they are elected. If 
142 no candidate receives a majority, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, 
143 and votes for that candidate are transferred to the next ranked choice on each ballot. 
144 This process continues until one candidate has a majority of the votes. Each ballot 
145 containing ranked choice voting shall include, in a clear and conspicuous manner, 
146 written instructions that explain how the ranked choice voting process functions and 
147 how to correctly mark the ballot. 

148 cc. Fraudulent: any intentional act or omission designed to deceive, mislead, or 
149 improperly influence the election process, where the actor knows the representation 
150 or conduct is false, and where the deception is capable of affecting a material aspect 
151 of the election, including voter decisions, candidate eligibility, ballot integrity, or the 
152 administration of voting procedures. 

153 1. Regardless of actual affect, if the actions undertaken by an individual has 
154 the reasonable capability to influence the election, it will fall under this 
155 definition. 

156 dd. Defamatory: a false statement, written or spoken, to a third party, presented as fact, 
157 and causes damage to the person’s reputation. 

158 1. A false statement regarding a candidate, elected official, party officer, or 
159 other public official, must prove actual malice to be considered defamatory. 

160 1. Actual malice shall be defined as a false statement either with 
161 knowledge of its falsity or with reckless disregard for the truth. 

162 2. A false statement regarding a private individual does not require proof of 
163 actual malice. 

164 ee. Officer: an individual who holds an office of trust, authority, or command. 

165 1. This definition will also encompass any individual who is considered by a 
166 political party to be an officer by their governing documents. 

167 Section 2. Amendment to Student Body Statutes Chapter 708, “Campaigning Rules and 
168 Campaign Materials”. 

169 Chapter 708 of the Florida State University Student Body Statutes is hereby amended to read as 
170 follows: 

171 Chapter 708 Campaigning Rules And Campaign Materials 

 Page 7 of 15 
172 1. Regulation of Campaign Material and Other Activities: 
173 

174 a. Campaign materials may be placed in university owned academic buildings in places 
175 provided for general information such as billboards or community posting boards. 
176 Any marking of university property must be approved by the proper university 
177 authority or authorities. 

178 b. Active campaigning by soliciting support from students is forbidden inside university 
179 academic buildings and residence halls. 

180 c. All material and activity located on FSU campuses shall be in accordance with rules 
181 and regulation of Campus Event Services, Union Posting Guidelines, University 
182 Housing Guidelines, the Student Conduct Code and any other relevant entities. 

183 d. There shall be no campaigning through the campus email system. 

184 1. A student may not use FSU email servers to campaign for political office. 
185 This includes sending emails from their own FSU email or to another 
186 student’s FSU email. 

187 e. Campaigning inside of university owned libraries, dining halls, and the Student Union 
188 is prohibited. 

189 2. Volunteer Registration 

190 a. All volunteers who are tasked with campaigning on behalf of a candidate and/or party 
191 will be required to be registered by the candidate and/or party as a registered 
192 campaigner through the Supervisor of Elections office. 

193 1. To register an individual, the candidate/party must provide their full name, 
194 FSUID, and major. 

195 2. In the case of a party registering their campaigners, the party must register 
196 their members and officers of the party separately. 

197 b. Candidates/political parties may submit amendments to their list of registered 
198 campaigners, removals and additions, by emailing the Supervisor of Elections. 

199 1. This amendment process is not allowed to be used by a political party to 
200 avoid liability of the party in cases pursuant to Section 710(5)(c). 

201 Section 3. Amendment to Student Body Statutes Chapter 710, “Violations and Penalties”. 

202 Chapter 710 of the Florida State University Student Body Statutes is hereby amended to read 
203 as follows: 

204 Chapter 710 Violations And Penalties 

205 1. Scope and Prosecution of Alleged Violations: 

 Page 8 of 15 
206 a. All candidates and political party members are bound by and may be prosecuted 
207 under this Code. 

208 b. Conviction of any person for a violation under this Code shall not preclude 
209 subsequent prosecution or violation of the Ethics Codes or the Student Conduct 
210 Code. 

211 c. The Attorney General shall represent the Supervisor of Elections in all proceedings 
212 of the Elections Commission and Supreme Court. 

213 2. Enforcement: 

214 a. The Supervisor of Elections, Deputy Supervisors, Elections Assistants, and all 
215 members of the Elections Commission shall enforce the Election Code. Failure to 
216 enforce the Election Code shall be an impeachable offense. 

217 3. Standing: 

218 a. Students or political parties who show actual injury shall have standing to contest the 
219 results of any election on grounds within or outside the scope of the Election Code 
220 until forty-eight (48) hours following the close of the polls. 

221 4. Reporting Procedures: 

222 a. All alleged violations shall be brought to the Supervisor of Elections in accordance 
223 with Section 703(2) of the Student Body Election Code, and must include: 

224 1. The name of the party or individual alleging the violation; 

225 2. The name of the party or individual who allegedly violated the Elections 
226 Code; 

227 3. The specific statute(s) in the Elections Code which was allegedly violated; 

228 4. Any and all evidence to support the claim of an alleged violation; and 

229 5. A short and plain statement describing the occurrence of the alleged 
230 violation. 

231 b. When an alleged violation is filed against an individual candidate, independent 
232 candidate, political party, or a member of a political party, the Supervisor of Elections 
233 shall notify the recipient(s) and listed witnesses of the alleged violation within twenty-
234 four (24) hours after receiving the alleged violation. 

235 c. All students will have the option to present their case directly to the elections 
236 commission, choose a third-party to represent them, or be appointed a law student 
237 by the Supreme Court to represent their case before the Elections Commission. 

238 d. The Supervisor of Elections and Deputy Supervisor(s) shall have the power to 
239 receive and review alleged violations. The time, place, and manner of such violations 
240 shall be recorded and submitted to the Elections Commission. 

241 e. All alleged violations and appeals must be presented to the Supervisor of Elections 
242 electronically by the end of two (2) business days from their discovery. 

 Page 9 of 15 
243 1. Any complaint that lists an alleged violation after two (2) business days 
244 from its original discovery shall be dismissed by the Supervisor of Elections. 

245 f. The final deadline for all alleged violations and appeals to be filed by an individual or 
246 political party for a particular election is forty-eight (48) hours following the close of 
247 polls from an election, unless it alleges a failure to submit a complete or rectified final 
248 expense statement. 

249 1. If an alleged violation is submitted less than twenty-four (24) hours before 
250 the deadline to submit alleged violations, the Supervisor of Elections shall 
251 be allowed to notify individuals of an alleged violation after the close of the 
252 filing deadline. 

253 2. The final deadline for an alleged violation and appeal to be filed by an 
254 individual or political party alleging a failure to submit a complete or rectified 
255 final expense statement is the Wednesday following an election by 4 p.m. 

256 g. The burden that a party alleging a violation of the Student Body Election Code must 
257 meet in order to prove a violation shall be by “clear and convincing evidence”. 

258 h. Students shall not be prohibited from properly registered campaign materials which 
259 are clothing, except in the Student Senate Chambers. 

260 1. Wearing clothing which is a campaign material is strictly prohibited in the 
261 Student Senate Chambers. The only exception to this rule is when the 
262 results of an election are read aloud to the Senate by the Supervisor of 
263 Elections on the day of an election. 

264 5. Implementation of Violations: 

265 a. Each occurrence, event, or time that violates the Election Code shall constitute an 
266 alleged Election violation that must be heard by the Elections Commission. Violations 
267 do not count against a candidate or political party until ruled upon by the Elections 
268 Commission. 

269 1. In the event that a party found to be responsible by the Elections 
270 Commission appeals to the Student Supreme Court, the violation will not be 
271 counted until the Supreme Court issues their ruling. 

272 b. Disqualification shall occur according to the following provisions: 

273 1. Party Disqualification: 

274 1. A political party that has either been found guilty of a schedule 4 
275 violation or has accumulated twenty-five (25) or more penalty points 
276 during a single election cycle shall be disqualified. A candidate or 
277 individual that has either been found guilty of a schedule 4 violation or 
278 has accumulated fifteen (15) or more penalty points during a single 
279 elction election cycle shall be disqualified. 

280 2. In the case that a political party is disqualified, all candidates running 
281 in that election with that party shall become disqualified. Any 
282 candidate disqualified shall be barred from running for an elected 
283 office or being a member of a political party for one (1) election cycle 
284 following their disqualification. 

 Page 10 of 15 
285 3. The disqualified political party is barred from participating in future 
286 elections for a period of four (4) years. 

287 4. All party officers and members of the party leadership board shall be 
288 barred from participating in student government elections as members 
289 of political parties or running for office for one (1) election cycle 
290 following their disqualification. 

291 2. Winning Candidate Disqualification: 

292 1. If a candidate who won an election is then disqualified, the Supervisor 
293 of Elections shall call a Special Election pursuant to Student Body 
294 Statute Section 705(2) for the office won by the disqualified candidate. 

295 3. Individual Disqualification: 

296 1. In the event the candidate or individual is barred from running in an 
297 election, participating in any political party, or advocating/campaigning 
298 for individual candidates, political parties, or ballot items for one (1) 
299 election cycle following their disqualification. 

300 4. Special Election After Disqualification: 

301 1. If there is a special election following disqualification of a candidate or 
302 political party, the following rules will be obeyed: 

303 a. Inability to use the political party’s name or logo on campaign 
304 materials and during campaigning. 

305 b. Inability to use the party funds. 

306 c. A disqualified political party cannot endorse a candidate or 
307 candidates. 

308 c. When an Election violation is alleged against a party as opposed to an individual, 
309 naming the party as the respondent, it must meet one or more of the following 
310 standards: 

311 1. The violation is perpetrated by any person acting as an officer of a party. 

312 2. The violation involved the collaboration of more than one member of the 
313 same party. 

314 3. The violation is in a series of violations which constitute a systematic 
315 attempt by a party to violate the Elections Code. 

316 4. The violation is part of a clear pattern of violations perpetrated by 
317 individuals internal to a party which represent systemic ignorance of the 
318 Elections Code. 

319 6. Violations of the Code: 

320 a. No violations will contest or come into contradiction with Section 710(4). 

 Page 11 of 15 
321 b. If a candidate or political party is accused of any election violation and does not 
322 challenge the validity of the allegation, they may be eligible for a reduced punishment 
323 in exchange for an admission of guilt to the Elections Commission. 

324 1. This section shall not apply if an individual, candidate, or political party is 
325 accused of a Schedule 3 Violation or Schedule 4 Violation. 

326 2. After admitting guilt to the Elections Commission, a respondent or petitioner 
327 cannot appeal the alleged violation to the Supreme Court. 

328 3. The vice-chair of the Commission shall move to approve reduced 
329 punishments by acclimation unless any member of the Elections 
330 Commission objects. If an objection is raised, the reduced punishment must 
331 be approved by a majority vote of no less than quorum. 

332 4. An individual, candidate, or political party may have up to three (3) 
333 punishments reduced per election cycle. Reduced punishments eliminate 
334 all points associated with a violation. 

335 c. Schedule one (1) Violations of this Code shall be assigned as follows: 

336 1. Removing, obscuring, or damaging another candidate’s or political party’s 
337 campaign materials within a given space such as a bulletin board or 
338 general flyer area. 

339 2. Engaging in any action against Chapter 709 of the Student Body Election 
340 code, including but not limited to violations of university posting guidelines. 

341 3. Using campaign materials which fail to comply with University regulations, 
342 building regulations, or fail to comply with such regulations in academic 
343 classrooms. 

344 4. Having posted campaign flyers in an academic building or classroom. 

345 5. Failing to remove campaign materials within thirty-six (36) hours of the 
346 closing of the polls, and campaign materials from previous election cycles 
347 that have failed to be removed. 

348 6. Submitting an incomplete Final Expense Statement, consistent with Section 
349 709(2)(f). 

350 1. If an allegation of an incomplete final expense statement is made, the 
351 recipient shall have until the Tuesday following the election by 4 p.m. 
352 Eastern Time to correct any issues with the document. If all issues are 
353 not corrected by the following Tuesday at 4 p.m. Eastern Time this 
354 violation will turn into a Schedule 4 Violation. 

355 d. Schedule two (2) Violations of this Code shall be assigned as follows: 

356 1. Bringing false or malicious charges against another candidate, political 
357 party, or political member. 

358 2. Posting, utilizing, or distributing, either electronically or physically, 
359 campaign material that is publicly defamatory against a candidate for an 
360 elected office of the student body, or is defamatory against any person or 
361 entity within the content of a campaign material. 

 Page 12 of 15 
362 1. This shall apply to political party’s executive board members, 
363 candidates, and/or dues-paying members in the current semester. 

364 3. Defacing or damaging official election materials created and distributed by 
365 the Supervisor or Elections. 

366 4. Campaigning prior to one (1) week before the election. 

367 5. Performing an activity that would intentionally place another party or 
368 candidate in violation of the election code. 

369 6. Using the past and/or present SGA logo on campaign items. 

370 7. Utilizing any Student Government owned equipment for express 
371 endorsement or support for or against any candidate, platform, political 
372 party, or ballot item. 

373 8. Campaigning physically or electronically using the resources, platforms, or 
374 authority of an SGA entity which is not a political party, Affiliated Project, or 
375 Agency. 

376 9. Tasking individuals to campaign as a candidate/political party without 
377 registering them as a registered campaigner under Section 708(2). 

378 e. Schedule three (3) Violations of this Code shall be assigned as follows: 

379 1. Vandalism or any unauthorized marking of university or private property for 
380 campaign purposes. 

381 2. Falsely representing oneself on behalf of the Supervisor of Elections or the 
382 SGA Office of Elections. 

383 3. Engaging in any action against Chapter 709 of the Election Code. 

384 4. Failing to appear at any elections commission hearing if listed as a 
385 petitioner without giving prior notice to the Supervisor of Elections, five (5) 
386 hours prior to the Elections Commission hearing, of inability to appear 

387 f. Schedule four (4) Violations of this Code shall be assigned as follows: 

388 1. Submitting a fraudulent final expense statement. This includes parties or 
389 individuals failing to submit a complete final expense statement by the 
390 Tuesday following the election at 4 p.m. Eastern Time. 

391 1. This is an allegation that can only be made by the Supervisor of 
392 Elections and/or the Deputy Supervisors of Elections. 

393 2. Providing another individual or group with or receiving personal login 
394 information (FSU ID and password) in which they use to cast votes for 
395 another person. These votes shall be considered fraudulent. 

396 3. Any attempt to perpetrate a fraudulent election. This shall include, but is not 
397 limited to, providing false information regarding filing or elections 
398 procedures, voting more than once, or attempting to vote with another 
399 person’s student identification (FSU ID). 

 Page 13 of 15 
400 4. Offering money, gift cards, or other forms of payment in exchange for votes 
401 in any election. 

402 5. Offering goods or services in exchange for votes, not including campaign 
403 materials as specified in Chapter 701 of the Election Code. 

404 6. Submitting a fraudulent volunteer registration form under Section 708(2). 

405 7. Tabulation of Election Violations: 

406 a. Violations shall be adjudicated by the appropriate body as they arise as much as 
407 reasonable efficiency will allow, but a decision to expel or disqualify a candidate from 
408 the ballot shall not be executed until after the final closing of the polls during a 
409 general election. 

410 8. Penalty Point System: 

411 a. Penalty Points shall be assigned with each violation. The Elections Commission shall 
412 hold the discretion to reduce penalties. The vice-chair of the Elections Commission 
413 shall assign penalty points in full accordance with Chapter 710 when no reduction 
414 applies. 

415 1. A political party that has either been found guilty of a schedule 4 violation or 
416 has accumulated twenty-five (25) or more penalty points during a single 
417 election cycle shal be disqualified by the Supervisor of Elections and the 
418 Elections Commission. 

419 2. A candidate or individual that has either been found guilty of a schedule 4 
420 violation or has accumulated fifteen (15) or more penalty points during a 
421 single election cycle shall be disqualified by the Supervisor of Elections and 
422 the Elections Commission. 

423 9. Schedule One (1) Violation Penalties: 

424 a. The following penalties shall be levied against those who have been found 
425 responsible for committing a Schedule One (1) violation: 

426 1. For the first instance of finding a Schedule One (1) Violation pursuant to the 
427 Elections Code, a one (1) point penalty shall be levied against an individual 
428 or political party. 

429 2. For the second and any additional findings of a Schedule One (1) Violation, 
430 three (3) point penalty shall be levied against an individual or political party. 

431 10. Schedule Two (2) Violation Penalties: 

432 a. The following penalties shall be levied against those who have been found 
433 responsible for committing a Schedule Two (2) violation: 

434 1. For the first instance of finding a Schedule Two (2) Violation, a three (3) 
435 point penalty shall be levied against an individual or political party. 

436 2. For the second and any additional findings of a Schedule Two (2) Violation, 
437 a four (4) point penalty shall be levied against an individual or political party. 

438 11. Schedule Three (3) Violation Penalties: 

 Page 14 of 15 
439 a. For all instances of finding a Schedule Three (3) Violation, a ten (10) point penalty 
440 shall be levied against an individual or political party. 

441 12. Schedule Four (4) Violation Penalties: 

442 a. Any person or political party found responsible for a Schedule Four (4) Violation shall 
443 be disqualified pursuant to Student Body Statute Section 710(5)(b). 

444 13. Additional Prosecution: 

445 a. Conviction of any person for violations under this Code shall not preclude 
446 subsequent persecution of that person for violation of the Ethics Code, the Student 
447 Honor Code, or the Student Conduct Code. 

448 Section 4. Effective Date. 

449 The provisions of this bill shall take effect upon the signature of the Vice President for Student 
450 Affairs.

Land Acknowledgement 
The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is 
located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can.

Bill #78-001 Sponsored by Riley Perantoni 
 This bill amends Chapter 701 to add definitions for the terms 
 “Fraudulent,” “Defamatory,” and “Officer” as used in the Student 
 Body Statutes. This bill amends Chapter 708 to codify a requirement 
 that parties send a list of specified volunteers and officers to the 
 Supervisor of Elections. This bill amends Chapter 710 to create 
 enforcement mechanisms against a violation of the amended section 
 of Chapter 708. (Assigned to Judiciary and Internal Affairs, 
 01.21.26) 

Bill #78-002 Sponsored by Destinee Britto, Jose Collantes 
 The following amendments to SBS 703.3.2 Definitions, SBS 709 
 Campaigning Finances, SBS 708 Campaigning Rules and 
 Campaigning Material are explained as establishing the following: 
 giving the Election Commission the appropriate authority to dismiss 
 violations that are deemed frivolous in nature, aligning financial 
 disclosure statement laws with rectified final expense statements, 
 and authenticating a list of all campus party-affiliated members with

sections.text:
THE SEVENTY-SEVENTH STUDENT SENATE 
 Calendar: November 5, 2025 
 Location: Senate Chambers 
 Time: 7:30 PM 
 Submit Public Comment Here 

 Call to Order 

 Pledge of Allegiance 

 Moment of Silent Reflection 
Land Acknowledgement 
The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is 
located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can. 

 Roll Call and Verification of Quorum 

 Presentations and Awards 
 • CHAW - Juan Miguel Abril & Stephan Ugwuagu 

 • Surprise Acknowledgment ✨

 • Corrections and Approval of Senate and Committee Minutes

 • Student Life Committee Minutes (11.2.25)

 • INCOMPLETE - Finance Committee Minutes (11.4.25) 

 • Remaining Balances (Attached) 

 Items Pulled from the Consent Calendar 

 Constitutional Amendments 

 Legislation on First Reading 
Resolution Sponsored by Isabella LoBianco 
#77-080 This resolution requests $4,327.60 in funding from SGA Senate 
 Projects to expand LIFT's visibility and engagement through branded 
 merchandise and wellness materials. (Passed in Student Life 
 11.2.25, Tabled in Budget 10.29.25) 

Bill #77-056 Sponsored by Jackson, Bella Rios 
 This bill amends Chapter 205, “Code of Ethics,” to allow students 
 with prior convictions, who have been reviewed and admitted to 
 Florida State University through the Judicial Review Committee, to 
 serve in Student Government. It reaffirms FSU’s belief in second 
 chances, personal growth, and the power of education to transform 
 lives. (Assigned to Judiciary 11.5.25) 

Bill #77-055 Sponsored by Bigenho, Goldstein 
 This legislation strengthens transparency, accessibility, and judicial 
 independence within the Student Government Association by 
 updating Chapter 203 of the Student Body Statutes. Developed in 
 partnership with the Office of the Attorney General and refined with 
 input from the Senate's Judiciary and Student Life Committees, it 
 improves how students are informed about upcoming meetings, 
 restores and modernizes online public comment in a manner 
 favorable to the Office of the Attorney General, expands 
 opportunities for virtual participation, and reinforces fairer Sunshine 
 enforcement across all branches of SGA. (Assigned to Judiciary 
 10.29.25,Tabled in Judiciary 10.30.25, Assigned to Student Life 
 10.29.25, Found Unfavorable in Student Life) 

 Legislation on Second Reading Allocation Sponsored by Vince Nucatola, Bella Rios 
Resolution This allocation resolution gives $4635.47 to various RSOs. 
#77-009 

Resolution Sponsored by Nathalia Benner, Ferris 
#77-081 This legislation seeks to encourage SGA to explore the opportunity 
 of fixing currently broken Legacy Walk Speakers. The purpose of 
 Legacy Walk is to provide a historical tour of campus, and with 
 repairing the speakers found throughout the tour, SGA can ensure 
 spaces on campus are fully functional to provide the tour 
 experience. (Placed on Second Reading by Senate President 
 11.05.25) 

Bill #77-053 Sponsored by Leila Jackson 
 Passage of the bill provides formal authorization for COGS officers to 
 be sworn in by the oath or affirmation that the Congress had 
 previously enacted. (Passed in Judiciary, 10.30.25) 

Proclamation Sponsored by Noam Druckmann, Elizabeth Cordero 
#77-026 This proclamation serves in efforts to create a safe, respectful, and 
 supportive campus environment. It acknowledges the prevalence of 
 sexual violence on college campuses and encourages FSU's 
 dedication to prevention, education, and express support for all 
 survivors. (Passed in Student Life, 11.2.25) 

Proclamation Sponsored by Leila Jackson, Mia Ferris 
#77-027 This Proclamation aims to solidify the FSU’s Student Senate on 
 furthering the education of financial literacy. As there are many 
 resources such as Unconquered by Debt, Office of Financial Aid, and 
 the Center for Health Advocacy and Wellness that are open to aiding 
 all members of the student body including first-generation students 
 and low-income families. (Passed in Student Life 11.2.25, Passed 
 in Finance 11.3.25) 

Resolution Sponsored by Angelica Moreno 
#77-079 This bill allocates $5,000 from Senate Projects to fund the MCAT 
 Test-Taking Strategies Workshop Series, coordinated by the 
 Interdisciplinary Medical Sciences (IMS) Division and the Office of 
 Pre-Health Advising. The series will include four expert-led 
 workshops designed to improve students' mastery of test-taking 
 strategies essential for MCAT success. The initiative seeks to 
 enhance academic preparedness, accessibility, and competitiveness 
 among FSU's pre-health students. (Passed in Student Life 11.2.25, 
 Passed in Budget 10.30.25)

 77th STUDENT SENATE

 Senate Bill/Resolution/Proclamation/PCA #: 27 
 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Ferris, Jackson 
 Co-sponsor(s): Add any Co-Sponsors here 

Short Title: Educating FSU students on financial literacy 

Summary of Legislation: 
This Proclamation aims to solidify the FSU’s Student Senate on furthering the education of 
financial literacy. As there are many resources such as Unconquered by Debt, Office of 
Financial Aid, and the Center for Health Advocacy and Wellness that are open to aiding all 
members of the student body including first-generation students and low-income families. 

Background Information: 
 According to recent studies from Auburn University in 2024 Only 25% of 18- to 29-year-olds in 
a 2025 survey reported feeling "strongly confident" in their financial knowledge, a drop from 
36% in 2023. The percentage of Gen Z who feel "not at all" financially literate increased from 
12% to 18% over the same period. According to the U.S. Department of Justice, in 2021 an 
estimated 23.9 million persons, or about 9% of all U.S. residents age 16 or older, reported that 
they had been victims of identity theft during the prior 12 months. Almost 4% of U.S. residents 
age 16 or older had experienced at least one incident involving the misuse of an existing credit 
card 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This proclamation aims to achieve more financial literacy among the student body as well as 
providing resources such as RFID Card Blocking Sleeves in the future to be distributed. 

Attachment(s): 
 • Attachment #1: Proposed Proclamation

 Senate Proclamation #: 27 
 
 Primary Sponsor(s): Ferris, Jackson 
 Co-Sponsor(s): Add any Co-Sponsors here 
 
 A PROCLAMATION 
 Educating FSU students on financial literacy 

 1 WHEREAS, the FSU Student Senate recognizes that there is a need to educate our student body on 
 2 financial literacy ; and 

 3 WHEREAS, there are many resources such as Unconquered by Debt, Office of Financial Aid, and the 
 4 Center for Health Advocacy and Wellness that are open to aiding all members of the student body 
 5 including first-generation students and low-income families ; and 

 6 WHEREAS, According to recent studies from Auburn University in 2024 Only 25% of 18- to 29-year-
 7 olds in a 2025 survey reported feeling "strongly confident" in their financial knowledge, a drop from 
 8 36% in 2023. The percentage of Gen Z who feel "not at all" financially literate increased from 12% 
 9 to 18% over the same period; and 

10 WHEREAS, According to the U.S. Department of Justice, in 2021 an estimated 23.9 million persons, or 
11 about 9% of all U.S. residents age 16 or older, reported that they had been victims of identity theft 
12 during the prior 12 months. Almost 4% of U.S. residents age 16 or older had experienced at least 
13 one incident involving the misuse of an existing credit card; and 

14 WHEREAS, the dangers of identity theft and fraud aren’t widely recognized, especially now with more 
15 common forms of payment such as tap payment; 

16 NOW THEREFORE BE IT PROCLAIMED by the 77th Student Senate at Florida State University 
17 that: The FSU Student Senate helps to further provide these resources, information, and points of 
18 contact to the student body; 

19 BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED that: The FSU Student Senate hopes to invest in providing physical 
20 resources such as RFID Card Blocking Sleeves to be distributed via Market Wednesday;

sections.heading: 2025-10-01 Student Senate Meeting Agenda
sections.text:
THE SEVENTY-SEVENTH STUDENT SENATE 
 Calendar: October 1, 2025 
 Location: Senate Chambers 
 Time: 7:30 PM 
 Submit Public Comment Here 

 Call to Order 

 Pledge of Allegiance 

 Moment of Silent Reflection 
Land Acknowledgement 
The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is 
located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can. 

 Roll Call and Verification of Quorum 

 Presentations and Awards 

 Public Comments from Students, RSOs, and Members of the Campus Community 
 • 2025-10-01 Public Comments 

 Messages from SGA Entities 
 • Carson Dale - Student Body President 

 Report of Senate Officers 
 • Isabella LoBianco - Student Senate President 

 • FSU General Counsel 
 Report of Senate Liaisons 

 Senate Confirmations

 9.26.25) 

 • Tanner Bigenho - Student Senate, Arts and Sciences Seat 5 (Passed Rules 
 9.27.25) 

 • Brooke Abbott - Student Senate, Entrepreneurship Seat 1 (Passed Rules 
 09.27.25) 

 • Olivia Nicholson - Student Senate, Anne’s College Seat 2 (Passed in Rules 
 09.27.25) 

 • Paola Verlage Ramirez - Student Senate, Criminology and Criminal Justice 
 Seat 3 (Passed Rules 09.27.25) 

 • Jasmine Gannaoui - Business Seat 13 (Passed in Rules 9.27.25) 

 Consent Calendar 
 • Corrections and Approval of Senate and Committee Minutes 

 • Judiciary Committee Minutes (09.25.2025) 

 • Rules Committee Minutes (09.26.2025) 

 • Student Life Committee Minutes (09.28.2025) 

 • Internal Affairs Committee Minutes (09.29.2025) 

 • Remaining Balances (Attached) 

 Items Pulled from the Consent Calendar 

 Constitutional Amendments 

 Legislation on First Reading 
Resolution Sponsored by Goldstein, Holliday 
#77-061 This resolution amends the Senate Rules of Procedure to establish 
 College Delegations, composed of all Senators from the same 
 academic college. It creates the position of Delegation Chair, elected 
 by each Delegation, with responsibilities for organizing Delegation 
 meetings, coordinating outreach to constituents, and serving as the 
 liaison to their college’s Dean and Student Leadership Council (if 
 applicable). (Assigned to Rules, 09.03.25) (Tabled in Rules 
 09.07.25, Tabled in Rules 09.19.25, Tabled in Rules 09.27.25) Resolution Sponsored by Sara Mendez Arango, Jackson 
#77-068 This resolution adds responsibility for organizing outreach and 
 tabling to the Student Life Committee including Market Wednesday. 
 This includes organizing who will table Market Wednesday, but 
 leaves it open for other senators. (Assigned to Student Life 
 10.01.25, Assigned to Rules 10.01.25) 

Resolution Sponsored by Ethan Bischof 
#77-069 This senate transfer resolution seeks to cover residual costs incurred 
 for the installation of a vending machine mini mart in Strozier that will 
 stock fresh food. This bill will transfer the sum of $2,710 to FSU 
 Facilities to install an outlet for the fridge and associated electrical 
 equipment (Work Order #2621191). $1,376.91 will be transferred to 
 FSU ITS to cover installation and procurement of a CASS security 
 camera (Work order #26009677). The total dollar amount requested 
 by this legislation is $4,086.91. (Assigned to Budget 10.01.25, 
 Student Life 10.01.25, Finance 10.01.25) 

Bill #77-046 Sponsored by Goldstein 
 This bill consolidates and restructures the financial governance 
 framework of the Student Senate by amending multiple chapters of 
 the Student Body Statutes. It eliminates the Senate Budget 
 Committee as a standing body, reassigns oversight to the Finance 
 Committee, and updates procedures for budget amendments, 
 transfers, reserve accounts, and fund usage. The legislation 
 establishes a standardized project proposal process for CAD Fund 
 requests and revises thresholds for Senate Projects and other 
 allocations. (Passed Judiciary 9.26.25, Passed SL 9.28.25, 
 Passed Rules 9.27.25, Passed Internal Affairs 2.29.25, Passed 
 Finance 2.29.25, Tabled Budget) 

Resolution Sponsored by Goldstein 
#77-065 This resolution amends the Senate Rules of Procedure to restructure 
 the Senate’s fiscal committees beginning with the 78th Student 
 Senate. It redefines the duties of the Finance and Budget 
 Committees, revises committee structures, and clarifies their 
 respective responsibilities regarding A&S Fee appropriations, 
 transfers, and oversight. (Passed Judiciary 9.26.25, Passed SL 
 9.28.25, Passed Rules 9.27.25, Passed Internal Affairs 2.29.25, 
 Passed Finance 2.29.25, Tabled Budget) 

Resolution Sponsored by Holliday 
#77-064 Replacing “Bureau Review” with “Department Review” and 
 Eliminating the Word “Bureau” from Senate Rules of Procedure. 
 (Tabled Rules, 09.27.25, Passed in Judiciary 9.26.25, Passed in 
 Internal Affairs 09.22.25) 

Bill #77-047 Sponsored by Goldstein, Rios 
 This bill creates the SGA Lending Library as a formally recognized affiliated project within Student Government, codified in Chapter 
 1118 of the Student Body Statutes. The library will provide students 
 access to essential, academic, recreational, and wellness items 
 through a structured partnership with FSU Libraries, with dedicated 
 funding and annual review mechanisms. ( Tabled in Budget 
 9.19.25, Tabled in Student Life 9.28.25, Tabled in Rules 9.27.25, 
 Passed in Judiciary 09.25.25, Passed in Internal Affairs 9.29.25, 
 Passed in Finance 09.29.25) 

 Legislation on Second Reading 
Proclamation Sponsored by Fernandez 
#77-022 Recognizing the Need for Kosher Food Accessibility at Florida State 
 University. (Assigned to Student Life 09.10.25) (Passed Student 
 Life, 09.14.25) 

Bill #77-048 Sponsored by Holliday 
 This piece of legislation elaborates on the Election Assistant position 
 in the Election Code to give the role more duties and general 
 responsibilities for future reference. (Passed in Internal Affairs 
 9.29.25, Passed in Judiciary 9.26.25) 

Allocation Sponsored by Bella Rios, Vince Nucatola 
Resolution This funding resolution provides allocations to various RSOs through 
#77-004 the RSOAC committee. (Editors note: Awaiting Cover Sheet)

 Advisor Announcements

Land Acknowledgement 
The Student Government of Florida State University acknowledges that it is 
located on land that is the ancestral and traditional territory of the Apalachee 
Nation, the Miccosukee Tribe of Florida, the Muscogee Creek Nation, and the 
Seminole Tribe of Florida. We pay respect to their Elders past and present and 
extend that respect to their descendants and to all Indigenous people. We 
recognize this land remains scarred by the histories and ongoing legacies of 
settler colonial violence, dispossession, and removal. In spite of all this, and with 
tremendous resilience, these Indigenous Nations have remained deeply 
connected to this territory, to their families, to their communities, and to their 
cultural ways of life. We recognize the ongoing relationships of care that these 
Indigenous Nations maintain with this land and extend our gratitude as we live and 
work as humble and respectful guests upon their territory. We encourage all to 
learn about and educate others on the contemporary work of the Indigenous 
Nations whose land we are on and to endeavor to support Indigenous sovereignty 
in all the ways that we can.

Short Title: The REACH (Redefining External Affairs for Coordination and Harmony) Act 

Summary of Legislation: This bill adds on to the Executive Departments Act by expanding on 
the Department of External Affairs, including establishing and elaborating on its Office of 
Governmental Affairs, Office of Public Relations, and Office of University Relations and their 
positions and duties. 

Background Information: This bill was made in consolidation with the Executive branch’s 
goal of reworking SGA’s internal structure to make the executive branch more communicative 
and connected. This includes restructuring bureaus into departments rather than keeping them 
as floating entities with limited executive oversight. This bill is a product of the Structural 
Reform Working Group within the Student Senate. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: This bill would formally establish the Office of Governmental 
Affairs, Office of Public Relations, and Office of University Relations while elaborating on the 
duties, structure, and responsibilities of the Department of External Affairs.

Short Title: Implementing Ranked Choice Voting for Elections with Three or More Candidates 

Summary of Legislation: The bill amends Chapters 701 and 713 of the Florida State 
University Student Body Statutes to introduce and define “Ranked Choice Voting” as a 
recognized electoral method. It establishes that Ranked Choice Voting will be used in any 
election where three or more candidates appear on the ballot for a single seat. This includes 
positions in the Student Senate, Congress of Graduate Students, Union Board, Campus 
Recreation Board, and future Student Government Association bodies to follow. This bill also 
clarifies the procedure for determining a winner in case of ties, assuming no individual 
candidate initially receives a majority of first-choice votes. 

Background Information: 

To correlate with any possible rise in electoral candidates in future elections, ranked-choice 
voting becomes an appropriate electoral structure for any rising political diversity that FSU may 
foster. The global use of Ranked Choice Voting has been shown to effectively capture voter 
intent when it comes to a greater variety of political candidates. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
Implementation of Ranked Choice Voting ensures that elected candidates have broader 
support from the student body by requiring a majority through a ranked system. It eliminates 
the need for potential runoff elections, streamlining the electoral process and reducing the 
administrative burden. The change encourages a more representative and inclusive voting 
system. Once signed by the Vice President for Student Affairs, this legislation will go into effect 
and apply to all future qualifying student elections.

 7 candidate receives a majority, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, and votes for 
 8 that candidate are transferred to the next ranked choice on each ballot. This process continues

Short Title: An Act Amending Chapter 615 “The Homecoming Executive Council” and 
Repealing Chapter 616 “The Homecoming Planning Commission” and Chapter 617 “The 
Homecoming Live Planning Committee” 

Summary of Legislation: This bill aims to remove the Homecoming Planning Commission 
from SGA statutes to better fit the current allocation of budget to the Homecoming Executive 
Council and updates Chapter 615 to reflect that change. This Bill also updates Chapter 617 
adding it as a new section under Chapter 615 to better fit the current structure of Homecoming 
Executive Council. 

Background Information: The Homecoming Planning Commission was established in 2003 
to serve as a governing body responsible for suballocating Activity and Service (A&S) fees to 
other organizations annually. Since the Commission’s creation, the process by which the 
Homecoming Executive Council receives funding has evolved. This creates an unnecessary 
procedural step in accessing funds already allocated during the annual A&S budget 
distribution. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: This bill would create a more streamlined process for the 
allocation of A&S fees to the Homecoming Executive Council every year.

Short Title: An Amendment to Chapter 401 “Forms of Legislation” – Clarifying Bills and 
Resolutions 

Summary of Legislation: 
This bill aims to clarify the contents of bills and resolutions. Bills shall now include the transfer 
of monetary funds and consent resolutions have been added to include the legislation from 
funding board including the Registered Student Organization Allocation Committee. 

Background Information: 
Transfer resolutions used to be a form of legislation used to transfer funds from senate 
between funding categories for SGA entities. That function is now categorized under bills. 
Consent resolutions are reserved for funding board (e.g. RSOAC) legislation. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
Bills shall continue to be signed by the same respective leadership, and consent resolutions 
shall be signed by senate leadership and copies of them are to be sent to the SG & A 
accounting office.

The Student Ombuds Office is committed to fulfilling Florida 
 State University’s mission by cultivating a campus climate 
grounded in respect, honesty, and integrity. As an independent, 
 informal, impartial, and confidential resource, the Student 
Ombuds Office serves students by offering a safe place to seek 
counsel, obtain resources, and ask questions about FSU policy. 
 The Student Ombuds Office welcomes all visitors from the 
 FSU student body.

o Objective: Provide students experiencing conflict, or who have complaints, with 
 confidential, informal, impartial, and independent consultation for the purpose of 
 equipping them with the resources and skills to advocate for themselves.
o Clarify the Student Ombuds’ role
 ØDiscuss the cornerstone principles of confidentiality, informality, impartiality, and 
 independence.
 § Confidentiality: Circumstances will not be disclosed without the visitor's consent, absent 
 compelling reasons (e.g., court order/Title IX/immediate threat to health & safety).
 § Informality: Listen, learn, and provide information to help students; the Student Ombuds

 § Impartiality: Act in a manner promoting fairness and equity to all parties. The Student 
 Ombuds may not advocate for students or the university.
 § Independence: Independent from any FSU administrative structure.
 ØDiscuss how the Student Ombuds Office functions and where the office fits into the greater 
 campus community.

Short Title: Funding for CEEGSA Orientation + Bowling & Billiards Night 

Summary of Legislation: 
This bill allocates $1,126.58 from the COGS Unallocated account to the Civil and 
Environmental Engineering Graduate Student Association (CEEGSA) to host an orientation 
and community-building event on September 26, 2025. The event will provide a welcoming 
space for new graduate students, promote faculty-student engagement, and strengthen 
departmental identity through interactive activities, dinner, and custom T-shirt distribution. 

Background Information: 
The Civil and Environmental Engineering Graduate Student Association (CEEGSA) is 
organizing an Orientation + Bowling & Billiards Night at the FSU Student Union. This event 
addresses the need for community-building and support for incoming graduate students while 
also fostering connections among returning students and faculty. The program includes 
orientation, recreational activities, catered dinner, and T-shirt distribution. Such events have 
historically been effective in strengthening departmental cohesion, promoting inclusivity, and 
increasing student engagement in graduate student life. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If approved, this legislation will provide financial support for venue rental, catering, and T-shirts 
for approximately 100 participants. It will help incoming students transition smoothly into 
graduate school, foster departmental identity, and enhance the overall graduate student 
experience in the College of Engineering.

Short Title: A bill allocating LSC Funds for the Fall 2025 Semester. 

Summary of Legislation: 
The bill allocates $98,339.13 from the Law School Council to the Council and to College of 
Law Student Organizations. 

Background Information: 
Every year, in the annual budget, the Congress allocates funds to the Law School Council (LSC) 
for LSC to distribute to the student organizations at the College of Law. In fall 2023, the Law 
School Governance Reform Act was passed, which mandated that LSC allocate its annual funds 
in a semesterly budget. 
 
As part of its budget process, LSC holds an initial informational session with student 
organizations walking through the budget process for the semester and answering any questions 
from the organizations. Organizations then have a period of time to submit budget requests to 
LSC. These requests are initially reviewed at a meeting of the LSC and Round One cuts are 
made. These cuts are made off of the submissions and are meant to bring down the volume of 
the initial request. Once the Round One cuts are provided to the organizations, each organization 
has a period of time to appeal the cuts and provide additional arguments for why that 
organization should receive more funding than initially proposed. LSC hears these arguments 
and incorporates them into a final allocation. 
 
The final allocations are then transmitted to the COGS Speaker, who works with the 
representatives from the College of Law to draft a bill based off of the allocations made by LSC. 
Typically, a representative from the College of Law sponsors the budget bill. 
 
The Congress, subject to veto by the university president or their designee, has final authority 
over the allocations made by LSC and may amend or reject the allocations as it sees fit. 

Effect of Proposed Legislation:

Passage of the bill allocates $98,339.13 from the Law School Council to the Council and to

Short Title: Repeal of the Civic Engagement Board 

Summary of Legislation: 
This bill would repeal all legislation pertaining to the Civic Engagement Board, ending its status 
as an affiliated project. 

Background Information:

Social Sciences and Public Policy. As SGA continues to undergo significant structural reforms- 
particularly in re-evaluating the roles and relevance of its affiliated projects, bureaus and other 
boards- it would be in the association’s best interest to repeal CEB’s designation as an 
affiliated project. In the future, efforts for a more streamlined, clearly defined, and non-
overlapping organizational framework can be created along with the rest of the executive 
changes.

Government. The Board would retain RSO status and autonomous operations, independent of 
SGA. It would be the first step in a series of internal changes redefining the current operational 
functions of SGA.

Short Title: Supporting Local Fee Increases for the 2025–2026 Academic Year

Summary of Legislation:
This resolution supports the recommendations of the 2025 Local Fees Committee to increase 
the Activity & Service (A&S) Fee, Health Fee, and Athletics Fee for the 2025–2026 academic 
year. It provides detailed justification based on inflation rates, minimum wage increases, and 
growing student enrollment. The resolution further endorses pre-authorized annual fee 
increases for subsequent academic years, consistent with statutory limits.

Background Information: 
The local fees at Florida State University (FSU), which include the Activity & Service Fee, 
Health Fee, and Athletics Fee, have remained unchanged since the 2013–2014 academic 
year. During this period, the Consumer Price Index has increased by approximately 37.2%, 
and Florida’s minimum wage has risen by 66.8%. Simultaneously, FSU's total student 
enrollment has grown by 5.4%. This resolution is presented to ensure that student services 
funded by these fees can be maintained and enhanced to meet growing demand and rising 
operational costs.

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
If enacted, this resolution would officially express the Student Senate’s support for the 
recommended local fee increases and urge the Florida State University Board of Trustees to 
approve these changes. It would also promote the sustainability of student services by aligning 
local fee revenues with inflationary and operational pressures.

Short Title: A Proclamation Condemning Hazing and Honoring the Life of Caleb Wilson

Summary of Legislation: 
This proclamation condemns the practice of hazing, specifically highlighting the tragic death of 
Caleb Wilson, a student at Southern University, who died due to hazing. The proclamation 
calls for stronger preventative measures, urges the University Administration to take action, 
and emphasizes the responsibility of student organizations to prevent harm in the name of 
tradition.

Background Information: 

Caleb Wilson, a 20-year-old student at Southern University, tragically lost his life due to 
fraternity hazing. Hazing continues to be a dangerous and unlawful practice that has led to the 
loss of many students’ lives across the nation. The proclamation aims to condemn hazing, 
honor Caleb Wilson’s life, and encourage stronger actions to prevent further tragedies. This 
issue has a significant impact on the broader university community and student organizations, 
including fraternities and sororities, who must address these harmful practices.

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 

If enacted, this proclamation will officially condemn the actions that led to Caleb Wilson’s death 
and encourage the University Administration to strengthen anti-hazing policies and educational 
efforts. It will also promote a culture of accountability within student organizations to ensure 
safety, transparency, and respect among students, preventing further hazing incidents.

Short Title: A Proclamation Supporting the Expansion of Brightline to North Florida and 
Advocating for a Financial Agreement to Benefit Students. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This proclamation expresses support for the expansion of Brightline to North Florida, including 
Tallahassee, Tampa, Jacksonville, and Gainesville, to improve transportation access for 
students at Florida State University (FSU) and other institutions in the region. It highlights the 
financial burdens many students face due to limited transit options and urges university 
leadership and state officials to advocate for a student financial assistance program for 
Brightline travel. The expansion and implementation of affordable student rates would enhance 
accessibility, sustainability, and academic and professional opportunities for students.

Background Information: 
Affordable and reliable transportation is a critical issue for students, particularly those from 
minority and lower-income backgrounds. North Florida lacks strong public transit connections 
to major metropolitan areas such as Orlando, Tampa, and Miami, making travel costly and 
inefficient for students without personal vehicles. Expanding Brightline and establishing a 
financial assistance program would significantly improve mobility, increase access to job and 
internship opportunities, and foster collaboration between Florida's universities.

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This proclamation calls for formal advocacy efforts from FSU leadership and state officials to 
ensure students benefit from expanded Brightline services. It also requests semesterly 
updates from relevant stakeholders, including Brightline leadership, the Florida Department of 
Transportation, and FSU Administration. Additionally, copies of this proclamation will be sent to 
university presidents, student government leaders, and key local and state officials to garner 
widespread support.

Summary of Legislation:

growth. These conditions begin during a child’s developmental period and can last throughout 
a lifetime. Awareness efforts not only validate the lived experiences of students with 
developmental disabilities but also celebrate their resilience, contributions, and achievements 
in higher education.

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation reaffirms the Senate’s commitment to creating a supportive environment for 
Florida State University students with developmental disabilities. By officially recognizing 
March as Developmental Disabilities Awareness Month, the Senate seeks to promote 
awareness, advocate for accessibility and inclusion, and celebrate the contributions of 
individuals with developmental disabilities within the FSU community. This proclamation 
reflects the university’s dedication to ensuring that all students, regardless of ability, have the 
resources and support needed to thrive academically, socially, and personally.

by a majority vote of the respective committee.

At times, committee election results are not the reflection of the prioritization of merit and 
experience for committee leadership. The appointment process of committee Chairs and Vice-
Chairs is also seen in our state government, where we would be able to reflect real-world 
systems. The Senate President is also held to a higher standard of nonpartisanship and meri-
based decision-making.

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation allows for the senate to choose during the organizational session whether to go 
with the election process or the appointment process. Chairs and Vice Chairs can also be 
removed by a majority vote of the respective committee. The Rules committee can also 
investigate a Chair or Vice Chair. When a committee leadership role goes vacant, the Senate 
President has the jurisdiction to appoint a new Chair or Vice Chair. Chair and Vice-Chair 
positions can also go up for re-election at any point after the organizational session. with a 2/3 
(two-thirds) vote. The Rules Committee shall also be chaired by the Senate President Pro-
Tempore.

Short Title: A Resolution Allocating $1,006.42 from Senate Projects to Students for Sensible 
Drug Policy for the Distribution of Fentanyl Testing Strips

Summary of Legislation: 
This resolution allocates $1,006.42 from the Senate Projects fund to Students for Sensible 
Drug Policy (SSDP) at Florida State University. The funds will be used to purchase and 
distribute 2,000 fentanyl testing strips at Greek Life chapters and nightclubs in an effort to 
reduce the risk of accidental overdoses within the student body and the broader community.

Background Information: 
The opioid crisis has led to a significant rise in accidental overdoses due to the presence of 
fentanyl in recreational drugs. Fentanyl, a potent synthetic opioid, is often mixed into 
substances without the knowledge of the user, leading to severe health risks and fatalities. 
FSU’s SSDP is dedicated to harm reduction initiatives that educate students and provide 
resources to mitigate these dangers. By distributing fentanyl testing strips, SSDP aims to 
empower individuals to make informed choices regarding substance safety. Senate Projects 
funding will allow the organization to expand its efforts and directly contribute to student well-
being.

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This Resolution would transfer $1,006.42 from Senate Projects to SSDP at FSU to purchase 
2000 fentanyl testing strips to distribute to students.

Why?
We distribute free fentanyl test strips to students in Tallahassee. Fentanyl test strips are a vital 
harm reduction resource on college campuses as they can identify the presence of fentanyl in 
recreational substances before a student consumes them. If having Narcan is the air bag, using 
fentanyl test strips is safe driving. Test strips are important in preventing accidental overdoses in 
the first place so that there is not a need to save someone's life with Narcan.
 We believe Fentanyl test strips should always be distributed alongside Narcan and we 
make extensive efforts to do so on campus and at local nightlife venues. Test strips are single 
use, and frequently students will require multiple at a time. This semester (fall 24) alone we 
have already distributed nearly 200 free fentanyl test strips and over 40 boxes of Narcan nasal

Bill #77-017 Sponsored by Noumena 
 This Elections Omnibus Bill proposes a comprehensive set of 
 updates to the Student Government Election Code, aimed at 
 resolving persistent technical and procedural issues. The bill focuses 
 on improving clarity, correcting outdated references, and eliminating 
 redundancy across multiple chapters of the Code. Notably, the 
 authority to appoint the Supervisor of Elections and their Deputy is 
 shifted from the Student Body President to the Supreme Court Chief 
 Justice, aligning the Code with recent constitutional amendments. 
 Several provisions regarding campaign materials and finance 
 reporting are also revised. The outdated campaign material registry 
 is removed, with oversight instead maintained through Final Expense 
 Statements. This reduces bureaucratic burden while preserving 
 financial accountability. Definitions of campaign expenses are 
 clarified to include fair market value, while exempting publicly 

 Page 3 of 102 available discounts. The bill also extends the time for the Elections 
 Commission to publish decisions from two to five business days, 
 ensuring thorough and reasoned rulings. Additional edits correct 
 inaccurate statute citations, eliminate duplicative language, and 
 remove provisions already covered by other sections of the Code or 
 by the Congress of Graduate Students' electoral procedures. 
 Collectively, these changes modernize the Election Code by 
 improving its legal precision, aligning it with governing documents, 
 and promoting transparency and fairness in the electoral process. 
 (Passed Unanimously in Internal Affairs 4.15.25, Passed 
 Unanimously in Judiciary 4.22.25, Passed Unanimously in 
 Finance 4.22.25, Tabled in Student Life 4.21.25)

Short Title: A Proclamation Condemning Hazing and Honoring the Life of Caleb Wilson

Summary of Legislation: 
This proclamation condemns the practice of hazing, specifically highlighting the tragic death of 
Caleb Wilson, a student at Southern University, who died due to hazing. The proclamation 
calls for stronger preventative measures, urges the University Administration to take action, 
and emphasizes the responsibility of student organizations to prevent harm in the name of 
tradition.

Background Information: 

Caleb Wilson, a 20-year-old student at Southern University, tragically lost his life due to 
fraternity hazing. Hazing continues to be a dangerous and unlawful practice that has led to the 
loss of many students’ lives across the nation. The proclamation aims to condemn hazing, 
honor Caleb Wilson’s life, and encourage stronger actions to prevent further tragedies. This 
issue has a significant impact on the broader university community and student organizations, 
including fraternities and sororities, who must address these harmful practices.

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 

If enacted, this proclamation will officially condemn the actions that led to Caleb Wilson’s death 
and encourage the University Administration to strengthen anti-hazing policies and educational 
efforts. It will also promote a culture of accountability within student organizations to ensure 
safety, transparency, and respect among students, preventing further hazing incidents.

Short Title: A Proclamation Supporting the Expansion of Brightline to North Florida and 
Advocating for a Financial Agreement to Benefit Students. 

Summary of Legislation: 
This proclamation expresses support for the expansion of Brightline to North Florida, including 
Tallahassee, Tampa, Jacksonville, and Gainesville, to improve transportation access for 
students at Florida State University (FSU) and other institutions in the region. It highlights the 
financial burdens many students face due to limited transit options and urges university 
leadership and state officials to advocate for a student financial assistance program for 
Brightline travel. The expansion and implementation of affordable student rates would enhance 
accessibility, sustainability, and academic and professional opportunities for students.

Background Information: 
Affordable and reliable transportation is a critical issue for students, particularly those from 
minority and lower-income backgrounds. North Florida lacks strong public transit connections 
to major metropolitan areas such as Orlando, Tampa, and Miami, making travel costly and 
inefficient for students without personal vehicles. Expanding Brightline and establishing a 
financial assistance program would significantly improve mobility, increase access to job and 
internship opportunities, and foster collaboration between Florida's universities.

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This proclamation calls for formal advocacy efforts from FSU leadership and state officials to 
ensure students benefit from expanded Brightline services. It also requests semesterly 
updates from relevant stakeholders, including Brightline leadership, the Florida Department of 
Transportation, and FSU Administration. Additionally, copies of this proclamation will be sent to 
university presidents, student government leaders, and key local and state officials to garner 
widespread support.

 Short Title: Title VII Reform: Comprehensive Amendments to the Election Code

 Summary of Legislation: 

 This Elections Omnibus Bill proposes a comprehensive set of updates to the Student 
 Government Election Code, aimed at resolving persistent technical and procedural issues. The 
 bill focuses on improving clarity, correcting outdated references, and eliminating redundancy 
 across multiple chapters of the Code. Notably, the authority to appoint the Supervisor of 
 Elections and their Deputy is shifted from the Student Body President to the Supreme Court 
 Chief Justice, aligning the Code with recent constitutional amendments. Several provisions 
 regarding campaign materials and finance reporting are also revised. The outdated campaign 
 material registry is removed, with oversight instead maintained through Final Expense 
 Statements. This reduces bureaucratic burden while preserving financial accountability. 
 Definitions of campaign expenses are clarified to include fair market value, while exempting 
 publicly available discounts. The bill also extends the time for the Elections Commission to 
 publish decisions from two to five business days, ensuring thorough and reasoned rulings. 
 Additional edits correct inaccurate statute citations, eliminate duplicative language, and 
 remove provisions already covered by other sections of the Code or by the Congress of 
 Graduate Students' electoral procedures. Collectively, these changes modernize the Election 
 Code by improving its legal precision, aligning it with governing documents, and promoting 
 transparency and fairness in the electoral process.

 Background Information: 

In recent years, the Student Government Association has undertaken efforts to modernize and 
clarify its governing documents, including the Election Code. While past reforms made 
meaningful progress, technical issues and outdated procedures have continued to cause 
confusion and inefficiencies during election cycles. Ambiguities in legal language, incorrect 
statute references, and redundant or unnecessary provisions have complicated enforcement 
and compliance. Additionally, procedural inconsistencies and outdated responsibilities—such 
as the appointment authority for election officials and the requirement to register campaign 
materials—no longer reflect the current governance structure or best practices for electoral 
transparency. The need for clearer rules and streamlined processes became especially evident 

 Page 49 of 102through recent election cycles, where inconsistencies in the Code impeded fair enforcement 
and created administrative burdens. This bill emerges from a continued commitment to uphold 
election integrity by ensuring the Election Code is legally sound, procedurally efficient, and 
consistent with constitutional amendments. The proposed changes are designed to reduce 
ambiguity, promote transparency, and realign responsibilities in a way that supports a fair and 
accountable student government election process.

 Effect of Proposed Legislation: 

If enacted, the Elections Omnibus Bill would revise the Student Government Election Code to 
address longstanding technical and procedural inconsistencies. Key changes include updating 
incorrect statute references, eliminating vague or redundant clauses, and clarifying ambiguous 
language—ultimately making the Code more accessible and enforceable. The bill transfers the 
authority to appoint the Supervisor of Elections and Deputy Supervisor from the Student Body 
President to the Supreme Court Chief Justice, aligning the Code with recent constitutional 
amendments. It also simplifies campaign finance procedures by removing the outdated 
requirement to register campaign materials, instead relying on final expense statements for 
financial transparency. Procedural timelines are also revised to allow more time for due 
process—for instance, extending the window for the Elections Commission to publish opinions 
from two to five business days. Several outdated or duplicative clauses, such as mandatory 
seminar rules for graduate candidates and unnecessary apportionment provisions, are removed 
to reduce confusion. Overall, the legislation modernizes the election framework, enhances 
accountability, and aligns legal procedures with practical enforcement, ensuring a clearer and 
fairer electoral process.

Short Title: Recognizing March as Developmental Disabilities Awareness Month

Summary of Legislation: 
This proclamation seeks to state the 77th Student Senate’s support for all members of the 
Florida State University community with developmental disabilities by officially recognizing 
March as Developmental Disabilities Awareness Month.

Background Information: 
Studies have shown that 1 in 5 undergraduate students have a developmental disability. 
Developmental disabilities can impact a child’s physical, emotional, social, and intellectual 
growth. These conditions begin during a child’s developmental period and can last throughout 
a lifetime. Awareness efforts not only validate the lived experiences of students with 
developmental disabilities but also celebrate their resilience, contributions, and achievements 
in higher education.

Effect of Proposed Legislation: 
This legislation reaffirms the Senate’s commitment to creating a supportive environment for 
Florida State University students with developmental disabilities. By officially recognizing 
March as Developmental Disabilities Awareness Month, the Senate seeks to promote 
awareness, advocate for accessibility and inclusion, and celebrate the contributions of 
individuals with developmental disabilities within the FSU community. This proclamation 
reflects the university’s dedication to ensuring that all students, regardless of ability, have the 
resources and support needed to thrive academically, socially, and personally.
